abstract: Distinctive electrocardiogram (EeG) patterns are created when the heart is beating normally and when a dangerous arrhythmia is present. Some devices which monitor the EeG and react to arrhythmias parameterize the ECG signal and make a diagnosis based on the parameters. The author discusses the use of a neural network to classify the EeG signals directly. without parameterization. The input to such a network must be translation-invariant. since the distinctive features of the EeG may appear anywhere in an arbritrarily-chosen EeG segment. The input must also be insensitive to the episode-to-episode and patient-to-patient variability in the rhythm pattern.

Some devices which monitor the EeG and react to arrhythmias parameterize the ECG signal and make a diagnosis based on the parameters. paragraphs: This paper discusses using a neural network to classify electrocardiogram signals directly. Normal heart activity and dangerous arrhythmias produce distinctive signal patterns. Some monitoring devices first turn the waveform into a set of parameters and diagnose from those values; the proposed approach instead makes the ECG signal itself the basis for neural classification.

A central requirement is translation invariance. When an ECG segment is selected arbitrarily, a diagnostic feature can occur at different positions within that segment. Its location should therefore not determine how the network interprets it. The input representation must preserve useful pattern information while allowing the same feature to be recognized wherever it appears.

The author also identifies variation across patients and across separate episodes as something the input must tolerate. Together, these requirements define the representation problem behind direct ECG classification: retain the distinctions relevant to rhythm diagnosis while reducing sensitivity to timing position and other rhythm variability. The contribution described is an approach organized around those necessary properties of the network's input.
summary.tldr: Direct neural ECG classification requires inputs that tolerate shifts in feature position and variation across patients and episodes.

title: Using a Translation-Invariant Neural Network to Diagnose Heart Arrhythmia

abstract: Multi-class classification problems can be efficiently solved by partitioning the original problem into sub-problems involving only two classes: for each pair of classes, a (potentially small) neural network is trained using only the data of these two classes. We show how to combine the outputs of the two-class neural networks in order to obtain posterior probabilities for the class decisions. The resulting probabilistic pairwise classifier is part of a handwriting recognition system which is currently applied to check reading. We present results on real world data bases and show that, from a practical point of view, these results compare favorably to other neural network approaches.
originalAbstract: Multi-class classification problems can be efficiently solved by partitioning the original problem into sub-problems involving only two classes: for each pair of classes, a (potentially small) neural network is trained using only the data of these two classes. We show how to combine the outputs of the two-class neural networks in order to obtain posterior probabilities for the class decisions. The resulting probabilistic pairwise classifier is part of a handwriting recognition system which is currently applied to check reading. We present results on real world data bases and show that, from a practical point of view, these results compare favorably to other neural network approaches.

paragraphs: The paper tackles classification with many possible classes by splitting it into decisions between pairs. For each pair of classes, a neural network learns using only examples belonging to those two classes. Each subproblem therefore has a narrower distinction to learn, and its network can potentially be relatively small.

The key contribution is a method for combining those pairwise outputs into posterior probabilities for the complete classification problem. The system must turn separate two-class judgments into probabilities over the available classes. Producing these probabilities gives the combined classifier more information to report than a collection of unrelated pairwise decisions.

The resulting classifier forms part of a handwriting recognition system used for reading checks. The authors evaluate it on real-world databases and report results that compare favorably, from a practical standpoint, with other neural network approaches. The paper thus connects a decomposition strategy to a probability-producing recognition system, showing how specialized two-class networks can contribute to a single multiclass decision in an applied setting.
summary.tldr: Pairwise neural classifiers are combined into multiclass posterior probabilities and applied to handwriting recognition for check reading.

title: Pairwise Neural Network Classifiers with Probabilistic Outputs

abstract: In this paper the problem of learning appropriate domain-specific bias is addressed. It is shown that this can be achieved by learning many related tasks from the same domain, and a theorem is given bounding the number tasks that must be learnt. A corollary of the theorem is that if the tasks are known to possess a common inter(cid:173) nal representation or preprocessing then the number of examples required per task for good generalisation when learning n tasks si(cid:173) multaneously scales like O(a + ~), where O(a) is a bound on the minimum number of examples requred to learn a single task, and O( a + b) is a bound on the number of examples required to learn each task independently. An experiment providing strong qualita(cid:173) tive support for the theoretical results is reported.

An experiment providing strong qualita(cid:173) tive support for the theoretical results is reported.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a learner can acquire assumptions that suit a particular domain. Such assumptions constitute model bias: they guide which explanations or predictors the learner considers appropriate. The proposed route is to learn many related tasks from that domain, allowing their common structure to inform the learning process.

The theoretical contribution bounds how many tasks must be learned to acquire an appropriate bias. A consequence concerns tasks known to share an internal representation or preprocessing step. Under that assumption, learning tasks together reduces the examples needed per task by distributing the burden of learning shared structure across the collection. The result separates task-specific requirements from the additional requirements associated with learning independently.

An experiment provides strong qualitative support for the theory. The stated significance is that related tasks can help establish how a domain should be represented, and that shared representation can improve generalization efficiency. The common-representation assumption is central to the sample-requirement result: the benefit comes from structure that the tasks can actually share.
summary.tldr: Learning related tasks together can acquire a useful domain bias and reduce per-task data requirements when the tasks share a representation.

title: Learning Model Bias

abstract: We propose an active learning method with hidden-unit reduction. which is devised specially for multilayer perceptrons (MLP). First, we review our active learning method, and point out that many Fisher-information-based methods applied to MLP have a critical problem: the information matrix may be singular. To solve this problem, we derive the singularity condition of an information ma(cid:173) trix, and propose an active learning technique that is applicable to MLP. Its effectiveness is verified through experiments.
originalAbstract: We propose an active learning method with hidden-unit reduction. which is devised specially for multilayer perceptrons (MLP). First, we review our active learning method, and point out that many Fisher-information-based methods applied to MLP have a critical problem: the information matrix may be singular. To solve this problem, we derive the singularity condition of an information ma(cid:173) trix, and propose an active learning technique that is applicable to MLP. Its effectiveness is verified through experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops an active learning method specifically for multilayer perceptrons. Active learning concerns choosing informative training examples, so the usefulness of the selection rule depends on how well it describes the network being trained. The authors identify a mathematical obstacle affecting many selection methods based on Fisher information.

That obstacle is a singular information matrix. Such a matrix lacks the independent information needed for some of the calculations that information-based methods rely on. The authors derive the condition under which this singularity occurs in multilayer perceptrons, making the source of the problem explicit instead of assuming the matrix is always suitable.

Their proposed solution incorporates hidden-unit reduction into an active learning technique applicable to these networks. This connects the choice of training examples with the structure of the model itself: the network representation matters to whether the selection criterion works. The abstract reports experimental verification of the method's effectiveness, supporting the practical relevance of addressing singularity when designing active learning for multilayer perceptrons.
summary.tldr: An active learning method uses hidden-unit reduction to address singular Fisher information matrices in multilayer perceptrons.

title: Active Learning in Multilayer Perceptrons

abstract: In many real world tasks, only a small fraction of the available inputs are important at any particular time. This paper presents a method for ascertaining the relevance of inputs by exploiting temporal coherence and predictability. The method pro(cid:173) posed in this paper dynamically allocates relevance to inputs by using expectations of their future values. As a model of the task is learned, the model is simulta(cid:173) neously extended to create task-specific predictions of the future values of inputs. Inputs which are either not relevant, and therefore not accounted for in the model, or those which contain noise, will not be predicted accurately. These inputs can be de-emphasized, and, in turn, a new, improved, model of the task created. The tech(cid:173) niques presented in this paper have yielded significant improvements for the vision-based autonomous control of a land vehicle, vision-based hand tracking in cluttered scenes, and the detection of faults in the etching of semiconductor wafers.

paragraphs: The paper addresses tasks in which only a small portion of the available input matters at a given moment. It proposes assigning relevance dynamically by using temporal coherence and predictions of future input values. The aim is to let the developing task model help determine which observations deserve continued emphasis.

As the system learns the task, it also learns task-specific predictions of its inputs. Inputs that are irrelevant to the model, or dominated by noise, are not predicted accurately. The system reduces their emphasis and learns an improved task model from the resulting allocation of attention. Prediction and relevance selection therefore form a feedback process during learning.

The authors report significant improvements in vision-based autonomous land-vehicle control, hand tracking amid clutter, and fault detection during semiconductor-wafer etching. These applications demonstrate the same principle across different tasks: expectations about incoming data can guide processing of that data. The approach uses predictability relative to the learned task model as evidence for allocating input relevance.
summary.tldr: Task-specific predictions guide input relevance, improving reported results in vehicle control, hand tracking, and manufacturing fault detection.

title: Using Expectation to Guide Processing: A Study of Three Real-World Applications

abstract: The encoding accuracy of a population of stochastically spiking neurons is studied for different distributions of their tuning widths. The situation of identical radially symmetric receptive fields for all neurons, which is usually considered in the literature, turns out to be disadvantageous from an information-theoretic point of view. Both a variability of tuning widths and a fragmentation of the neural population into specialized subpopulations improve the encoding accuracy.
originalAbstract: The encoding accuracy of a population of stochastically spiking neurons is studied for different distributions of their tuning widths. The situation of identical radially symmetric receptive fields for all neurons, which is usually considered in the literature, turns out to be disadvantageous from an information-theoretic point of view. Both a variability of tuning widths and a fragmentation of the neural population into specialized subpopulations improve the encoding accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper examines how accurately a population of neurons can encode stimuli with multiple dimensions when the neurons spike stochastically. It focuses on tuning widths, which describe how broadly a neuron responds across stimuli. The question is how the distribution of these widths across a population affects the information carried by its activity.

A commonly studied arrangement gives every neuron an identical, radially symmetric receptive field. The authors find this uniform arrangement disadvantageous from an information-theoretic perspective. Their comparison makes the organization of the population central: encoding accuracy depends on how response properties are distributed among neurons, including whether those properties are all alike.

Two changes improve encoding accuracy in the study: allowing tuning widths to vary and dividing the population into specialized subpopulations. The results identify diversity and specialization as useful features of the analyzed neural representation. They suggest that evaluating a population only through identical receptive fields can overlook encoding benefits available when neurons have different widths or take on specialized representational roles.
summary.tldr: Variable tuning widths and specialized subpopulations improve encoding accuracy in the studied populations of stochastically spiking neurons.

title: Neural Representation of Multi-Dimensional Stimuli

abstract: We present evidence that several higher-order statistical proper(cid:173) ties of natural images and signals can be explained by a stochastic model which simply varies scale of an otherwise stationary Gaus(cid:173) sian process. We discuss two interesting consequences. The first is that a variety of natural signals can be related through a com(cid:173) mon model of spherically invariant random processes, which have the attractive property that the joint densities can be constructed from the one dimensional marginal. The second is that in some cas(cid:173) es the non-stationarity assumption and only second order methods can be explicitly exploited to find a linear basis that is equivalent to independent components obtained with higher-order methods. This is demonstrated on spectro-temporal components of speech.

paragraphs: The paper presents evidence that several complex statistical properties of natural images and signals can arise from a comparatively simple process. The proposed model changes the scale of an otherwise stationary Gaussian process. These scale changes introduce non-stationarity, allowing the signal's statistical behavior to vary rather than remain fixed.

One consequence is a common description of different natural signals through spherically invariant random processes. For this model family, the joint probability densities can be constructed from a one-dimensional marginal density. This connects the behavior of multiple signal components to a simpler distributional description and provides a shared framework for signals that exhibit the relevant properties.

A second consequence concerns finding useful linear components. In some cases, exploiting non-stationarity with second-order methods produces a basis equivalent to independent components obtained through higher-order methods. The authors demonstrate this on speech components spanning spectral and temporal structure. The finding shows that changing signal statistics can sometimes supply information otherwise extracted using higher-order statistical analysis.
summary.tldr: Varying the scale of a Gaussian process can explain several natural-signal statistics and sometimes enable second-order recovery of independent-component-equivalent bases.

title: Higher-Order Statistical Properties Arising from the Non-Stationarity of Natural Signals

abstract: In this paper we consider formulations of multi-class problems based on a generalized notion of a margin and using output coding. This includes, but is not restricted to, standard multi-class SVM formulations. Differ- ently from many previous approaches we learn the code as well as the embedding function. We illustrate how this can lead to a formulation that allows for solving a wider range of problems with for instance many classes or even “missing classes”. To keep our optimization problems tractable we propose an algorithm capable of solving them using two- class classiﬁers, similar in spirit to Boosting.

This includes, but is not restricted to, standard multi-class SVM formulations. Differ- ently from many previous approaches we learn the code as well as the embedding function. We illustrate how this can lead to a formulation that allows for solving a wider range of problems with for instance many classes or even “missing classes”. To keep our optimization problems tractable we propose an algorithm capable of solving them using two- class classiﬁers, similar in spirit to Boosting.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification problems with multiple possible classes. It combines output coding, which represents class outputs through codes, with a generalized notion of a margin. The resulting framework includes standard multiclass support vector machine formulations while also allowing other ways to express the classification problem.

The distinguishing choice is to learn both the output code and the embedding function. Rather than treating the code as a fixed part of the task, the formulation makes it another object to adapt. The authors illustrate how this flexibility can accommodate a wider range of problems, including situations with many classes or what they call missing classes.

Learning these components creates optimization problems that must remain computationally manageable. The proposed algorithm solves them using two-class classifiers, in a manner related in spirit to boosting. The contribution therefore joins a more adaptable representation of multiclass outputs with a practical decomposition strategy: binary classification serves as a building block for the broader learning problem.
summary.tldr: Learning output codes together with embeddings broadens multiclass classification formulations while allowing optimization through binary classifiers.

title: Adapting Codes and Embeddings for Polychotomies

abstract: The Bayesian paradigm provides a natural and effective means of exploit- ing prior knowledge concerning the time-frequency structure of sound signals such as speech and music—something which has often been over- looked in traditional audio signal processing approaches. Here, after con- structing a Bayesian model and prior distributions capable of taking into account the time-frequency characteristics of typical audio waveforms, we apply Markov chain Monte Carlo methods in order to sample from the resultant posterior distribution of interest. We present speech enhance- ment results which compare favourably in objective terms with standard time-varying ﬁltering techniques (and in several cases yield superior per- formance, both objectively and subjectively); moreover, in contrast to such methods, our results are obtained without an assumption of prior knowledge of the noise power.
originalAbstract: The Bayesian paradigm provides a natural and effective means of exploit- ing prior knowledge concerning the time-frequency structure of sound signals such as speech and music—something which has often been over- looked in traditional audio signal processing approaches. Here, after con- structing a Bayesian model and prior distributions capable of taking into account the time-frequency characteristics of typical audio waveforms, we apply Markov chain Monte Carlo methods in order to sample from the resultant posterior distribution of interest. We present speech enhance- ment results which compare favourably in objective terms with standard time-varying ﬁltering techniques (and in several cases yield superior per- formance, both objectively and subjectively); moreover, in contrast to such methods, our results are obtained without an assumption of prior knowledge of the noise power.

paragraphs: Speech and music have structure in how their frequency content changes over time. This paper uses that structure as prior knowledge in a Bayesian approach to audio enhancement. The authors construct a probabilistic model and prior distributions that can account for characteristic time-frequency patterns in audio waveforms.

Combining those priors with the observed signal produces a posterior distribution describing the quantities to be estimated. The authors use Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to draw samples from that posterior. This makes the learned estimate depend on both the recording and assumptions about plausible sound structure, with inference carried out through sampling.

The reported speech enhancement results compare favorably on objective measures with standard time-varying filters. In several cases, the method also performs better both objectively and subjectively. A particularly relevant feature is that these results do not assume advance knowledge of the noise power. The evidence supports the value of structured audio priors without claiming superiority in every tested situation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian time-frequency modeling improves speech enhancement in reported comparisons without requiring prior knowledge of noise power.

title: Bayesian Estimation of Time-Frequency Coefficients for Audio Signal Enhancement

abstract: We develop \name\ (STM), a nonparametric Bayesian model of parsed documents. \Shortname\ generates words that are both thematically and syntactically constrained, which combines the semantic insights of topic models with the syntactic information available from parse trees. Each word of a sentence is generated by a distribution that combines document-specific topic weights and parse-tree specific syntactic transitions. Words are assumed generated in an order that respects the parse tree. We derive an approximate posterior inference method based on variational methods for hierarchical Dirichlet processes, and we report qualitative and quantitative results on both synthetic data and hand-parsed documents.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian model for documents that already have parse trees. Its purpose is to combine thematic information with grammatical structure. Topic models supply a way to represent what a document discusses, while parse trees provide relationships that constrain how its words fit together syntactically.

In the proposed model, each word is generated from a distribution combining document-specific topic weights with syntactic transitions associated with the parse tree. Word generation follows an order consistent with that tree. The model therefore makes both document context and syntactic relationships part of the same account of how words arise.

The authors derive approximate posterior inference using variational methods for hierarchical Dirichlet processes. This supplies a way to infer the model's hidden structure from parsed observations. They report qualitative and quantitative results on synthetic data and hand-parsed documents. The contribution is the joint formulation and its inference method, with those evaluations examining a model in which thematic and syntactic constraints act together at the level of individual words.
summary.tldr: Syntactic Topic Models combine document topics and parse-tree transitions in a Bayesian account of word generation.

title: Syntactic Topic Models

abstract: The learning of appropriate distance metrics is a critical problem in classification. In this work, we propose a boosting-based technique, termed BoostMetric, for learning a Mahalanobis distance metric. One of the primary difficulties in learning such a metric is to ensure that the Mahalanobis matrix remains positive semidefinite. Semidefinite programming is sometimes used to enforce this constraint, but does not scale well. BoostMetric is instead based on a key observation that any positive semidefinite matrix can be decomposed into a linear positive combination of trace-one rank-one matrices. BoostMetric thus uses rank-one positive semidefinite matrices as weak learners within an efficient and scalable boosting-based learning process. The resulting method is easy to implement, does not require tuning, and can accommodate various types of constraints. Experiments on various datasets show that the proposed algorithm compares favorably to those state-of-the-art methods in terms of classification accuracy and running time.

paragraphs: The paper proposes BoostMetric, a boosting-based method for learning a Mahalanobis distance used in classification. Such a distance is controlled by a matrix that must remain positive semidefinite. Enforcing that constraint through semidefinite programming can be computationally difficult as the problem grows, motivating a different construction.

The key observation is that every positive semidefinite matrix can be expressed as a positively weighted combination of trace-one, rank-one matrices. BoostMetric uses these simpler matrices as weak learners. Building the distance matrix from positive combinations of these components preserves the required mathematical property within the boosting process.

The authors describe the resulting method as scalable, easy to implement, requiring no tuning, and able to accommodate several kinds of constraints. Experiments on multiple datasets compare favorably with leading methods in classification accuracy and running time. The significance lies in connecting a matrix constraint to a constructive learning procedure: a valid distance matrix can be assembled from simple valid pieces, while the empirical results support the practical value of that approach.
summary.tldr: BoostMetric learns valid Mahalanobis distance matrices by boosting simple rank-one positive semidefinite components.

title: Positive Semidefinite Metric Learning with Boosting

abstract: We consider the problem of optimizing the sum of a smooth convex function and a non-smooth convex function using proximal-gradient methods, where an error is present in the calculation of the gradient of the smooth term or in the proximity operator with respect to the second term. We show that the basic proximal-gradient method, the basic proximal-gradient method with a strong convexity assumption, and the accelerated proximal-gradient method achieve the same convergence rates as in the error-free case, provided the errors decrease at an appropriate rate. Our experimental results on a structured sparsity problem indicate that sequences of errors with these appealing theoretical properties can lead to practical performance improvements.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of optimizing the sum of a smooth convex function and a non-smooth convex function using proximal-gradient methods, where an error is present in the calculation of the gradient of the smooth term or in the proximity operator with respect to the second term. We show that the basic proximal-gradient method, the basic proximal-gradient method with a strong convexity assumption, and the accelerated proximal-gradient method achieve the same convergence rates as in the error-free case, provided the errors decrease at an appropriate rate. Our experimental results on a structured sparsity problem indicate that sequences of errors with these appealing theoretical properties can lead to practical performance improvements.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization objectives made by adding a smooth convex function to a nonsmooth convex function. Proximal-gradient methods handle these two parts through different computations. In practice, either the gradient calculation for the smooth part or the proximity operation for the nonsmooth part may be approximate, raising the question of how those errors affect convergence.

The authors analyze three settings: the basic method, the basic method under strong convexity, and an accelerated method. They show that each can retain its corresponding error-free convergence rate when the computational errors decrease at a suitable rate. The guarantee therefore links the accuracy required of individual operations to the progress of the overall optimization.

Experiments on a structured sparsity problem indicate that error sequences satisfying these theoretical requirements can also improve practical performance. This makes controlled approximation a useful algorithmic choice rather than merely an unavoidable defect. The key condition is that errors must shrink appropriately; the result does not say that arbitrary inaccuracies preserve convergence speed.
summary.tldr: Proximal-gradient methods retain their error-free convergence rates when approximation errors decrease appropriately, with experiments indicating practical benefits.

title: Convergence Rates of Inexact Proximal-Gradient Methods for Convex Optimization

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of modeling the dynamic structure of human activities in the attributes space. A video sequence is first represented in a semantic feature space, where each feature encodes the probability of occurrence of an activity attribute at a given time. A generative model, denoted the binary dynamic system (BDS), is proposed to learn both the distribution and dynamics of different activities in this space. The BDS is a non-linear dynamic system, which extends both the binary principal component analysis (PCA) and classical linear dynamic systems (LDS), by combining binary observation variables with a hidden Gauss-Markov state process. In this way, it integrates the representation power of semantic modeling with the ability of dynamic systems to capture the temporal structure of time-varying processes. An algorithm for learning BDS parameters, inspired by a popular LDS learning method from dynamic textures, is proposed. A similarity measure between BDSs, which generalizes the Binet-Cauchy kernel for LDS, is then introduced and used to design activity classifiers. The proposed method is shown to outperform similar classifiers derived from the kernel dynamic system (KDS) and state-of-the-art approaches for dynamics-based or attribute-based action recognition.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes human activities by modeling how meaningful attributes evolve through a video. Each time point is represented by features giving the probabilities that particular activity attributes occur. This creates a semantic description of the sequence, allowing recognition to use both the attributes present and their temporal organization.

The authors introduce a generative model called the binary dynamic system. It combines binary observation variables with a hidden Gauss-Markov state process, extending ideas from binary principal component analysis and linear dynamic systems. The resulting nonlinear model learns both the distribution of activity attributes and how they change over time.

The paper supplies a parameter-learning algorithm inspired by work on dynamic textures and a similarity measure between binary dynamic systems that generalizes the Binet-Cauchy kernel for linear systems. This measure is then used to construct activity classifiers. The proposed approach outperforms the compared kernel dynamic-system classifiers and state-of-the-art dynamics-based or attribute-based recognition methods. The results support modeling semantic content and temporal structure together.
summary.tldr: A binary dynamic system models changing semantic attributes in video and improves activity recognition over the compared approaches.

title: Recognizing Activities by Attribute Dynamics

abstract: We address a central problem of neuroanatomy, namely, the automatic segmentation of neuronal structures depicted in stacks of electron microscopy (EM) images. This is necessary to efficiently map 3D brain structure and connectivity. To segment {\em biological} neuron membranes, we use a special type of deep {\em artificial} neural network as a pixel classifier. The label of each pixel (membrane or non-membrane) is predicted from raw pixel values in a square window centered on it. The input layer maps each window pixel to a neuron. It is followed by a succession of convolutional and max-pooling layers which preserve 2D information and extract features with increasing levels of abstraction. The output layer produces a calibrated probability for each class. The classifier is trained by plain gradient descent on a $512 \times 512 \times 30$ stack with known ground truth, and tested on a stack of the same size (ground truth unknown to the authors) by the organizers of the ISBI 2012 EM Segmentation Challenge. Even without problem-specific post-processing, our approach outperforms competing techniques by a large margin in all three considered metrics, i.e. \emph{rand error}, \emph{warping error} and \emph{pixel error}. For pixel error, our approach is the only one outperforming a second human observer.

For pixel error, our approach is the only one outperforming a second human observer.

paragraphs: Mapping brain structure and connectivity requires identifying neuronal structures in stacks of electron microscopy images. This paper addresses a central part of that task: deciding which pixels belong to neuronal membranes. It uses a deep neural network to classify each pixel from the raw image values in a square neighborhood centered on that pixel.

Successive convolutional and max-pooling layers preserve two-dimensional information while extracting increasingly abstract features. The output gives calibrated probabilities for membrane and non-membrane classes. The network is trained with ordinary gradient descent on a labeled image stack, connecting local visual context directly to the desired segmentation labels.

Challenge organizers evaluate the method on an equally sized stack whose ground truth was unknown to the authors. Without problem-specific post-processing, it outperforms competing techniques by a large margin on rand error, warping error, and pixel error. On pixel error specifically, it is the only approach reported to outperform a second human observer. That human comparison applies to this metric in the evaluation, rather than establishing superiority across all aspects of anatomical reconstruction.
summary.tldr: A deep pixel classifier segments neuronal membranes from raw microscopy images and leads the reported challenge evaluation across three metrics.

title: Deep Neural Networks Segment Neuronal Membranes in Electron Microscopy Images

abstract: Entropy rate quantifies the amount of disorder in a stochastic process. For spiking neurons, the entropy rate places an upper bound on the rate at which the spike train can convey stimulus information, and a large literature has focused on the problem of estimating entropy rate from spike train data. Here we present Bayes Least Squares and Empirical Bayesian entropy rate estimators for binary spike trains using Hierarchical Dirichlet Process (HDP) priors. Our estimator leverages the fact that the entropy rate of an ergodic Markov Chain with known transition probabilities can be calculated analytically, and many stochastic processes that are non-Markovian can still be well approximated by Markov processes of sufficient depth. Choosing an appropriate depth of Markov model presents challenges due to possibly long time dependencies and short data sequences: a deeper model can better account for long time-dependencies, but is more difficult to infer from limited data. Our approach mitigates this difficulty by using a hierarchical prior to share statistical power across Markov chains of different depths. We present both a fully Bayesian and empirical Bayes entropy rate estimator based on this model, and demonstrate their performance on simulated and real neural spike train data.

paragraphs: The entropy rate of a neuronal spike train measures its disorder and bounds how rapidly it can convey stimulus information. Estimating that rate is difficult when recordings are short and spikes have dependencies extending far into the past. This paper develops Bayesian estimators for binary spike trains that address this tension.

The method uses Markov models because an ergodic Markov chain’s entropy rate can be calculated analytically when its transition probabilities are known. This sharing mitigates the difficulty of choosing between temporal detail and reliable estimation. The contribution is a way to pool evidence across temporal depths while estimating a quantity that constrains the information capacity of spike trains.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Bayesian estimators share information across Markov model depths to estimate spike-train entropy rates from limited recordings.

title: Spike train entropy-rate estimation using hierarchical Dirichlet process priors

abstract: We provide a general theory of the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm for inferring high dimensional latent variable models. In particular, we make two contributions: (i) For parameter estimation, we propose a novel high dimensional EM algorithm which naturally incorporates sparsity structure into parameter estimation. With an appropriate initialization, this algorithm converges at a geometric rate and attains an estimator with the (near-)optimal statistical rate of convergence. (ii) Based on the obtained estimator, we propose a new inferential procedure for testing hypotheses for low dimensional components of high dimensional parameters. For a broad family of statistical models, our framework establishes the first computationally feasible approach for optimal estimation and asymptotic inference in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models require learning from data when some relevant variables are unobserved. This paper develops a general theory for expectation-maximization in high-dimensional versions of these models. It addresses both obtaining accurate parameter estimates and using those estimates to test hypotheses about selected components of the parameter.

For estimation, the authors propose an EM algorithm that incorporates sparsity into the learning process. With an appropriate initialization, it converges geometrically and reaches an estimator with a near-optimal or optimal statistical convergence rate. These are distinct benefits: geometric convergence concerns progress across algorithmic iterations, while the statistical rate describes the accuracy attainable from the data.

The second contribution builds an inferential procedure on the resulting estimator. It supports hypothesis tests for low-dimensional parts of a parameter that is high-dimensional overall. For a broad family of statistical models, the authors present the framework as the first computationally feasible route to optimal estimation and asymptotic inference in high dimensions. The initialization requirement is central to the stated convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-aware EM framework combines fast convergence from appropriate initialization with strong estimation guarantees and asymptotic hypothesis testing.

title: High Dimensional EM Algorithm: Statistical Optimization and Asymptotic Normality

abstract: Learning of low dimensional structure in multidimensional data is a canonical problem in machine learning. One common approach is to suppose that the observed data are close to a lower-dimensional smooth manifold. There are a rich variety of manifold learning methods available, which allow mapping of data points to the manifold. However, there is a clear lack of probabilistic methods that allow learning of the manifold along with the generative distribution of the observed data. The best attempt is the Gaussian process latent variable model (GP-LVM), but identifiability issues lead to poor performance. We solve these issues by proposing a novel Coulomb repulsive process (Corp) for locations of points on the manifold, inspired by physical models of electrostatic interactions among particles. Combining this process with a GP prior for the mapping function yields a novel electrostatic GP (electroGP) process. Focusing on the simple case of a one-dimensional manifold, we develop efficient inference algorithms, and illustrate substantially improved performance in a variety of experiments including filling in missing frames in video.

paragraphs: High-dimensional observations may lie near a smooth structure with far fewer dimensions. Many manifold-learning methods map observations onto such a structure, but this paper seeks a probabilistic model that learns both the structure and the distribution generating the observations. It identifies identifiability problems in Gaussian process latent variable models as an obstacle to that goal.

The authors introduce a Coulomb repulsive process for the locations of points on the manifold, inspired by electrostatic interactions between particles. They combine this process with a Gaussian process prior for the function mapping those locations into the observation space. The resulting electrostatic Gaussian process couples the arrangement of latent points with a probabilistic mapping to observed data.

The paper focuses on one-dimensional manifolds, or curves, and develops efficient inference algorithms for this case. Experiments show substantially improved performance across several tasks, including filling in missing video frames. The contribution is a probabilistic curve-learning construction that addresses the identified ambiguities in latent locations, with practical evidence from the one-dimensional setting studied.
summary.tldr: An electrostatic Gaussian process combines repulsive latent locations with a probabilistic mapping to improve learning of one-dimensional manifolds.

title: Probabilistic Curve Learning: Coulomb Repulsion and the Electrostatic Gaussian Process

abstract: We describe a convergence acceleration technique for generic optimization problems. Our scheme computes estimates of the optimum from a nonlinear average of the iterates produced by any optimization method. The weights in this average are computed via a simple and small linear system, whose solution can be updated online. This acceleration scheme runs in parallel to the base algorithm, providing improved estimates of the solution on the fly, while the original optimization method is running. Numerical experiments are detailed on classical classification problems.

Numerical experiments are detailed on classical classification problems.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to accelerate optimization by using the sequence of estimates an optimizer already produces. Instead of treating each iterate only as a step toward the next one, the method combines iterates to form an additional estimate of the optimum. The scheme is described for generic optimization problems and can work alongside any base optimization method.

The combination is a nonlinear average whose weights are obtained by solving a small linear system. That system can be updated online as the base algorithm continues. The method therefore has a concrete computational mechanism for turning the evolving sequence into new solution estimates, without requiring the original optimization run to finish first.

The acceleration runs in parallel with the underlying optimizer and provides improved estimates on the fly. Numerical experiments examine the approach on classical classification problems. The contribution is a broadly applicable mechanism for extracting more useful estimates from an ongoing optimization trajectory, with empirical evaluation in classification rather than a stated universal improvement rate for every possible optimizer.
summary.tldr: An online nonlinear combination of optimization iterates produces improved solution estimates while the base optimizer continues running.

title: Regularized Nonlinear Acceleration

abstract: This paper focuses on style transfer on the basis of non-parallel text. This is an instance of a broad family of problems including machine translation, decipherment, and sentiment modification. The key challenge is to separate the content from other aspects such as style. We assume a shared latent content distribution across different text corpora, and propose a method that leverages refined alignment of latent representations to perform style transfer. The transferred sentences from one style should match example sentences from the other style as a population. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this cross-alignment method on three tasks: sentiment modification, decipherment of word substitution ciphers, and recovery of word order.

paragraphs: Changing a sentence's style while retaining its content is difficult when training texts do not come in matched pairs. This paper studies that non-parallel setting, where examples from different corpora must supply the information needed for transfer without directly showing corresponding rewrites.

The approach assumes that the corpora share a latent distribution of content. Under this assumption, it uses refined alignment of hidden representations to separate content from other properties, including style. A central requirement is population-level agreement: sentences transferred into a target style should collectively resemble examples from that style. This provides a training objective even when individual source and target sentences are not paired.

The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of cross-alignment on sentiment modification, word-substitution cipher decipherment, and word-order recovery. These tasks test transformations involving different aspects of text while sharing the challenge of recovering underlying content. The findings support the proposed alignment approach across those examples, with the shared latent-content distribution remaining an explicit modeling assumption.
summary.tldr: Cross-alignment learns text transformations from unpaired corpora by assuming shared latent content and matching transferred sentences to the target population.

title: Style Transfer from Non-Parallel Text by Cross-Alignment

abstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) is a non-parametric inference algorithm that evolves a set of particles to fit a given distribution of interest. We analyze the non-asymptotic properties of SVGD, showing that there exists a set of functions, which we call the Stein matching set, whose expectations are exactly estimated by any set of particles that satisfies the fixed point equation of SVGD. This set is the image of Stein operator applied on the feature maps of the positive definite kernel used in SVGD. Our results provide a theoretical framework for analyzing the properties of SVGD with different kernels, shedding insight into optimal kernel choice. In particular, we show that SVGD with linear kernels yields exact estimation of means and variances on Gaussian distributions, while random Fourier features enable probabilistic bounds for distributional approximation. Our results offer a refreshing view of the classical inference problem as fitting Stein’s identity or solving the Stein equation, which may motivate more efficient algorithms.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent approximates a target distribution by moving a collection of particles. This paper asks what such a finite collection can represent exactly. The authors identify a Stein matching set of functions whose expectations are estimated exactly whenever the particles satisfy SVGD's fixed-point equation.

The matching set comes from applying the Stein operator to the feature maps of SVGD's positive-definite kernel. This makes the kernel's role concrete: its features determine a collection of quantities that fixed-point particles match. Random Fourier features provide probabilistic bounds on distributional approximation. These results connect kernel choice to approximation properties and recast inference as matching Stein identities or solving a Stein equation, a perspective the authors suggest may inspire more efficient algorithms.
summary.tldr: SVGD fixed points exactly match expectations of a kernel-dependent function set, clarifying how kernel choice affects inference.

title: Stein Variational Gradient Descent as Moment Matching

abstract: The backpropagation of error algorithm (BP) is impossible to implement in a real brain. The recent success of deep networks in machine learning and AI, however, has inspired proposals for understanding how the brain might learn across multiple layers, and hence how it might approximate BP. As of yet, none of these proposals have been rigorously evaluated on tasks where BP-guided deep learning has proved critical, or in architectures more structured than simple fully-connected networks. Here we present results on scaling up biologically motivated models of deep learning on datasets which need deep networks with appropriate architectures to achieve good performance. We present results on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet datasets and explore variants of target-propagation (TP) and feedback alignment (FA) algorithms, and explore performance in both fully- and locally-connected architectures. We also introduce weight-transport-free variants of difference target propagation (DTP) modified to remove backpropagation from the penultimate layer. Many of these algorithms perform well for MNIST, but for CIFAR and ImageNet we find that TP and FA variants perform significantly worse than BP, especially for networks composed of locally connected units, opening questions about whether new architectures and algorithms are required to scale these approaches. Our results and implementation details help establish baselines for biologically motivated deep learning schemes going forward.

paragraphs: Algorithms inspired by biological learning aim to explain how learning across multiple layers might work without directly implementing backpropagation in a brain. This paper asks whether proposed alternatives can scale to tasks and architectures where deep learning is particularly important. It evaluates their performance beyond simple fully connected networks.

The study tests variants of target propagation and feedback alignment on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, using both fully connected and locally connected architectures. It also introduces variants of difference target propagation that avoid weight transport and remove backpropagation from the penultimate layer. These changes address specific implementation features relevant to the biological motivation of the algorithms.

The results show that success on the simpler task does not establish scalability to the harder settings studied. The paper supplies experimental baselines and implementation details, while raising the possibility that different algorithms or architectures are needed to scale these approaches.
summary.tldr: Biologically motivated alternatives to backpropagation perform well on MNIST but struggle to match it on the larger tasks and architectures tested.

title: Assessing the Scalability of Biologically-Motivated Deep Learning Algorithms and Architectures

abstract: This paper considers the learning of Boolean rules in either disjunctive normal form (DNF, OR-of-ANDs, equivalent to decision rule sets) or conjunctive normal form (CNF, AND-of-ORs) as an interpretable model for classification. An integer program is formulated to optimally trade classification accuracy for rule simplicity. Column generation (CG) is used to efficiently search over an exponential number of candidate clauses (conjunctions or disjunctions) without the need for heuristic rule mining. This approach also bounds the gap between the selected rule set and the best possible rule set on the training data. To handle large datasets, we propose an approximate CG algorithm using randomization. Compared to three recently proposed alternatives, the CG algorithm dominates the accuracy-simplicity trade-off in 8 out of 16 datasets. When maximized for accuracy, CG is competitive with rule learners designed for this purpose, sometimes finding significantly simpler solutions that are no less accurate.

paragraphs: The paper learns classifiers expressed as Boolean rules, making their decisions easier to inspect. It considers two structures: alternatives made from groups of jointly required conditions, and jointly required groups of alternatives. An integer program explicitly balances prediction accuracy against rule simplicity, so the learning objective includes the cost of a complicated explanation.

The challenge is that there are exponentially many possible clauses to consider. Column generation searches this space without requiring a preliminary heuristic rule-mining procedure. It also provides a bound on how far the selected rules are from the best possible training-data solution. For larger datasets, the authors introduce an approximate version that uses randomization.

Against three alternatives, the method achieves a better accuracy–simplicity trade-off on eight of sixteen datasets. When tuned primarily for accuracy, it remains competitive with specialized rule learners and sometimes produces substantially simpler rules with no loss of accuracy. These findings support its usefulness for selecting readable classifiers, while the optimization-gap bound concerns the training objective specifically.
summary.tldr: Column generation learns interpretable Boolean classifiers while balancing accuracy and simplicity and bounding their training-objective optimality gap.

title: Boolean Decision Rules via Column Generation

abstract: We study in this paper the problems of both image captioning and text-to-image generation, and present a novel turbo learning approach to jointly training an image-to-text generator (a.k.a. CaptionBot) and a text-to-image generator (a.k.a. DrawingBot). The key idea behind the joint training is that image-to-text generation and text-to-image generation as dual problems can form a closed loop to provide informative feedback to each other. Based on such feedback, we introduce a new loss metric by comparing the original input with the output produced by the closed loop. In addition to the old loss metrics used in CaptionBot and DrawingBot, this extra loss metric makes the jointly trained CaptionBot and DrawingBot better than the separately trained CaptionBot and DrawingBot. Furthermore, the turbo-learning approach enables semi-supervised learning since the closed loop can provide peudo-labels for unlabeled samples. Experimental results on the COCO dataset demonstrate that the proposed turbo learning can significantly improve the performance of both CaptionBot and DrawingBot by a large margin.

paragraphs: Image captioning converts an image into text, while text-to-image generation works in the opposite direction. This paper treats the two tasks as complementary sources of training feedback. Its turbo-learning approach jointly trains an image-to-text generator, called CaptionBot, and a text-to-image generator, called DrawingBot.

The generators form a closed loop: an input passes through one model and then the other, returning to its original type. The authors introduce an additional loss that compares the original input with the result of that round trip. This feedback supplements the losses already used to train each generator and connects their learning processes.

The same loop can generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled examples, enabling semi-supervised learning. On COCO, the authors report large, significant performance improvements for both generators compared with training them separately. The contribution is therefore useful in two related ways: the paired tasks provide an additional learning signal for one another, and their outputs make otherwise unlabeled samples usable within the joint training approach.
summary.tldr: Turbo learning jointly trains captioning and image-generation models through closed-loop feedback, improving both and enabling semi-supervised learning.

title: Turbo Learning for CaptionBot and DrawingBot

abstract: When the linear measurements of an instance of low-rank matrix recovery satisfy a restricted isometry property (RIP) --- i.e. they are approximately norm-preserving --- the problem is known to contain no spurious local minima, so exact recovery is guaranteed. In this paper, we show that moderate RIP is not enough to eliminate spurious local minima, so existing results can only hold for near-perfect RIP. In fact, counterexamples are ubiquitous: every $x$ is the spurious local minimum of a rank-1 instance of matrix recovery that satisfies RIP. One specific counterexample has RIP constant $\delta=1/2$, but causes randomly initialized stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to fail 12\% of the time. SGD is frequently able to avoid and escape spurious local minima, but this empirical result shows that it can occasionally be defeated by their existence. Hence, while exact recovery guarantees will likely require a proof of no spurious local minima, arguments based solely on norm preservation will only be applicable to a narrow set of nearly-isotropic instances.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix recovery reconstructs a matrix from linear measurements. One route to proving exact recovery uses restricted isometry, meaning the measurements approximately preserve relevant norms. This paper examines how strong that property must be to rule out spurious local minima: locally attractive solutions that do not give the desired recovery.

The authors show that moderate restricted isometry does not suffice. Their counterexample construction makes any chosen x a spurious local minimum of some rank-one recovery instance satisfying restricted isometry. This claim concerns a corresponding constructed instance for each x. It demonstrates that merely having norm-preserving measurements does not by itself establish a favorable optimization landscape.

In one counterexample with restricted isometry constant one half, randomly initialized stochastic gradient descent fails in 12 percent of runs. Although SGD often avoids or escapes spurious minima, this experiment shows they can sometimes defeat it. The authors conclude that landscape guarantees based only on norm preservation apply to a narrow range of nearly isotropic instances, and suggest that exact recovery guarantees will likely need proofs excluding spurious minima.
summary.tldr: Counterexamples show that moderate restricted isometry does not eliminate spurious local minima in nonconvex matrix recovery.

title: How Much Restricted Isometry is Needed In Nonconvex Matrix Recovery?

abstract: This paper presents a new class of gradient methods for distributed machine learning that adaptively skip the gradient calculations to learn with reduced communication and computation. Simple rules are designed to detect slowly-varying gradients and, therefore, trigger the reuse of outdated gradients. The resultant gradient-based algorithms are termed Lazily Aggregated Gradient --- justifying our acronym LAG used henceforth. Theoretically, the merits of this contribution are: i) the convergence rate is the same as batch gradient descent in strongly-convex, convex, and nonconvex cases; and, ii) if the distributed datasets are heterogeneous (quantified by certain measurable constants), the communication rounds needed to achieve a targeted accuracy are reduced thanks to the adaptive reuse of lagged gradients. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data corroborate a significant communication reduction compared to alternatives.

Simple rules are designed to detect slowly-varying gradients and, therefore, trigger the reuse of outdated gradients. The resultant gradient-based algorithms are termed Lazily Aggregated Gradient --- justifying our acronym LAG used henceforth. Theoretically, the merits of this contribution are: i) the convergence rate is the same as batch gradient descent in strongly-convex, convex, and nonconvex cases; and, ii) if the distributed datasets are heterogeneous (quantified by certain measurable constants), the communication rounds needed to achieve a targeted accuracy are reduced thanks to the adaptive reuse of lagged gradients. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data corroborate a significant communication reduction compared to alternatives.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can require repeated gradient calculations and communication between machines. This paper asks when previously computed gradients can remain useful enough to reuse. Its Lazily Aggregated Gradient methods, or LAG, adaptively skip some fresh calculations, reducing both computation and the communication associated with supplying new gradients.

The method uses simple rules to detect gradients that change slowly. When those rules permit it, the algorithm reuses an older gradient in the aggregate update. The theoretical analysis establishes the same convergence rate as batch gradient descent across strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex cases, showing that selective reuse can preserve the rate of optimization progress.

The communication guarantee has an additional condition: the distributed datasets must have heterogeneity captured by specified measurable constants. Under that condition, LAG reduces the communication rounds needed to reach a target accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real data also report substantial communication savings over alternatives. The result makes selective gradient refreshes a principled way to reduce distributed training costs.
summary.tldr: LAG selectively reuses older gradients to reduce distributed learning costs while preserving batch gradient descent’s convergence rate.

title: LAG: Lazily Aggregated Gradient for Communication-Efficient Distributed Learning

abstract: Although the popular MNIST dataset \citep{mnist} is derived from the NIST database \citep{nist-sd19}, precise processing steps of this derivation have been lost to time. We propose a reconstruction that is accurate enough to serve as a replacement for the MNIST dataset, with insignificant changes in accuracy. We trace each MNIST digit to its NIST source and its rich metadata such as writer identifier, partition identifier, etc. We also reconstruct the complete MNIST test set with 60,000 samples instead of the usual 10,000. Since the balance 50,000 were never distributed, they enable us to investigate the impact of twenty-five years of MNIST experiments on the reported testing performances. Our results unambiguously confirm the trends observed by \citet{recht2018cifar,recht2019imagenet}: although the misclassification rates are slightly off, classifier ordering and model selection remain broadly reliable. We attribute this phenomenon to the pairing benefits of comparing classifiers on the same digits.

We propose a reconstruction that is accurate enough to serve as a replacement for the MNIST dataset, with insignificant changes in accuracy. We trace each MNIST digit to its NIST source and its rich metadata such as writer identifier, partition identifier, etc. We also reconstruct the complete MNIST test set with 60,000 samples instead of the usual 10,000. Since the balance 50,000 were never distributed, they enable us to investigate the impact of twenty-five years of MNIST experiments on the reported testing performances. Our results unambiguously confirm the trends observed by \citet{recht2018cifar,recht2019imagenet}: although the misclassification rates are slightly off, classifier ordering and model selection remain broadly reliable. We attribute this phenomenon to the pairing benefits of comparing classifiers on the same digits.

paragraphs: MNIST was derived from the NIST handwriting database, but the exact processing steps were no longer available. This paper reconstructs that derivation closely enough to produce a replacement dataset with insignificant accuracy changes. It also traces each MNIST digit back to its source, recovering associated information such as writer and partition identifiers.

The reconstruction yields a complete test set containing 60,000 examples, compared with the familiar 10,000. The other 50,000 had never been distributed. That makes them useful for examining whether many years of experimentation on the established benchmark have affected how well reported test performance reflects performance on additional digits.

The authors find that misclassification rates shift slightly, while the ordering of classifiers and the usefulness of model selection remain broadly reliable. They attribute this stability to comparing classifiers on the same digits, which provides paired comparisons. The result distinguishes the accuracy of a reported error rate from the reliability of a comparison between models.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing MNIST uncovers 50,000 undistributed test digits and finds that classifier rankings remain broadly reliable despite slight error-rate shifts.

title: Cold Case: The Lost MNIST Digits

abstract: When maximum likelihood estimation is infeasible, one often turns to score matching, contrastive divergence, or minimum probability flow to obtain tractable parameter estimates. We provide a unifying perspective of these techniques as minimum Stein discrepancy estimators, and use this lens to design new diffusion kernel Stein discrepancy (DKSD) and diffusion score matching (DSM) estimators with complementary strengths. We establish the consistency, asymptotic normality, and robustness of DKSD and DSM estimators, then derive stochastic Riemannian gradient descent algorithms for their efficient optimisation. The main strength of our methodology is its flexibility, which allows us to design estimators with desirable properties for specific models at hand by carefully selecting a Stein discrepancy. We illustrate this advantage for several challenging problems for score matching, such as non-smooth, heavy-tailed or light-tailed densities.

paragraphs: Estimating a probabilistic model's parameters can be difficult when maximum likelihood is infeasible. Existing alternatives include score matching, contrastive divergence, and minimum probability flow. This paper presents a common perspective on these techniques: each can be viewed through parameter estimation based on minimizing a Stein discrepancy.

The authors use that perspective to construct diffusion kernel Stein discrepancy and diffusion score matching estimators, abbreviated DKSD and DSM. Their central design idea is flexibility. Choosing a suitable discrepancy allows an estimator to be adapted to desirable properties of the model being fitted, rather than treating the estimation objective as a fixed choice across all models.

The paper establishes consistency, asymptotic normality, and robustness for the proposed estimators, and derives stochastic Riemannian gradient methods for efficient optimization. It illustrates the benefits on densities that pose difficulties for score matching, including nonsmooth, heavy-tailed, and light-tailed cases. The contribution combines a unifying interpretation of existing methods with new estimators, theoretical analysis, and optimization procedures that turn discrepancy selection into a practical modeling decision.
summary.tldr: A Stein-discrepancy framework unifies parameter-estimation methods and yields flexible new estimators with theoretical guarantees and efficient optimization.

title: Minimum Stein Discrepancy Estimators

abstract: To train Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to generate realistic imagery requires a loss function that reflects human perception of image similarity. We propose such a loss function based on Watson's perceptual model, which computes a weighted distance in frequency space and accounts for luminance and contrast masking. We extend the model to color images, increase its robustness to translation by using the Fourier Transform, remove artifacts due to splitting the image into blocks, and make it differentiable. In experiments, VAEs trained with the new loss function generated realistic, high-quality image samples. Compared to using the Euclidean distance and the Structural Similarity Index, the images were less blurry; compared to deep neural network based losses, the new approach required less computational resources and generated images with less artifacts.

paragraphs: Training an image generator requires a way to measure how closely its output resembles a target image. For variational autoencoders, the paper argues that this measurement should reflect human visual perception. It develops a training loss from Watson’s perceptual model, which compares images through weighted differences in frequency space and accounts for how luminance and contrast can mask visible differences.

The authors adapt this perceptual model for neural network training in several ways. They extend it to color images, use the Fourier transform to improve robustness to translation, eliminate artifacts associated with dividing images into blocks, and make the calculation differentiable. These changes let the perceptual comparison directly guide updates to the generator.

In the reported experiments, variational autoencoders trained with this loss produced realistic, high-quality samples. Their images were less blurry than those obtained with Euclidean distance or the Structural Similarity Index. Compared with losses based on deep neural networks, the approach used fewer computational resources and produced fewer artifacts, supporting its usefulness as a perceptually motivated training objective.
summary.tldr: An adapted Watson perceptual loss improves generated image quality while reducing computation relative to deep-network-based losses in the reported experiments.

title: A Loss Function for Generative Neural Networks Based on Watson’s Perceptual Model

abstract: Double descent refers to the phase transition that is exhibited by the generalization error of unregularized learning models when varying the ratio between the number of parameters and the number of training samples. The recent success of highly over-parameterized machine learning models such as deep neural networks has motivated a theoretical analysis of the double descent phenomenon in classical models such as linear regression which can also generalize well in the over-parameterized regime. We provide the first exact non-asymptotic expressions for double descent of the minimum norm linear estimator. Our approach involves constructing a special determinantal point process which we call surrogate random design, to replace the standard i.i.d. design of the training sample. This surrogate design admits exact expressions for the mean squared error of the estimator while preserving the key properties of the standard design. We also establish an exact implicit regularization result for over-parameterized training samples. In particular, we show that, for the surrogate design, the implicit bias of the unregularized minimum norm estimator precisely corresponds to solving a ridge-regularized least squares problem on the population distribution. In our analysis we introduce a new mathematical tool of independent interest: the class of random matrices for which determinant commutes with expectation.

paragraphs: Double descent describes how generalization error changes as a model moves between regimes with fewer and more parameters than training examples. This paper analyzes the phenomenon for the minimum-norm linear estimator. Its goal is an exact description at finite sample sizes, rather than an expression that only becomes accurate in a large-sample limit.

The central construction replaces ordinary independent sampling with a special determinantal point process called surrogate random design. This sampling model preserves key properties of the standard design while allowing exact expressions for mean squared error. The resulting double-descent formulas therefore apply to the constructed surrogate design, an essential part of what makes the analysis possible.

For over-parameterized samples under this design, the authors also establish an exact relationship between the estimator's implicit bias and ridge-regularized least squares on the population distribution. This connects a solution chosen without explicit regularization to a regularized population problem. The analysis additionally introduces random matrices for which taking a determinant commutes with taking an expectation.
summary.tldr: A specially constructed sampling design yields exact finite-sample formulas for double descent and implicit regularization in minimum-norm linear regression.

title: Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design

abstract: Pairwise alignment of DNA sequencing data is a ubiquitous task in bioinformatics and typically represents a heavy computational burden. State-of-the-art approaches to speed up this task use hashing to identify short segments (k-mers) that are shared by pairs of reads, which can then be used to estimate alignment scores. However, when the number of reads is large, accurately estimating alignment scores for all pairs is still very costly. Moreover, in practice, one is only interested in identifying pairs of reads with large alignment scores. In this work, we propose a new approach to pairwise alignment estimation based on two key new ingredients. The first ingredient is to cast the problem of pairwise alignment estimation under a general framework of rank-one crowdsourcing models, where the workers' responses correspond to k-mer hash collisions. These models can be accurately solved via a spectral decomposition of the response matrix. The second ingredient is to utilise a multi-armed bandit algorithm to adaptively refine this spectral estimator only for read pairs that are likely to have large alignments. The resulting algorithm iteratively performs a spectral decomposition of the response matrix for adaptively chosen subsets of the read pairs.

paragraphs: Comparing pairs of DNA reads can become expensive when a sequencing dataset contains many reads. Hashing shared short sequences, called k-mers, helps estimate alignment scores, but estimating every pair accurately still requires substantial work. This paper focuses on the more targeted objective of finding pairs with large alignment scores.

The first ingredient is a statistical reformulation. The authors express alignment estimation through rank-one crowdsourcing models, treating k-mer hash collisions as the responses that would otherwise come from workers. A spectral decomposition of the resulting response matrix provides a way to estimate the model accurately. This connects alignment evidence to a structured matrix estimation problem.

The second ingredient decides where to spend additional estimation effort. A multi-armed bandit algorithm selects read pairs that appear likely to have strong alignments, and the spectral estimate is refined on adaptively chosen subsets. The resulting procedure repeatedly combines estimation with selective attention. Its central contribution is organizing computation around promising pairs instead of pursuing equally precise scores for every possible pair.
summary.tldr: The method combines spectral estimation with adaptive selection to concentrate DNA alignment computation on read pairs likely to match strongly.

title: Adaptive Learning of Rank-One Models for Efficient Pairwise Sequence Alignment

abstract: In the real world, object categories usually have a hierarchical granularity tree. Nowadays, most researchers focus on recognizing categories in a specific granularity, \emph{e.g.,} basic-level or sub(ordinate)-level. Compared with basic-level categories, the sub-level categories provide more valuable information, but its training annotations are harder to acquire. Therefore, an attractive problem is how to transfer the knowledge learned from basic-level annotations to sub-level recognition. In this paper, we introduce a new task, named Hierarchical Granularity Transfer Learning (HGTL), to recognize sub-level categories with basic-level annotations and semantic descriptions for hierarchical categories. Different from other recognition tasks, HGTL has a serious granularity gap,~\emph{i.e.,} the two granularities share an image space but have different category domains, which impede the knowledge transfer. To this end, we propose a novel Bi-granularity Semantic Preserving Network (BigSPN) to bridge the granularity gap for robust knowledge transfer. Explicitly, BigSPN constructs specific visual encoders for different granularities, which are aligned with a shared semantic interpreter via a novel subordinate entropy loss. Experiments on three benchmarks with hierarchical granularities show that BigSPN is an effective framework for Hierarchical Granularity Transfer Learning.
