paragraphs: Object categories can be organized into hierarchies, with broad categories containing more specific subcategories. Fine-grained labels provide richer information but are harder to obtain. This paper introduces Hierarchical Granularity Transfer Learning, a task that uses broad-category image annotations and semantic descriptions of hierarchical categories to recognize more specific categories.

The main obstacle is a granularity gap: the images occupy the same visual space, but the broad and specific levels have different category domains. The proposed Bi-granularity Semantic Preserving Network addresses this by constructing separate visual encoders for the different levels. A shared semantic interpreter connects them, with a subordinate entropy loss used to align their representations.

This design gives each granularity its own visual representation while using category semantics to support transfer between levels. Experiments on three benchmarks with hierarchical categories show that the network is effective for the proposed task. The findings support using broadly labeled images together with semantic descriptions to learn finer distinctions, reducing reliance on the harder-to-acquire subcategory annotations.
summary.tldr: BigSPN transfers broad-category supervision to finer recognition by aligning granularity-specific visual encoders through shared category semantics.

title: Hierarchical Granularity Transfer Learning

abstract: We present a differentially private learner for halfspaces over a finite grid $G$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with sample complexity $\approx d^{2.5}\cdot 2^{\log^*|G|}$, which improves the state-of-the-art result of [Beimel et al., COLT 2019] by a $d^2$ factor. The building block for our learner is a new differentially private algorithm for approximately solving the linear feasibility problem: Given a feasible collection of $m$ linear constraints of the form $Ax\geq b$, the task is to {\em privately} identify a solution $x$ that satisfies {\em most} of the constraints. Our algorithm is iterative, where each iteration determines the next coordinate of the constructed solution $x$.

The building block for our learner is a new differentially private algorithm for approximately solving the linear feasibility problem: Given a feasible collection of $m$ linear constraints of the form $Ax\geq b$, the task is to {\em privately} identify a solution $x$ that satisfies {\em most} of the constraints. paragraphs: A halfspace classifier separates points according to which side of a linear boundary they occupy. This paper studies learning such classifiers under differential privacy when the inputs lie on a finite grid in d-dimensional space. The aim is to reduce the number of training examples required while retaining the privacy guarantee.

The proposed learner has sample complexity approximately d to the power 2.5 times 2 raised to log-star of the grid size. Log-star denotes the number of repeated logarithms needed to reduce a quantity to a small constant. The result improves the prior state of the art by a factor of d squared, reducing the dimension-dependent sample requirement.

The key ingredient is a new private algorithm for approximate linear feasibility. Given a collection of linear inequalities that can all be satisfied, it privately constructs a point satisfying most of them. The algorithm determines one coordinate at each iteration. This coordinatewise construction supplies the building block for the improved learner, with the feasibility guarantee explicitly allowing some constraints to remain unsatisfied.
summary.tldr: A coordinatewise private feasibility algorithm reduces the sample complexity of learning halfspaces over finite grids by a factor of d squared.

title: Private Learning of Halfspaces: Simplifying the Construction and Reducing the Sample Complexity

abstract: Counterpoint is an important concept in Western music theory. In the past century, there have been significant interests in incorporating counterpoint into Chinese folk music composition. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning-based system, named FolkDuet, towards the online countermelody generation for Chinese folk melodies. With no existing data of Chinese folk duets, FolkDuet employs two reward models based on out-of-domain data, i.e. Bach chorales, and monophonic Chinese folk melodies. An interaction reward model is trained on the duets formed from outer parts of Bach chorales to model counterpoint interaction, while a style reward model is trained on monophonic melodies of Chinese folk songs to model melodic patterns. With both rewards, the generator of FolkDuet is trained to generate countermelodies while maintaining the Chinese folk style. The entire generation process is performed in an online fashion, allowing real-time interactive human-machine duet improvisation. Experiments show that the proposed algorithm achieves better subjective and objective results than the baselines.

paragraphs: FolkDuet generates a countermelody alongside a Chinese folk melody in real time. The challenge is to learn both how two musical lines interact and how to preserve Chinese folk style when no Chinese folk duet dataset is available. The paper addresses this with reinforcement learning guided by two separately learned rewards.

An interaction reward learns counterpoint relationships from duets formed using the outer parts of Bach chorales. A style reward learns melodic patterns from single-line Chinese folk songs. Together, these rewards train the generator to produce a complementary line while retaining the intended melodic style, drawing different kinds of musical knowledge from different sources.

Generation takes place online, allowing interactive human-machine duet improvisation rather than requiring the complete melody in advance. Experiments report better subjective and objective results than the baselines. The contribution demonstrates how separate rewards for musical interaction and style can guide generation when examples of their desired combination are unavailable.
summary.tldr: FolkDuet combines rewards learned from Bach and Chinese folk melodies to generate interactive countermelodies without folk-duet training data.

title: When Counterpoint Meets Chinese Folk Melodies

abstract: We study the problem of semi-supervised learning on graphs, for which graph neural networks (GNNs) have been extensively explored. However, most existing GNNs inherently suffer from the limitations of over-smoothing, non-robustness, and weak-generalization when labeled nodes are scarce. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective framework—GRAPH RANDOM NEURAL NETWORKS (GRAND)—to address these issues. In GRAND, we first design a random propagation strategy to perform graph data augmentation. Then we leverage consistency regularization to optimize the prediction consistency of unlabeled nodes across different data augmentations. Extensive experiments on graph benchmark datasets suggest that GRAND significantly outperforms state-of- the-art GNN baselines on semi-supervised node classification. Finally, we show that GRAND mitigates the issues of over-smoothing and non-robustness, exhibiting better generalization behavior than existing GNNs. The source code of GRAND is publicly available at https://github.com/Grand20/grand.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised node classification uses a graph with labels available for only some nodes. Existing graph neural networks can struggle when labels are scarce, when their predictions are insufficiently robust, or when repeated propagation makes node representations overly similar. The paper introduces Graph Random Neural Networks, or GRAND, to address these issues.

GRAND first creates augmented graph data using a randomized propagation strategy. It then applies consistency regularization to predictions for unlabeled nodes across those different augmentations. The training objective encourages a node's prediction to remain consistent across augmented views, allowing unlabeled nodes to contribute directly to the learning process.

Experiments on graph benchmarks suggest that GRAND substantially outperforms the state-of-the-art graph neural network baselines considered for semi-supervised node classification. The authors also report reduced over-smoothing and improved robustness and generalization. These findings support the combination of randomized propagation and prediction consistency as a practical framework for learning on graphs, particularly in the scarce-label setting studied by the paper.
summary.tldr: GRAND combines randomized graph propagation with consistency across augmented views to improve semi-supervised node classification.

title: Graph Random Neural Networks for Semi-Supervised Learning on Graphs

abstract: We present Grammar-Based Grounded Language Learning (G2L2), a lexicalist approach toward learning a compositional and grounded meaning representation of language from grounded data, such as paired images and texts. At the core of G2L2 is a collection of lexicon entries, which map each word to a tuple of a syntactic type and a neuro-symbolic semantic program. For example, the word shiny has a syntactic type of adjective; its neuro-symbolic semantic program has the symbolic form $\lambda x.\textit{filter}(x, \textbf{SHINY})$, where the concept SHINY is associated with a neural network embedding, which will be used to classify shiny objects. Given an input sentence, G2L2 first looks up the lexicon entries associated with each token. It then derives the meaning of the sentence as an executable neuro-symbolic program by composing lexical meanings based on syntax. The recovered meaning programs can be executed on grounded inputs. To facilitate learning in an exponentially-growing compositional space, we introduce a joint parsing and expected execution algorithm, which does local marginalization over derivations to reduce the training time. We evaluate G2L2 on two domains: visual reasoning and language-driven navigation. Results show that G2L2 can generalize from small amounts of data to novel compositions of words.

paragraphs: Understanding a new combination of familiar words requires a system to reuse what those words mean. Grammar-Based Grounded Language Learning, or G2L2, addresses this through a learned lexicon. Each word is associated with a syntactic type and a semantic program, linking grammatical composition with meanings grounded in inputs such as images.

The semantic programs combine symbolic operations with neural representations. For instance, an adjective can correspond to a filtering operation whose underlying visual concept is recognized through a learned embedding. To interpret a sentence, G2L2 retrieves the entries for its words and combines them according to syntax. The result is an executable program that acts on grounded inputs.

Learning these combinations is challenging because the space of possible compositions grows exponentially. The authors introduce an algorithm that combines parsing with expected execution and locally marginalizes over derivations to reduce training time. Evaluations cover visual reasoning and navigation directed by language. The reported results show that G2L2 can learn from small amounts of data and generalize to new combinations of words in these domains.
summary.tldr: G2L2 learns word-level programs that compose through grammar, supporting generalization to new word combinations from small amounts of grounded data.

title: Grammar-Based Grounded Lexicon Learning

abstract: The increasing computational requirements of deep neural networks (DNNs) have led to significant interest in obtaining DNN models that are sparse, yet accurate. Recent work has investigated the even harder case of sparse training, where the DNN weights are, for as much as possible, already sparse to reduce computational costs during training. Existing sparse training methods are often empirical and can have lower accuracy relative to the dense baseline. In this paper, we present a general approach called Alternating Compressed/DeCompressed (AC/DC) training of DNNs, demonstrate convergence for a variant of the algorithm, and show that AC/DC outperforms existing sparse training methods in accuracy at similar computational budgets; at high sparsity levels, AC/DC even outperforms existing methods that rely on accurate pre-trained dense models. An important property of AC/DC is that it allows co-training of dense and sparse models, yielding accurate sparse-dense model pairs at the end of the training process. This is useful in practice, where compressed variants may be desirable for deployment in resource-constrained settings without re-doing the entire training flow, and also provides us with insights into the accuracy gap between dense and compressed models.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks retain only a portion of their weights, making them attractive when computation is limited. Obtaining sparsity during training could also reduce training costs. The difficulty is maintaining accuracy: existing sparse training methods can fall behind dense models, and many rely primarily on empirical design choices.

AC/DC alternates between compressed and decompressed training. Its distinctive practical property is that dense and sparse models are trained together, producing an accurate pair at the end of one training process. This gives practitioners both a full model and a compressed option for deployment in settings with fewer resources, without repeating the entire training workflow.

The authors establish convergence for a variant of the algorithm and report better accuracy than existing sparse training methods at similar computational budgets. At high sparsity, AC/DC also outperforms existing methods that start from accurate pretrained dense models. The paired outputs additionally provide a way to examine the accuracy difference between dense and compressed networks within the same training approach.
summary.tldr: AC/DC alternates compressed and decompressed training to produce accurate sparse–dense model pairs while improving accuracy at comparable sparse-training budgets.

title: AC/DC: Alternating Compressed/DeCompressed Training of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Daniely and Schacham recently showed that gradient descent finds adversarial examples on random undercomplete two-layers ReLU neural networks. The term “undercomplete” refers to the fact that their proof only holds when the number of neurons is a vanishing fraction of the ambient dimension. We extend their result to the overcomplete case, where the number of neurons is larger than the dimension (yet also subexponential in the dimension). In fact we prove that a single step of gradient descent suffices. We also show this result for any subexponential width random neural network with smooth activation function.

paragraphs: This paper studies how easily gradient methods can find adversarial examples for randomly constructed neural networks with two layers. The starting point is an earlier result for ReLU networks whose hidden layer is small relative to the input dimension. More precisely, that earlier proof required the number of neurons to become a vanishing fraction of the dimension.

The authors extend the result to networks whose hidden layer can contain more neurons than there are input dimensions. Their proof still imposes a growth restriction: the width must be subexponential in the dimension. Within the setting they analyze, a single gradient descent step is sufficient to find an adversarial example, strengthening the previous conclusion about gradient descent.

They also establish a corresponding result for random networks with smooth activation functions and subexponential width. The contribution therefore broadens both the permitted network sizes and activation choices. These are theoretical findings about random networks in the stated setting; they explain why increasing width within that range need not prevent a simple gradient attack from succeeding.
summary.tldr: For the random two-layer networks studied, one gradient step finds adversarial examples even when network width exceeds input dimension, subject to a subexponential width restriction.

title: A single gradient step finds adversarial examples on random two-layers neural networks

abstract: Programs, consisting of semantic and structural information, play an important role in the communication between humans and agents. Towards learning general program executors to unify perception, reasoning, and decision making, we formulate program-guided tasks which require learning to execute a given program on the observed task specification. Furthermore, we propose Program-Guided Transformers (ProTo), which integrates both semantic and structural guidance of a program by leveraging cross-attention and masked self-attention to pass messages between the specification and routines in the program. ProTo executes a program in a learned latent space and enjoys stronger representation ability than previous neural-symbolic approaches. We demonstrate that ProTo significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods on GQA visual reasoning and 2D Minecraft policy learning datasets. Additionally, ProTo demonstrates better generalization to unseen, complex, and human-written programs.

paragraphs: Programs communicate both what operations mean and how those operations are organized. The broader aim is a general program executor that brings perception, reasoning, and decision making into a shared framework.

The proposed Program-Guided Transformer, or ProTo, incorporates both semantic and structural guidance. Cross-attention and masked self-attention pass information between the task specification and routines in the program. Execution occurs in a learned latent space, giving the model a representation-based way to carry out the program. The authors describe this as offering stronger representation ability than earlier neural-symbolic approaches.

Experiments report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods on GQA visual reasoning and 2D Minecraft policy learning. ProTo also shows better generalization to unseen, complex, and human-written programs. These findings support the usefulness of treating program meaning and organization as complementary guidance, across both a visual reasoning task and a task requiring learned behavior.
summary.tldr: ProTo uses program semantics and structure to guide transformer-based execution, improving visual reasoning, policy learning, and generalization to new programs.

title: ProTo: Program-Guided Transformer for Program-Guided Tasks

abstract: Diet planning, a basic and regular human activity, is important to all individuals. Children, adults, the healthy, and the infirm all profit from diet planning. Many recent attempts have been made to develop machine learning (ML) applications related to diet planning. However, given the complexity and difficulty of implementing this task, no high-quality diet-level dataset exists at present. Professionals, particularly dietitians and physicians, would benefit greatly from such a dataset and ML application. In this work, we create and publish the Korean Menus–Ingredients–Nutrients–Diets (MIND) dataset for a ML application regarding diet planning and dietary health research. The nature of diet planning entails both explicit (nutrition) and implicit (composition) requirements. Thus, the MIND dataset was created by integrating input from experts who considered implicit data requirements for diet solution with the capabilities of an operations research (OR) model that specifies and applies explicit data requirements for diet solution and a controllable generative machine that automates the high-quality diet generation process. MIND consists of data from 1,500 South Korean daily diets, 3,238 menus, and 3,036 ingredients. MIND considers the daily recommended dietary intake of 14 major nutrients. MIND can be easily downloaded and analyzed using the Python package dietkit accessible via the package installer for Python. MIND is expected to contribute to the use of ML in solving medical, economic, and social problems associated with diet planning. Furthermore, our approach of integrating data from experts with OR and ML models is expected to promote the use of ML in other fields that require the generation of high-quality synthetic professional task data, especially since the use of ML to automate and support professional tasks has become a highly valuable service.

The MIND dataset addresses the need for data at this complete-diet level. Its creation process combines professional input with computational methods so that generating diets accounts for more than numerical nutrient targets alone.

Experts contribute knowledge about implicit composition requirements, while an operations research model specifies and applies explicit requirements. A controllable generative model automates diet generation within this combined approach. The resulting Korean Menus–Ingredients–Nutrients–Diets dataset includes 1,500 South Korean daily diets, 3,238 menus, and 3,036 ingredients, and considers recommended daily intake for 14 major nutrients.

They also propose the combination of expert input, optimization, and controlled generation as a promising approach for creating synthetic data for other professional tasks, presenting that broader impact as an expectation.
summary.tldr: MIND combines expert judgment, optimization, and controlled generation to create a dataset of nutritionally informed South Korean diets.

title: MIND dataset for diet planning and dietary healthcare with machine learning: Dataset creation using combinatorial optimization and controllable generation with domain experts

abstract: Imitation learning is a class of promising policy learning algorithms that is free from many practical issues with reinforcement learning, such as the reward design issue and the exploration hardness. However, the current imitation algorithm struggles to achieve both high performance and high in-environment sample efficiency simultaneously. Behavioral Cloning (BC) does not need in-environment interactions, but it suffers from the covariate shift problem which harms its performance. Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) turns imitation learning into a distribution matching problem. It can achieve better performance on some tasks but it requires a large number of in-environment interactions. Inspired by the recent success of EfficientZero in RL, we propose EfficientImitate (EI), a planning-based imitation learning method that can achieve high in-environment sample efficiency and performance simultaneously. Our algorithmic contribution in this paper is two-fold. First, we extend AIL into the MCTS-based RL. Second, we show the seemingly incompatible two classes of imitation algorithms (BC and AIL) can be naturally unified under our framework, enjoying the benefits of both. We benchmark our method not only on the state-based DeepMind Control Suite but also on the image version which many previous works find highly challenging. Experimental results show that EI achieves state-of-the-art results in performance and sample efficiency. EI shows over 4x gain in performance in the limited sample setting on state-based and image-based tasks and can solve challenging problems like Humanoid, where previous methods fail with a small amount of interactions. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhaohengyin/EfficientImitate.

paragraphs: Behavioral cloning learns without new environment interactions but can suffer when its actions lead away from demonstration states. Adversarial imitation can improve behavior through distribution matching, yet often needs many interactions. EfficientImitate aims to combine strong performance with a smaller interaction budget.

The framework extends adversarial imitation to reinforcement learning based on Monte Carlo tree search and unifies it with behavioral cloning. Planning provides the common structure through which the two imitation approaches can contribute their respective advantages.

On state-based and image-based DeepMind Control tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and sample efficiency. In limited-sample settings, performance improves by over 4x, and the method solves challenging tasks such as Humanoid where earlier methods fail with few interactions. The abstract does not give the precise interaction budgets or define every reported aggregate, so the gains remain specific to the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: EfficientImitate combines planning, behavioral cloning, and adversarial imitation to reduce environment interactions.

title: Planning for Sample Efficient Imitation Learning

abstract: We consider a preference learning setting where every participant chooses an ordered list of $k$ most preferred items among a displayed set of candidates. (The set can be different for every participant.) We identify a distance-based ranking model for the population's preferences and their (ranked) choice behavior. The ranking model resembles the Mallows model but uses a new distance function called Reverse Major Index (RMJ). We find that despite the need to sum over all permutations, the RMJ-based ranking distribution aggregates into (ranked) choice probabilities with simple closed-form expression. We develop effective methods to estimate the model parameters and showcase their generalization power using real data, especially when there is a limited variety of display sets.

paragraphs: Preference data often consists of a short ranked selection rather than a complete ordering of every available item. This paper studies participants who choose their k favorite items, in order, from a displayed candidate set. Different participants may see different sets, so the model must connect these partial observations to population-level preferences.

The authors introduce a distance-based ranking distribution resembling the Mallows model but using a new distance called Reverse Major Index. A central result concerns converting that full ranking distribution into probabilities for the choices people actually report. Although this aggregation involves all permutations, the resulting ranked-choice probabilities have simple closed-form expressions.

This makes the model useful for handling partial ranked selections without leaving their probabilities as an unwieldy sum over complete rankings. The paper develops methods for estimating the model's parameters and evaluates their generalization on real data. The reported strength is especially relevant when the observed data contains only a limited variety of candidate display sets, where learning preferences from restricted presentation patterns is important.
summary.tldr: A new ranking distance yields simple ranked-choice probabilities and supports preference estimation from varying candidate sets.

title: On A Mallows-type Model For (Ranked) Choices

abstract: We propose and analyze a reinforcement learning principle thatapproximates the Bellman equations by enforcing their validity onlyalong a user-defined space of test functions. Focusing onapplications to model-free offline RL with function approximation, weexploit this principle to derive confidence intervals for off-policyevaluation, as well as to optimize over policies within a prescribedpolicy class. We prove an oracle inequality on our policyoptimization procedure in terms of a trade-off between the value anduncertainty of an arbitrary comparator policy. Different choices oftest function spaces allow us to tackle different problems within acommon framework. We characterize the loss of efficiency in movingfrom on-policy to off-policy data using our procedures, and establishconnections to concentrability coefficients studied in past work. Weexamine in depth the implementation of our methods with linearfunction approximation, and provide theoretical guarantees withpolynomial-time implementations even when Bellman closure does nothold.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to evaluate or improve decisions. This paper introduces a principle for approximating the Bellman equations, which express consistency between values and the rewards and future values they imply. Instead of enforcing those equations everywhere, the method enforces them along a user-selected space of test functions.

The authors use this principle for model-free learning with function approximation. It supports both confidence intervals for evaluating policies from data collected under other policies and optimization within a chosen policy class. Their policy-optimization guarantee compares the result against an arbitrary alternative policy through a tradeoff between that policy's value and its uncertainty.

Choosing different test-function spaces lets the same framework address different problems. The analysis also characterizes the efficiency lost when moving from on-policy to off-policy data and connects it to established measures of data coverage. For linear function approximation, the authors provide polynomial-time implementations with theoretical guarantees even without Bellman closure, a property concerning whether Bellman updates stay within the function class.
summary.tldr: Testing Bellman consistency against selected functions enables offline policy evaluation and optimization with guarantees, including linear settings without Bellman closure.

title: Bellman Residual Orthogonalization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Most existing point cloud completion methods assume the input partial point cloud is clean, which is not practical in practice, and are Most existing point cloud completion methods assume the input partial point cloud is clean, which is not the case in practice, and are generally based on supervised learning. In this paper, we present an unsupervised generative adversarial autoencoding network, named UGAAN, which completes the partial point cloud contaminated by surroundings from real scenes and cutouts the object simultaneously, only using artificial CAD models as assistance. The generator of UGAAN learns to predict the complete point clouds on real data from both the discriminator and the autoencoding process of artificial data. The latent codes from generator are also fed to discriminator which makes encoder only extract object features rather than noises. We also devise a refiner for generating better complete cloud with a segmentation module to separate the object from background. We train our UGAAN with one real scene dataset and evaluate it with the other two. Extensive experiments and visualization demonstrate our superiority, generalization and robustness. Comparisons against the previous method show that our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance on unsupervised point cloud completion and segmentation on real data.

paragraphs: Real-world partial point clouds can include surrounding clutter as well as missing object geometry. UGAAN tackles both problems together: it completes the object and separates it from its background. The method uses unsupervised learning on real data with artificial CAD models as assistance, addressing the clean-input assumption common in earlier completion methods.

Its generator learns to produce complete point clouds through signals from a discriminator and from autoencoding artificial data. The discriminator also receives latent codes from the generator, encouraging the encoder to capture object features instead of noise. A refiner improves the completed cloud and includes a segmentation module that distinguishes object points from background.

The authors train on one real-scene dataset and evaluate on two others, examining transfer beyond the training dataset. Experiments and visualizations support their claims of generalization and robustness, and comparisons report state-of-the-art unsupervised completion and segmentation on real data. The combined design matters because completion and object separation are treated as related parts of reconstructing an object from a contaminated observation.
summary.tldr: UGAAN uses adversarial learning and artificial CAD models to jointly complete partial real-world point clouds and separate objects from clutter.

title: Unsupervised Point Cloud Completion and Segmentation by Generative Adversarial Autoencoding Network

abstract: Contrastive learning is a method of learning visual representations by training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to increase the similarity between representations of positive pairs (transformations of the same image) and reduce the similarity between representations of negative pairs (transformations of different images). Here we explore Energy-Based Contrastive Learning (EBCLR) that leverages the power of generative learning by combining contrastive learning with Energy-Based Models (EBMs). EBCLR can be theoretically interpreted as learning the joint distribution of positive pairs, and it shows promising results on small and medium-scale datasets such as MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Specifically, we find EBCLR demonstrates from $\times 4$ up to $\times 20$ acceleration compared to SimCLR and MoCo v2 in terms of training epochs. Furthermore, in contrast to SimCLR, we observe EBCLR achieves nearly the same performance with $254$ negative pairs (batch size $128$) and $30$ negative pairs (batch size $16$) per positive pair, demonstrating the robustness of EBCLR to small numbers of negative pairs. Hence, EBCLR provides a novel avenue for improving contrastive learning methods that usually require large datasets with a significant number of negative pairs per iteration to achieve reasonable performance on downstream tasks. Code: https://github.com/1202kbs/EBCLR

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds image representations by bringing transformed versions of the same image closer together and separating versions of different images. Energy-Based Contrastive Learning, or EBCLR, combines this objective with energy-based generative modeling. The paper gives the combination a theoretical interpretation as learning the joint distribution of two transformed views of the same image.

The authors evaluate EBCLR on small and medium-scale datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. They report acceleration ranging from fourfold to twentyfold relative to SimCLR and MoCo v2 when measured in training epochs. This result concerns the number of epochs needed in the reported comparisons, rather than a stated measurement of elapsed computing time.

EBCLR also achieves nearly unchanged performance when the number of negative pairs per positive pair falls from 254 to 30, corresponding to batch sizes of 128 and 16. The authors contrast this behavior with SimCLR. Together, the results suggest that combining generative and contrastive learning can reduce dependence on large numbers of negative examples in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: EBCLR combines contrastive and energy-based learning, reporting fewer training epochs and resilience to smaller negative-pair sets on small and medium-scale datasets.

title: Energy-Based Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

abstract: Network architecture plays a key role in the deep learning-based computer vision system. The widely-used convolutional neural network and transformer treat the image as a grid or sequence structure, which is not flexible to capture irregular and complex objects. In this paper, we propose to represent the image as a graph structure and introduce a new \emph{Vision GNN} (ViG) architecture to extract graph-level feature for visual tasks. We first split the image to a number of patches which are viewed as nodes, and construct a graph by connecting the nearest neighbors. Based on the graph representation of images, we build our ViG model to transform and exchange information among all the nodes. ViG consists of two basic modules: Grapher module with graph convolution for aggregating and updating graph information, and FFN module with two linear layers for node feature transformation. Both isotropic and pyramid architectures of ViG are built with different model sizes. Extensive experiments on image recognition and object detection tasks demonstrate the superiority of our ViG architecture. We hope this pioneering study of GNN on general visual tasks will provide useful inspiration and experience for future research. The PyTorch code is available at \url{https://github.com/huawei-noah/Efficient-AI-Backbones} and the MindSpore code is available at \url{https://gitee.com/mindspore/models}.

paragraphs: Vision GNN represents an image as a graph, motivated by the difficulty of describing irregular and complex objects through fixed grids or sequences. The method divides an image into patches and treats each patch as a node. Connecting nearest neighbors creates a graph through which the model can exchange information.

The architecture has two main components. A Grapher module uses graph convolution to aggregate and update information, while a feed-forward module with two linear layers transforms node features. Together, these operations let the model combine information across connected patches and refine each patch's representation. The resulting graph-level features are used for visual tasks.

The authors build both isotropic and pyramid versions at different model sizes, exploring the graph-based design across multiple architectural configurations. Extensive image-recognition and object-detection experiments demonstrate advantages for the proposed architecture. The contribution is therefore both a representation choice and an implemented family of vision models. The reported results support graph neural networks as an effective approach for the evaluated general visual tasks.
summary.tldr: Vision GNN models image patches as connected graph nodes and learns visual features through graph convolution and feature transformations.

title: Vision GNN: An Image is Worth Graph of Nodes

abstract: We study survival analysis in the dynamic setting: We seek to model the time to an event of interest given sequences of states. Taking inspiration from temporal-difference learning, a central idea in reinforcement learning, we develop algorithms that estimate a discrete-time survival model by exploiting a temporal-consistency condition. Intuitively, this condition captures the fact that the survival distribution at consecutive states should be similar, accounting for the delay between states. Our method can be combined with any parametric survival model and naturally accommodates right-censored observations. We demonstrate empirically that it achieves better sample-efficiency and predictive performance compared to approaches that directly regress the observed survival outcome.

Taking inspiration from temporal-difference learning, a central idea in reinforcement learning, we develop algorithms that estimate a discrete-time survival model by exploiting a temporal-consistency condition. Intuitively, this condition captures the fact that the survival distribution at consecutive states should be similar, accounting for the delay between states. paragraphs: Survival analysis predicts how long it will take for an event to occur. In a dynamic setting, that prediction can use a sequence of changing states rather than a single observation. This paper asks how relationships between successive states can improve learning of the distribution over event times.

The authors develop discrete-time survival algorithms inspired by temporal-difference learning. Their central condition is temporal consistency: predictions from consecutive states should align after accounting for the time that passed between them. This gives the learning procedure a relationship to exploit across the sequence, beyond directly fitting each prediction to an observed survival outcome.

The method can be combined with any parametric survival model and naturally handles right-censored observations, where observation ends before the event is seen. Empirical comparisons show better sample efficiency and predictive performance than approaches that directly regress observed outcomes. The findings indicate that temporal relationships can supply useful learning structure: the sequence contributes through consistency between neighboring predictions as well as through the recorded event information.
summary.tldr: Enforcing consistency between successive survival predictions improves sample efficiency and prediction in experiments while accommodating censored observations.

title: Temporally-Consistent Survival Analysis

abstract: Algorithmic fairness has received increased attention in socially sensitive domains. While rich literature on mean fairness has been established, research on quantile fairness remains sparse but vital. To fulfill great needs and advocate the significance of quantile fairness, we propose a novel framework to learn a real-valued quantile function under the fairness requirement of Demographic Parity with respect to sensitive attributes, such as race or gender, and thereby derive a reliable fair prediction interval. Using optimal transport and functional synchronization techniques, we establish theoretical guarantees of distribution-free coverage and exact fairness for the induced prediction interval constructed by fair quantiles. A hands-on pipeline is provided to incorporate flexible quantile regressions with an efficient fairness adjustment post-processing algorithm. We demonstrate the superior empirical performance of this approach on several benchmark datasets. Our results show the model’s ability to uncover the mechanism underlying the fairness-accuracy trade-off in a wide range of societal and medical applications.

paragraphs: Fairness research often examines average predictions, but averages alone do not describe how predictions behave across a distribution. This paper focuses on quantiles, which describe different positions within that distribution. It learns real-valued quantile functions subject to demographic parity with respect to sensitive attributes, such as race or gender, and uses them to construct prediction intervals.

The approach combines optimal transport and functional synchronization to coordinate the fairness adjustment. The authors establish theoretical guarantees of distribution-free coverage and exact fairness for the resulting intervals. Coverage concerns whether an interval contains the outcome being predicted; fairness here refers specifically to the demographic-parity requirement used in the framework.

The paper also provides a practical pipeline that pairs flexible quantile regression methods with an efficient post-processing adjustment. This makes the fairness mechanism usable alongside different quantile predictors. Benchmark experiments report superior empirical performance, and the authors use the results to investigate the relationship between fairness and accuracy. The contribution therefore connects fairness across predicted distributions with uncertainty expressed through intervals.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs prediction intervals from fair quantiles, with theoretical guarantees of coverage and demographic parity.

title: Conformalized Fairness via Quantile Regression

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that are based on the message passing (MP) paradigm generally exchange information between 1-hop neighbors to build node representations at each layer. In principle, such networks are not able to capture long-range interactions (LRI) that may be desired or necessary for learning a given task on graphs. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in development of Transformer-based methods for graphs that can consider full node connectivity beyond the original sparse structure, thus enabling the modeling of LRI. However, MP-GNNs that simply rely on 1-hop message passing often fare better in several existing graph benchmarks when combined with positional feature representations, among other innovations, hence limiting the perceived utility and ranking of Transformer-like architectures. Here, we present the Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB) with 5 graph learning datasets: $\texttt{PascalVOC-SP}$, $\texttt{COCO-SP}$, $\texttt{PCQM-Contact}$, $\texttt{Peptides-func}$ and $\texttt{Peptides-struct}$ that arguably require LRI reasoning to achieve strong performance in a given task. We benchmark both baseline GNNs and Graph Transformer networks to verify that the models which capture long-range dependencies perform significantly better on these tasks. Therefore, these datasets are suitable for benchmarking and exploration of MP GNNs and Graph Transformer architectures that are intended to capture LRI.

summary.tldr: LRGB introduces five graph datasets on which models capturing long-range dependencies show a clear performance advantage.

title: Long Range Graph Benchmark

abstract: Humans and other animals are capable of improving their learning performance as they solve related tasks from a given problem domain, to the point of being able to learn from extremely limited data. While synaptic plasticity is generically thought to underlie learning in the brain, the precise neural and synaptic mechanisms by which learning processes improve through experience are not well understood. Here, we present a general-purpose, biologically-plausible meta-learning rule which estimates gradients with respect to the parameters of an underlying learning algorithm by simply running it twice. Our rule may be understood as a generalization of contrastive Hebbian learning to meta-learning and notably, it neither requires computing second derivatives nor going backwards in time, two characteristic features of previous gradient-based methods that are hard to conceive in physical neural circuits. We demonstrate the generality of our rule by applying it to two distinct models: a complex synapse with internal states which consolidate task-shared information, and a dual-system architecture in which a primary network is rapidly modulated by another one to learn the specifics of each task. For both models, our meta-learning rule matches or outperforms reference algorithms on a wide range of benchmark problems, while only using information presumed to be locally available at neurons and synapses. We corroborate these findings with a theoretical analysis of the gradient estimation error incurred by our rule.

This paper approaches that question through mechanisms that could plausibly operate in neural circuits. It introduces a rule that estimates gradients for the parameters of an underlying learning algorithm by running that algorithm twice and using a contrastive procedure.

The rule extends the idea of contrastive Hebbian learning to meta-learning. It avoids computing second derivatives and running computations backward through time, both of which pose difficulties for a physical neural implementation. Its updates use information presumed to be available locally at neurons and synapses, making that locality an explicit part of the proposed biological plausibility.

The authors test the rule in two different models: synapses with internal states that retain information shared across tasks, and a two-system architecture in which one network rapidly modulates another. In both cases, it matches or exceeds reference algorithms on benchmark problems. A theoretical analysis of gradient estimation error complements those experiments, supporting the rule as a computational proposal rather than establishing that brains implement it.
summary.tldr: A contrastive meta-learning rule estimates gradients from two runs while using locally available information and avoiding second derivatives.

title: A contrastive rule for meta-learning

abstract: Backpropagation (BP) is the most successful and widely used algorithm in deep learning. However, the computations required by BP are challenging to reconcile with known neurobiology. This difficulty has stimulated interest in more biologically plausible alternatives to BP. One such algorithm is the inference learning algorithm (IL). IL trains predictive coding models of neural circuits and has achieved equal performance to BP on supervised and auto-associative tasks. In contrast to BP, however, the mathematical foundations of IL are not well-understood. Here, we develop a novel theoretical framework for IL. Our main result is that IL closely approximates an optimization method known as implicit stochastic gradient descent (implicit SGD), which is distinct from the explicit SGD implemented by BP. Our results further show how the standard implementation of IL can be altered to better approximate implicit SGD. Our novel implementation considerably improves the stability of IL across learning rates, which is consistent with our theory, as a key property of implicit SGD is its stability. We provide extensive simulation results that further support our theoretical interpretations and find IL achieves quicker convergence when trained with mini-batch size one while performing competitively with BP for larger mini-batches when combined with Adam.

This paper develops a framework for understanding what kind of optimization inference learning performs.

It closely approximates this method, which differs from the explicit stochastic gradient descent associated with backpropagation. These findings tie an alternative learning mechanism to an established optimization framework and use that connection to improve its behavior.
summary.tldr: A theoretical connection to implicit stochastic gradient descent explains inference learning and motivates a more stable implementation.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Inference Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are often categorized as either on-policy or off-policy depending on whether they use data from a target policy of interest or from a different behavior policy. In this paper, we study a subtle distinction between on-policy data and on-policy sampling in the context of the RL sub-problem of policy evaluation. We observe that on-policy sampling may fail to match the expected distribution of on-policy data after observing only a finite number of trajectories and this failure hinders data-efficient policy evaluation. Towards improved data-efficiency, we show how non-i.i.d., off-policy sampling can produce data that more closely matches the expected on-policy data distribution and consequently increases the accuracy of the Monte Carlo estimator for policy evaluation. We introduce a method called Robust On-Policy Sampling and demonstrate theoretically and empirically that it produces data that converges faster to the expected on-policy distribution compared to on-policy sampling. Empirically, we show that this faster convergence leads to lower mean squared error policy value estimates.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the value of a particular decision-making policy. A natural approach collects trajectories by following that policy directly. This paper highlights that a finite collection obtained this way may still represent the policy's expected data distribution poorly, reducing the accuracy of the resulting value estimate.

The authors distinguish the desired distribution of on-policy data from the act of sampling on-policy. They show how dependent, off-policy sampling can produce a collection that more closely matches the expected on-policy distribution. Their method, Robust On-Policy Sampling, uses this distinction to improve the data supplied to a Monte Carlo policy-value estimator.

Theoretical and empirical results show that the method's data converges faster to the expected on-policy distribution than data gathered through on-policy sampling. Experiments also show lower mean squared error in estimated policy values. The result makes the finite dataset itself central to sampling design: following the target policy is one way to gather data, but a different sampling process can better represent its expected behavior within the observed sample.
summary.tldr: Robust On-Policy Sampling uses dependent off-policy sampling to better match target-policy data distributions and improve value estimates.

title: Robust On-Policy Sampling for Data-Efficient Policy Evaluation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Label efficiency has become an increasingly important objective in deep learning applications. Active learning aims to reduce the number of labeled examples needed to train deep networks, but the empirical performance of active learning algorithms can vary dramatically across datasets and applications. It is difficult to know in advance which active learning strategy will perform well or best in a given application. To address this, we propose the first adaptive algorithm selection strategy for deep active learning. For any unlabeled dataset, our (meta) algorithm TAILOR (Thompson ActIve Learning algORithm selection) iteratively and adaptively chooses among a set of candidate active learning algorithms. TAILOR uses novel reward functions aimed at gathering class-balanced examples. Extensive experiments in multi-class and multi-label applications demonstrate TAILOR's effectiveness in achieving accuracy comparable or better than that of the best of the candidate algorithms. Our implementation of TAILOR is open-sourced at https://github.com/jifanz/TAILOR.

paragraphs: Active learning tries to reduce labeling work by choosing which examples should receive labels. Its practical difficulty is that a strategy that works well on one dataset can perform poorly on another. This paper addresses that selection problem: instead of requiring someone to choose a single active learning algorithm in advance, it proposes a method that adapts the choice during learning.

The method, TAILOR, operates above a collection of candidate active learning algorithms. At successive steps, it chooses which candidate to use. Its reward functions encourage collecting examples with a more balanced distribution across classes. This connects algorithm selection to a concrete concern in imbalanced datasets: the examples gathered for training may otherwise represent some classes much better than others.

Experiments cover both multi-class and multi-label applications. In those evaluations, TAILOR achieves accuracy comparable to or better than the best candidate algorithm. The finding supports adaptive selection as a practical response to uncertainty about which strategy will work, rather than establishing that one candidate is universally strongest.
summary.tldr: TAILOR adaptively selects active learning algorithms using rewards that encourage class balance, matching or improving on the best candidate in the reported experiments.

title: Algorithm Selection for Deep Active Learning with Imbalanced Datasets

abstract: We present PrimDiffusion, the first diffusion-based framework for 3D human generation. Devising diffusion models for 3D human generation is difficult due to the intensive computational cost of 3D representations and the articulated topology of 3D humans. To tackle these challenges, our key insight is operating the denoising diffusion process directly on a set of volumetric primitives, which models the human body as a number of small volumes with radiance and kinematic information. This volumetric primitives representation marries the capacity of volumetric representations with the efficiency of primitive-based rendering. Our PrimDiffusion framework has three appealing properties: **1)** compact and expressive parameter space for the diffusion model, **2)** flexible representation that incorporates human prior, and **3)** decoder-free rendering for efficient novel-view and novel-pose synthesis. Extensive experiments validate that PrimDiffusion outperforms state-of-the-art methods in 3D human generation. Notably, compared to GAN-based methods, our PrimDiffusion supports real-time rendering of high-quality 3D humans at a resolution of $512\times512$ once the denoising process is done. We also demonstrate the flexibility of our framework on training-free conditional generation such as texture transfer and 3D inpainting.

paragraphs: Generating three-dimensional humans with diffusion models is challenging because 3D representations can be computationally expensive and human bodies have articulated structure. PrimDiffusion addresses these issues through its representation: it models the body as a collection of small volumes carrying radiance and kinematic information, then performs diffusion directly over those volumetric primitives.

This design provides a compact but expressive parameter space and incorporates prior structure about humans. It also supports rendering without a decoder, enabling synthesis from new viewpoints and in new poses. The approach combines the representational capacity of volumes with the rendering efficiency associated with primitives, making representation design central to both generation and subsequent use.

Experiments report better 3D human generation than the compared state-of-the-art methods. After denoising is complete, the generated humans can be rendered in real time at 512 by 512 resolution; the real-time claim applies to rendering after generation. The authors also demonstrate conditional generation without additional training, including texture transfer and 3D inpainting, illustrating the flexibility of the representation.
summary.tldr: PrimDiffusion generates 3D humans through volumetric primitives, enabling flexible manipulation and real-time rendering after denoising.

title: PrimDiffusion: Volumetric Primitives Diffusion for 3D Human Generation

abstract: The hippocampus plays a critical role in learning, memory, and spatial representation, processes that depend on the NMDA receptor (NMDAR). Inspired by recent findings that compare deep learning models to the hippocampus, we propose a new nonlinear activation function that mimics NMDAR dynamics. NMDAR-like nonlinearity shifts short-term working memory into long-term reference memory in transformers, thus enhancing a process that is similar to memory consolidation in the mammalian brain. We design a navigation task assessing these two memory functions and show that manipulating the activation function (i.e., mimicking the Mg$^{2+}$-gating of NMDAR) disrupts long-term memory processes. Our experiments suggest that place cell-like functions and reference memory reside in the feed-forward network layer of transformers and that nonlinearity drives these processes. We discuss the role of NMDAR-like nonlinearity in establishing this striking resemblance between transformer architecture and hippocampal spatial representation.

This paper investigates a computational analogy by designing a transformer activation function inspired by receptor dynamics. This is evidence for a proposed correspondence between model components and hippocampal spatial-memory functions. The study uses that correspondence to explore memory consolidation computationally; the stated findings remain an experimentally supported analogy between the transformer and biological memory mechanisms.
summary.tldr: An NMDA-receptor-inspired activation gives transformers memory behavior resembling consolidation, with navigation experiments linking nonlinearity to long-term reference memory.

title: Transformer as a hippocampal memory consolidation model based on NMDAR-inspired nonlinearity

abstract: Reward functions are difficult to design and often hard to align with human intent. Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms address these problems by learning reward functions from human feedback. However, the majority of preference-based RL methods na\"ively combine supervised reward models with off-the-shelf RL algorithms. Contemporary approaches have sought to improve performance and query complexity by using larger and more complex reward architectures such as transformers. Instead of using highly complex architectures, we develop a new and parameter-efficient algorithm, Inverse Preference Learning (IPL), specifically designed for learning from offline preference data. Our key insight is that for a fixed policy, the $Q$-function encodes all information about the reward function, effectively making them interchangeable. Using this insight, we completely eliminate the need for a learned reward function. Our resulting algorithm is simpler and more parameter-efficient. Across a suite of continuous control and robotics benchmarks, IPL attains competitive performance compared to more complex approaches that leverage transformer-based and non-Markovian reward functions while having fewer algorithmic hyperparameters and learned network parameters. Our code is publicly released.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses human feedback to address the difficulty of specifying rewards that reflect human intent. A common design first learns a reward model and then combines it with an existing reinforcement learning algorithm. Inverse Preference Learning develops a more integrated approach specifically for learning from offline preference data.

The key observation concerns a fixed policy: its Q-function contains all the information about the reward function, making the two interchangeable in the sense used by the method. IPL uses this relationship to eliminate a separately learned reward function. This reduces the learned machinery needed to turn preferences into a decision-making policy.

Across continuous-control and robotics benchmarks, IPL achieves performance competitive with more complex approaches using transformer-based and non-Markovian reward functions. It also uses fewer learned network parameters and algorithmic hyperparameters. The result suggests that, in the evaluated offline setting, exploiting the relationship between rewards and action values can provide an effective alternative to increasing reward-model complexity.
summary.tldr: Inverse Preference Learning uses the reward information encoded in a Q-function to learn from offline preferences without a separate reward model.

title: Inverse Preference Learning: Preference-based RL without a Reward Function

abstract: Over the last several years, there has been significant progress in developing neural solvers for the Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem and applying them to generative modelling. This new research field is justifiably fruitful as it is interconnected with the practically well-performing diffusion models and theoretically grounded entropic optimal transport (EOT). Still, the area lacks non-trivial tests allowing a researcher to understand how well the methods solve SB or its equivalent continuous EOT problem. We fill this gap and propose a novel way to create pairs of probability distributions for which the ground truth OT solution is known by the construction. Our methodology is generic and works for a wide range of OT formulations, in particular, it covers the EOT which is equivalent to SB (the main interest of our study). This development allows us to create continuous benchmark distributions with the known EOT and SB solutions on high-dimensional spaces such as spaces of images. As an illustration, we use these benchmark pairs to test how well existing neural EOT/SB solvers actually compute the EOT solution. Our code for constructing benchmark pairs under different setups is available at: https://github.com/ngushchin/EntropicOTBenchmark

paragraphs: Neural methods for the Schrödinger Bridge problem connect generative modeling with diffusion models and entropic optimal transport. Evaluating these methods requires knowing whether they solve the underlying mathematical problem accurately. The paper addresses a shortage of challenging test cases with known answers, which makes that question difficult to assess directly.

The authors introduce a construction that produces pairs of probability distributions together with their correct transport solution. Because the answer is known by construction, researchers can compare a solver's output against a reference solution. The approach applies to a broad range of optimal transport formulations, including the entropic formulation equivalent to the Schrödinger Bridge problem.

The construction supports continuous distributions in high-dimensional spaces, including image spaces. The authors use resulting distribution pairs to examine how accurately existing neural solvers recover the entropic transport solution. The contribution is therefore an evaluation method and benchmark construction framework: it makes mathematical solution quality directly testable in settings relevant to modern generative modeling.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs continuous transport benchmarks with known solutions so researchers can directly evaluate neural Schrödinger Bridge and entropic transport solvers.

title: Building the Bridge of Schrödinger: A Continuous Entropic Optimal Transport Benchmark

abstract: For each of $T$ time steps, $m$ experts report probability distributions over $n$ outcomes; we wish to learn to aggregate these forecasts in a way that attains a no-regret guarantee. We focus on the fundamental and practical aggregation method known as *logarithmic pooling* -- a weighted average of log odds -- which is in a certain sense the optimal choice of pooling method if one is interested in minimizing log loss (as we take to be our loss function). We consider the problem of learning the best set of parameters (i.e. expert weights) in an online adversarial setting. We assume (by necessity) that the adversarial choices of outcomes and forecasts are consistent, in the sense that experts report calibrated forecasts. Imposing this constraint creates a (to our knowledge) novel semi-adversarial setting in which the adversary retains a large amount of flexibility. In this setting, we present an algorithm based on online mirror descent that learns expert weights in a way that attains $O(\sqrt{T} \log T)$ expected regret as compared with the best weights in hindsight.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine repeated probability forecasts from multiple experts. At each time step, experts provide distributions over possible outcomes, and the learner chooses how much weight to give each expert. The aggregation rule is logarithmic pooling, which combines forecasts through weighted log odds and is evaluated using logarithmic loss.

The aim is to learn weights whose cumulative loss stays close to that of the best fixed weights chosen after all outcomes are known. The setting permits adversarial forecasts and outcomes, but imposes a necessary consistency condition: experts must report calibrated forecasts. This creates a semi-adversarial problem that retains substantial adversarial flexibility while restricting which sequences are allowed.

Using online mirror descent, the authors obtain expected regret of O(√T log T) over T rounds. Since this grows more slowly than T, the expected regret per round tends toward zero. The result establishes a no-regret guarantee for logarithmic pooling in the stated calibrated setting, despite the difficulty posed by unbounded losses.
summary.tldr: An online mirror-descent method learns logarithmic-pooling weights with sublinear expected regret under a calibration constraint on expert forecasts.

title: No-Regret Learning with Unbounded Losses: The Case of Logarithmic Pooling

abstract: This paper investigates the logistic bandit problem, a variant of the generalized linear bandit model that utilizes a logistic model to depict the feedback from an action. While most existing research focuses on the binary logistic bandit problem, the multinomial case, which considers more than two possible feedback values, offers increased practical relevance and adaptability for use in complex decision-making problems such as reinforcement learning. In this paper, we provide an algorithm that enjoys both statistical and computational efficiency for the logistic bandit problem. In the binary case, our method improves the state-of-the-art binary logistic bandit method by reducing the per-round computation cost from $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ with respect to the time horizon $T$, while still preserving the minimax optimal guarantee up to logarithmic factors. In the multinomial case, with $K+1$ potential feedback values, our algorithm achieves an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ regret bound with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ computational cost per round. The result not only improves the $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{\kappa T})$ bound for the best-known tractable algorithm—where the large constant $\kappa$ increases exponentially with the diameter of the parameter domain—but also reduces the $\mathcal{O}(T)$ computational complexity demanded by the previous method.

While most existing research focuses on the binary logistic bandit problem, the multinomial case, which considers more than two possible feedback values, offers increased practical relevance and adaptability for use in complex decision-making problems such as reinforcement learning. In this paper, we provide an algorithm that enjoys both statistical and computational efficiency for the logistic bandit problem. In the binary case, our method improves the state-of-the-art binary logistic bandit method by reducing the per-round computation cost from $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ with respect to the time horizon $T$, while still preserving the minimax optimal guarantee up to logarithmic factors. In the multinomial case, with $K+1$ potential feedback values, our algorithm achieves an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ regret bound with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ computational cost per round. The result not only improves the $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{\kappa T})$ bound for the best-known tractable algorithm—where the large constant $\kappa$ increases exponentially with the diameter of the parameter domain—but also reduces the $\mathcal{O}(T)$ computational complexity demanded by the previous method.

paragraphs: Logistic bandits model sequential decisions in which an action produces feedback governed by a logistic model. The binary version has two possible feedback outcomes, while the multinomial version supports more than two. This paper develops an algorithm that improves the balance between learning performance and the computation required at each decision round.

For binary feedback, the algorithm reduces per-round computation from logarithmic in the time horizon T to constant with respect to T. It retains a minimax-optimal guarantee up to logarithmic factors. This means its stated computational cost does not grow with the length of the interaction in the way the compared method’s cost does.

For K+1 feedback outcomes, the regret bound scales as K times the square root of T, ignoring logarithmic factors. This removes a square-root dependence on a potentially large parameter-domain constant from the previous tractable bound. Per-round computation also becomes constant with respect to T, compared with the previous linear dependence. These are simultaneous improvements in the statistical guarantee and horizon-dependent computational cost.
summary.tldr: A logistic bandit algorithm improves multinomial regret guarantees while keeping per-round computation constant with respect to the time horizon.

title: Online (Multinomial) Logistic Bandit: Improved Regret and Constant Computation Cost

abstract: In this work, we reveal a strong implicit bias of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) that drives overly expressive networks to much simpler subnetworks, thereby dramatically reducing the number of independent parameters, and improving generalization. To reveal this bias, we identify _invariant sets_, or subsets of parameter space that remain unmodified by SGD. We focus on two classes of invariant sets that correspond to simpler (sparse or low-rank) subnetworks and commonly appear in modern architectures. Our analysis uncovers that SGD exhibits a property of _stochastic attractivity_ towards these simpler invariant sets. We establish a sufficient condition for stochastic attractivity based on a competition between the loss landscape's curvature around the invariant set and the noise introduced by stochastic gradients. Remarkably, we find that an increased level of noise strengthens attractivity, leading to the emergence of attractive invariant sets associated with saddle-points or local maxima of the train loss. We observe empirically the existence of attractive invariant sets in trained deep neural networks, implying that SGD dynamics often collapses to simple subnetworks with either vanishing or redundant neurons. We further demonstrate how this simplifying process of _stochastic collapse_ benefits generalization in a linear teacher-student framework. Finally, through this analysis, we mechanistically explain why early training with large learning rates for extended periods benefits subsequent generalization.

The findings link gradient noise, reduced effective model complexity, and learning behavior through a specific dynamical account.
summary.tldr: Gradient noise can attract SGD toward simpler subnetworks, providing a mechanism for reduced complexity and improved generalization.

title: Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks

abstract: Informational parsimony provides a useful inductive bias for learning representations that achieve better generalization by being robust to noise and spurious correlations. We propose *information gating* as a way to learn parsimonious representations that identify the minimal information required for a task. When gating information, we can learn to reveal as little information as possible so that a task remains solvable, or hide as little information as possible so that a task becomes unsolvable. We gate information using a differentiable parameterization of the signal-to-noise ratio, which can be applied to arbitrary values in a network, e.g., erasing pixels at the input layer or activations in some intermediate layer. When gating at the input layer, our models learn which visual cues matter for a given task. When gating intermediate layers, our models learn which activations are needed for subsequent stages of computation. We call our approach *InfoGating*. We apply InfoGating to various objectives such as multi-step forward and inverse dynamics models, Q-learning, and behavior cloning, highlighting how InfoGating can naturally help in discarding information not relevant for control. Results show that learning to identify and use minimal information can improve generalization in downstream tasks. Policies based on InfoGating are considerably more robust to irrelevant visual features, leading to improved pretraining and finetuning of RL models.

paragraphs: A control policy can become unreliable when it depends on visual details that are irrelevant to its task. InfoGating addresses this by learning which information is needed to solve the task. It explores two complementary objectives: revealing as little information as possible while keeping the task solvable, or hiding as little as possible to make it unsolvable.

The method controls information through a differentiable signal-to-noise parameterization. Applied to input pixels, it learns which visual cues matter; applied inside a network, it learns which activations later computations need. This makes the same information-selection idea applicable at different stages of a model rather than restricting it to preprocessing observations.

The authors apply InfoGating to forward and inverse dynamics objectives, Q-learning, and behavior cloning. Their results show that learning to identify and use minimal information can improve generalization on downstream tasks. Policies using InfoGating are reported to be considerably more robust to irrelevant visual features, with improvements in reinforcement learning pretraining and finetuning. The findings support information parsimony as a useful bias for control representations.
summary.tldr: InfoGating learns which information a control task needs, improving robustness to irrelevant visual features and downstream generalization.

title: Ignorance is Bliss: Robust Control via Information Gating

abstract: The theory underlying robust distributed learning algorithms, designed to resist adversarial machines, matches empirical observations when data is homogeneous. Under data heterogeneity however, which is the norm in practical scenarios, established lower bounds on the learning error are essentially vacuous and greatly mismatch empirical observations. This is because the heterogeneity model considered is too restrictive and does not cover basic learning tasks such as least-squares regression. We consider in this paper a more realistic heterogeneity model, namely $(G,B)$-gradient dissimilarity, and show that it covers a larger class of learning problems than existing theory. Notably, we show that the breakdown point under heterogeneity is lower than the classical fraction $\frac{1}{2}$. We also prove a new lower bound on the learning error of any distributed learning algorithm. We derive a matching upper bound for a robust variant of distributed gradient descent, and empirically show that our analysis reduces the gap between theory and practice.
