paragraphs: Robust distributed learning aims to train successfully even when some participating machines behave adversarially. Existing theory aligns with observations when machines have homogeneous data, but becomes much less informative when their data differ. The authors trace this gap to restrictive heterogeneity assumptions that exclude even basic problems such as least-squares regression.

The paper instead adopts a model called (G,B)-gradient dissimilarity, which covers a broader class of learning problems. Under this model, the authors show that the breakdown point is below the classical one-half fraction. In other words, data heterogeneity lowers the threshold of adversarial participation beyond which the learning guarantee breaks down.

They also prove a lower bound on the learning error achievable by any distributed learning algorithm and obtain a matching upper bound for a robust form of distributed gradient descent. This match identifies a tight error characterization within the model. Empirical results show that the analysis brings theoretical predictions closer to practice, clarifying both achievable performance and the effects of heterogeneity.
summary.tldr: A broader heterogeneity model yields tight distributed-learning error bounds and an adversarial breakdown threshold below one half.

title: Robust Distributed Learning: Tight Error Bounds and Breakdown Point under Data Heterogeneity

abstract: Sequence memory is an essential attribute of natural and artificial intelligence that enables agents to encode, store, and retrieve complex sequences of stimuli and actions. Computational models of sequence memory have been proposed where recurrent Hopfield-like neural networks are trained with temporally asymmetric Hebbian rules. However, these networks suffer from limited sequence capacity (maximal length of the stored sequence) due to interference between the memories. Inspired by recent work on Dense Associative Memories, we expand the sequence capacity of these models by introducing a nonlinear interaction term, enhancing separation between the patterns. We derive novel scaling laws for sequence capacity with respect to network size, significantly outperforming existing scaling laws for models based on traditional Hopfield networks, and verify these theoretical results with numerical simulation. Moreover, we introduce a generalized pseudoinverse rule to recall sequences of highly correlated patterns. Finally, we extend this model to store sequences with variable timing between states' transitions and describe a biologically-plausible implementation, with connections to motor neuroscience.

paragraphs: Sequence memory requires a system to store patterns together with the order in which they should be recalled. Recurrent Hopfield-like networks can learn such sequences through temporally asymmetric learning rules, but interference between memories limits the sequence length they can hold. This paper changes the interactions within these networks to reduce that interference.

Inspired by dense associative memories, the authors introduce a nonlinear interaction term that increases separation between patterns. They derive new laws describing how maximum sequence length scales with network size and verify them numerically. These laws improve substantially on the existing scaling results for models based on traditional Hopfield networks.

The paper also introduces a generalized pseudoinverse learning rule for recalling sequences whose patterns are highly correlated. A further extension allows different amounts of time between successive states, expanding the model beyond a fixed transition rhythm. Together with a proposed biologically plausible implementation and connections to motor neuroscience, these contributions address sequence length, pattern similarity, and timing as distinct requirements of sequence memory.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear interactions expand Hopfield-like sequence capacity, with additional mechanisms for correlated patterns and variable transition timing.

title: Long Sequence Hopfield Memory

abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to enhancing explainable image retrieval, particularly in situations where a fine-tuning set is unavailable. The widely-used SPatial verification (SP) method, despite its efficacy, relies on a spatial model and the hypothesis-testing strategy for instance recognition, leading to inherent limitations, including the assumption of planar structures and neglect of topological relations among features. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a pioneering technique that replaces the spatial model with a topological one within the RANSAC process. We propose bio-inspired saccade and fovea functions to verify the topological consistency among features, effectively circumventing the issues associated with SP's spatial model. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms SP, achieving state-of-the-art performance in non-fine-tuning retrieval. Furthermore, our approach can enhance performance when used in conjunction with fine-tuned features. Importantly, our method retains high explainability and is lightweight, offering a practical and adaptable solution for a variety of real-world applications.

paragraphs: Image retrieval often needs to verify whether matching features correspond to the same instance. Conventional spatial verification uses a spatial model within a hypothesis-testing process, bringing assumptions such as planar structure and overlooking topological relationships among features. This paper develops an alternative intended especially for cases without a fine-tuning dataset.

The method replaces the spatial model inside RANSAC with a topological model. Bio-inspired saccade and fovea functions check whether relationships among features are topologically consistent. This changes the basis of verification so that feature relationships can contribute without relying on the spatial model's planar assumptions.

Experiments show a significant improvement over spatial verification and state-of-the-art retrieval performance in the setting without fine-tuning. The approach can also improve retrieval when paired with features that have been fine-tuned. The authors describe it as lightweight and highly explainable, making the verification procedure itself an important part of the contribution. Its results support topological consistency as a practical source of evidence for instance matching across the evaluated retrieval settings.
summary.tldr: Topological RANSAC verifies feature relationships to improve explainable image retrieval, including when no fine-tuning set is available.

title: Topological RANSAC for instance verification and retrieval without fine-tuning

abstract: Robotic perception requires the modeling of both 3D geometry and semantics. Existing methods typically focus on estimating 3D bounding boxes, neglecting finer geometric details and struggling to handle general, out-of-vocabulary objects. 3D occupancy prediction, which estimates the detailed occupancy states and semantics of a scene, is an emerging task to overcome these limitations.To support 3D occupancy prediction, we develop a label generation pipeline that produces dense, visibility-aware labels for any given scene. This pipeline comprises three stages: voxel densification, occlusion reasoning, and image-guided voxel refinement. We establish two benchmarks, derived from the Waymo Open Dataset and the nuScenes Dataset, namely Occ3D-Waymo and Occ3D-nuScenes benchmarks. Furthermore, we provide an extensive analysis of the proposed dataset with various baseline models. Lastly, we propose a new model, dubbed Coarse-to-Fine Occupancy (CTF-Occ) network, which demonstrates superior performance on the Occ3D benchmarks.The code, data, and benchmarks are released at \url{https://tsinghua-mars-lab.github.io/Occ3D/}.

paragraphs: Robotic perception needs to describe both the shape of a scene and what its contents mean. Three-dimensional bounding boxes provide limited geometric detail and struggle with objects outside a predefined vocabulary. Occupancy prediction instead estimates detailed occupied-space states and their semantics, motivating datasets that support this richer description of the environment.

Occ3D introduces a pipeline for generating dense labels that account for visibility. Its three stages are voxel densification, occlusion reasoning, and refinement guided by images. Together, these stages address how to construct detailed scene labels while reasoning about which parts of the environment are visible or obscured.

The authors use the pipeline to establish Occ3D-Waymo and Occ3D-nuScenes from the corresponding driving datasets. They analyze performance with several baseline models and introduce a Coarse-to-Fine Occupancy network, CTF-Occ, which performs better on the proposed benchmarks. The contribution includes both the infrastructure for evaluating detailed occupancy prediction and a model demonstrating improved results within that evaluation setting.
summary.tldr: Occ3D provides dense, visibility-aware occupancy benchmarks and a coarse-to-fine model for detailed three-dimensional driving-scene perception.

title: Occ3D: A Large-Scale 3D Occupancy Prediction Benchmark for Autonomous Driving

abstract: In recent years, domains such as natural language processing and image recognition have popularized the paradigm of using large datasets to pretrain representations that can be effectively transferred to downstream tasks. In this work we evaluate how such a paradigm should be done in imitation learning, where both pretraining and finetuning data are trajectories collected by experts interacting with an unknown environment. Namely, we consider a setting where the pretraining corpus consists of multitask demonstrations and the task for each demonstration is set by an unobserved latent context variable. The goal is to use the pretraining corpus to learn a low dimensional representation of the high dimensional (e.g., visual) observation space which can be transferred to a novel context for finetuning on a limited dataset of demonstrations. Among a variety of possible pretraining objectives, we argue that inverse dynamics modeling -- i.e., predicting an action given the observations appearing before and after it in the demonstration -- is well-suited to this setting. We provide empirical evidence of this claim through evaluations on a variety of simulated visuomotor manipulation problems. While previous work has attempted various theoretical explanations regarding the benefit of inverse dynamics modeling, we find that these arguments are insufficient to explain the empirical advantages often observed in our settings, and so we derive a novel analysis using a simple but general environment model.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to pretrain representations for imitation learning from expert demonstrations. Its setting includes demonstrations of multiple tasks, with each task determined by an unobserved context variable. The aim is to compress high-dimensional observations into a representation that can transfer to a new context using only a limited set of demonstrations.

The authors argue for inverse dynamics as a pretraining objective: given the observations immediately before and after an action, predict that action. This connects representation learning directly to the actions within expert trajectories. Both pretraining and subsequent fine-tuning use demonstrations collected through interaction with an unknown environment.

Experiments on several simulated visuomotor manipulation problems provide evidence that this objective is well suited to the setting. The authors also examine existing theoretical accounts and find them insufficient to explain the empirical advantages they observe. They develop a new analysis using a simple but general environment model, pairing evidence about transfer performance with a revised explanation of why inverse dynamics can help.
summary.tldr: Predicting actions between observations provides useful pretrained representations for transferring imitation learning across latent task contexts.

title: Inverse Dynamics Pretraining Learns Good Representations for Multitask Imitation

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) is an approach that enables RL agents to learn from preference, which is particularly useful when formulating a reward function is challenging. Existing PbRL methods generally involve a two-step procedure: they first learn a reward model based on given preference data and then employ off-the-shelf reinforcement learning algorithms using the learned reward model. However, obtaining an accurate reward model solely from preference information, especially when the preference is from human teachers, can be difficult. Instead, we propose a PbRL algorithm that directly learns from preference without requiring any reward modeling. To achieve this, we adopt a contrastive learning framework to design a novel policy scoring metric that assigns a high score to policies that align with the given preferences. We apply our algorithm to offline RL tasks with actual human preference labels and show that our algorithm outperforms or is on par with the existing PbRL methods. Notably, on high-dimensional control tasks, our algorithm surpasses offline RL methods that learn with ground-truth reward information. Finally, we show that our algorithm can be successfully applied to fine-tune large language models.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning lets an agent learn from judgments about which behavior is better when writing a reward function is difficult. A common approach first converts those judgments into a learned reward model, then optimizes a policy using that model. This paper targets the difficulty of recovering accurate rewards from preferences, especially judgments supplied by people.

The proposed algorithm learns a policy directly from preference data. It uses a contrastive-learning framework to construct a policy score, assigning higher scores to policies that agree with the supplied preferences. This removes the separate reward-modeling stage and makes preference agreement the basis for assessing candidate behavior.

On offline reinforcement-learning tasks with actual human preference labels, the algorithm matches or exceeds the evaluated preference-based methods. In the reported high-dimensional control tasks, it also outperforms offline methods supplied with ground-truth rewards. The authors additionally demonstrate language-model fine-tuning. Together, these findings show that the direct approach can work across control and language settings, without establishing that preferences always outperform explicit reward information.
summary.tldr: A contrastive policy-scoring method learns directly from preferences and performs competitively in offline control and language-model fine-tuning.

title: Direct Preference-based Policy Optimization without Reward Modeling

abstract: We introduce Cap3D, an automatic approach for generating descriptive text for 3D objects. This approach utilizes pretrained models from image captioning, image-text alignment, and LLM to consolidate captions from multiple views of a 3D asset, completely side-stepping the time-consuming and costly process of manual annotation. We apply Cap3D to the recently introduced large-scale 3D dataset, Objaverse, resulting in 660k 3D-text pairs. Our evaluation, conducted using 41k human annotations from the same dataset, demonstrates that Cap3D surpasses human-authored descriptions in terms of quality, cost, and speed. Through effective prompt engineering, Cap3D rivals human performance in generating geometric descriptions on 17k collected annotations from the ABO dataset. Finally, we finetune Text-to-3D models on Cap3D and human captions, and show Cap3D outperforms; and benchmark the SOTA including Point·E, Shape·E, and DreamFusion.

paragraphs: Describing large collections of 3D objects manually is expensive and slow. Cap3D automates that process by combining pretrained image-captioning models, image-text alignment models, and a language model. It consolidates captions from multiple views of each object into descriptive text, using existing model capabilities to avoid manual annotation of the collection.

Applied to Objaverse, the approach produces 660,000 pairs of 3D objects and text. An evaluation using 41,000 human annotations from that dataset finds Cap3D superior to human-authored descriptions in quality, cost, and speed. A separate evaluation using 17,000 ABO annotations finds that, with effective prompting, it rivals human performance on geometric descriptions.

The paper also tests the captions as training material for text-to-3D models. Fine-tuning with Cap3D captions outperforms fine-tuning with human captions in the reported evaluation, and the authors benchmark Point·E, Shape·E, and DreamFusion. These findings connect automatic caption generation to downstream modeling value: the generated text is evaluated both as a description of an object and as a resource for learning to generate 3D content.
summary.tldr: Cap3D combines pretrained models to generate large-scale 3D captions that perform well in human comparisons and text-to-3D training.

title: Scalable 3D Captioning with Pretrained Models

abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning (TKGR) is the process of utilizing temporal information to capture complex relations within a Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) to infer new knowledge. Conventional methods in TKGR typically depend on deep learning algorithms or temporal logical rules. However, deep learning-based TKGRs often lack interpretability, whereas rule-based TKGRs struggle to effectively learn temporal rules that capture temporal patterns. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated extensive knowledge and remarkable proficiency in temporal reasoning. Consequently, the employment of LLMs for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning (TKGR) has sparked increasing interest among researchers. Nonetheless, LLMs are known to function as black boxes, making it challenging to comprehend their reasoning process. Additionally, due to the resource-intensive nature of fine-tuning, promptly updating LLMs to integrate evolving knowledge within TKGs for reasoning is impractical. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose a Large Language Models-guided Dynamic Adaptation (LLM-DA) method for reasoning on TKGs. Specifically, LLM-DA harnesses the capabilities of LLMs to analyze historical data and extract temporal logical rules. These rules unveil temporal patterns and facilitate interpretable reasoning. To account for the evolving nature of TKGs, a dynamic adaptation strategy is proposed to update the LLM-generated rules with the latest events. This ensures that the extracted rules always incorporate the most recent knowledge and better generalize to the predictions on future events. Experimental results show that without the need of fine-tuning, LLM-DA significantly improves the accuracy of reasoning over several common datasets, providing a robust framework for TKGR tasks.

To account for the evolving nature of TKGs, a dynamic adaptation strategy is proposed to update the LLM-generated rules with the latest events. This ensures that the extracted rules always incorporate the most recent knowledge and better generalize to the predictions on future events. Experimental results show that without the need of fine-tuning, LLM-DA significantly improves the accuracy of reasoning over several common datasets, providing a robust framework for TKGR tasks.

paragraphs: Temporal knowledge graph reasoning uses time-dependent relationships to infer new knowledge. The paper describes a tension between deep learning methods, whose reasoning can be difficult to interpret, and rule-based methods, which can struggle to learn useful temporal patterns. Language models offer temporal reasoning capabilities, but directly updating them through fine-tuning is resource intensive.

LLM-DA uses a language model to analyze historical data and extract temporal logical rules. These rules make the patterns used for reasoning explicit. The method then dynamically updates the generated rules using recent events, allowing evolving knowledge to enter the reasoning process without repeatedly fine-tuning the language model.

This separates the extraction of temporal knowledge from its continuing adaptation as the graph changes. The authors report significant accuracy improvements on several common datasets without fine-tuning. The findings support using language models to help construct interpretable rules and maintaining those rules as new events arrive, with the aim of improving predictions about future events in changing knowledge graphs.
summary.tldr: LLM-DA extracts temporal rules with language models and updates those rules with new events to improve knowledge graph reasoning without fine-tuning.

title: Large Language Models-guided Dynamic Adaptation for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning

abstract: The sampling problem under local differential privacy has recently been studied with potential applications to generative models, but a fundamental analysis of its privacy-utility trade-off (PUT) remains incomplete. In this work, we define the fundamental PUT of private sampling in the minimax sense, using the $f$-divergence between original and sampling distributions as the utility measure. We characterize the exact PUT for both finite and continuous data spaces under some mild conditions on the data distributions, and propose sampling mechanisms that are universally optimal for all $f$-divergences. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the superiority of our mechanisms over baselines, in terms of theoretical utilities for finite data space and of empirical utilities for continuous data space.

paragraphs: Private sampling seeks to produce samples while satisfying local differential privacy, creating a trade-off between privacy and fidelity to the original distribution. The paper gives this trade-off a precise minimax formulation. In this formulation, utility is measured by an f-divergence, a family of measures for differences between probability distributions.

The authors characterize the exact privacy-utility trade-off for both finite and continuous data spaces under mild conditions on the distributions. They also construct sampling mechanisms that are optimal across all f-divergences within the stated setting. This makes the result broader than an optimization for just one selected measure of distributional discrepancy, while retaining the assumptions of the analysis.

Numerical experiments compare the proposed mechanisms with baselines. The reported advantages concern theoretical utility measures for finite spaces and empirical utility measures for continuous spaces. Together, the analysis and experiments connect a fundamental performance target with mechanisms designed to attain it. The work also identifies private sampling as potentially relevant to generative models, without making an application-specific performance claim.
summary.tldr: Under stated distributional conditions, the paper derives exact minimax privacy-utility trade-offs and sampling mechanisms optimal across all f-divergences.

title: Exactly Minimax-Optimal Locally Differentially Private Sampling

abstract: Human Mesh Recovery (HMR) is the task of estimating a parameterized 3D human mesh from an image. There is a kind of methods first training a regression model for this problem, then further optimizing the pretrained regression model for any specific sample individually at test time. However, the pretrained model may not provide an ideal optimization starting point for the test-time optimization. Inspired by meta-learning, we incorporate the test-time optimization into training, performing a step of test-time optimization for each sample in the training batch before really conducting the training optimization over all the training samples. In this way, we obtain a meta-model, the meta-parameter of which is friendly to the test-time optimization. At test time, after several test-time optimization steps starting from the meta-parameter, we obtain much higher HMR accuracy than the test-time optimization starting from the simply pretrained regression model. Furthermore, we find test-time HMR objectives are different from training-time objectives, which reduces the effectiveness of the learning of the meta-model. To solve this problem, we propose a dual-network architecture that unifies the training-time and test-time objectives. Our method, armed with meta-learning and the dual networks, outperforms state-of-the-art regression-based and optimization-based HMR approaches, as validated by the extensive experiments. The codes are available at https://github.com/fmx789/Meta-HMR.

paragraphs: Human mesh recovery estimates a parameterized three-dimensional body from an image. Some methods train a regression model and then optimize it separately for each test example. The paper identifies a mismatch in that workflow: a model trained to predict well immediately may provide a poor starting point for the optimization that follows.

The authors incorporate that later optimization into training. For each sample in a training batch, they take a sample-specific optimization step before performing the overall training update. This meta-learning procedure learns parameters intended to support subsequent adaptation. They also introduce a dual-network architecture to unify training and test-time objectives, whose differences otherwise weaken the meta-learning process.

Experiments also report improvements over state-of-the-art regression-based and optimization-based approaches. The findings support training the initialization around its eventual use, while aligning the objectives used to learn and adapt it.
summary.tldr: Training through sample-specific optimization and aligning objectives with dual networks improves the starting point for test-time human mesh recovery.

title: Incorporating Test-Time Optimization into Training with Dual Networks for Human Mesh Recovery

abstract: Current state-of-the-art methods for differentially private model training are based on matrix factorization techniques. However, these methods suffer from high computational overhead because they require numerically solving a demanding optimization problem to determine an approximately optimal factorization prior to the actual model training. In this work, we present a new matrix factorization approach, BSR, which overcomes this computational bottleneck. By exploiting properties of the standard matrix square root, BSR allows to efficiently handle also large-scale problems. For the key scenario of stochastic gradient descent with momentum and weight decay, we even derive analytical expressions for BSR that render the computational overhead negligible. We prove bounds on the approximation quality that hold both in the centralized and in the federated learning setting. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that models trained using BSR perform on par with the best existing methods, while completely avoiding their computational overhead.

paragraphs: Some leading approaches to differentially private training require a matrix factorization before model training can begin. Finding a sufficiently good factorization involves a demanding numerical optimization problem. This preparation can impose substantial computational costs, even before accounting for the work of actually learning the model.

The paper introduces BSR, a factorization approach that uses properties of the standard matrix square root to avoid that bottleneck. It is designed to handle large problems efficiently. For stochastic gradient descent with momentum and weight decay, the authors derive analytical expressions, making the additional preparation cost negligible in this particular training setting.

The contribution includes bounds on approximation quality for both centralized and federated learning. These bounds provide theoretical support for replacing the expensive factorization procedure. Numerical experiments find that BSR-trained models perform comparably to the strongest existing methods while avoiding their factorization overhead. The stated benefit is therefore maintaining competitive model performance with much cheaper preparation; it does not mean that the underlying model training itself becomes computationally free.
summary.tldr: BSR makes matrix factorization for private model training inexpensive while retaining performance comparable to leading methods.

title: Banded Square Root Matrix Factorization for Differentially Private Model Training

abstract: Data-driven inference of the generative dynamics underlying a set of observed time series is of growing interest in machine learning and the natural sciences. In neuroscience, such methods promise to alleviate the need to handcraft models based on biophysical principles and allow to automatize the inference of inter-individual differences in brain dynamics. Recent breakthroughs in training techniques for state space models (SSMs) specifically geared toward dynamical systems (DS) reconstruction (DSR) enable to recover the underlying system including its geometrical (attractor) and long-term statistical invariants from even short time series. These techniques are based on control-theoretic ideas, like modern variants of teacher forcing (TF), to ensure stable loss gradient propagation while training. However, as it currently stands, these techniques are not directly applicable to data modalities where current observations depend on an entire history of previous states due to a signal’s filtering properties, as common in neuroscience (and physiology more generally). Prominent examples are the blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) or Ca$^{2+}$ imaging data. Such types of signals render the SSM's decoder model non-invertible, a requirement for previous TF-based methods.Here, exploiting the recent success of control techniques for training SSMs, we propose a novel algorithm that solves this problem and scales exceptionally well with model dimensionality and filter length. We demonstrate its efficiency in reconstructing dynamical systems, including their state space geometry and long-term temporal properties, from just short BOLD time series.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an underlying dynamical system from recorded brain signals. The goal goes beyond predicting the next observation: it includes reconstructing the geometry of the system’s behavior and its long-term statistical properties. Learning these dynamics directly from recordings could reduce the need to build brain models manually from biophysical principles.

A central obstacle is that some measurements combine information from many previous hidden states. Functional MRI’s BOLD signal and calcium imaging have this filtering behavior. As a result, a current observation cannot simply be inverted to recover the current state, which prevents direct application of earlier training methods based on teacher forcing.

The authors introduce a control-inspired algorithm that accommodates this obstacle while scaling well with both model dimensionality and filter length. They demonstrate reconstruction of state-space geometry and long-term temporal behavior from short BOLD time series. The contribution is therefore a way to train dynamical models when the measurement process spreads information across time, extending reconstruction methods to an important neuroimaging setting.
summary.tldr: A control-inspired training algorithm reconstructs underlying dynamics from short neuroimaging recordings whose measurements depend on a history of hidden states.

title: A scalable generative model for dynamical system reconstruction from neuroimaging data

abstract: The number of large language models (LLMs) with varying parameter scales and vocabularies is increasing. While they deliver powerful performance, they also face a set of common optimization needs to meet specific requirements or standards, such as instruction following or avoiding the output of sensitive information from the real world. However, how to reuse the fine-tuning outcomes of one model to other models to reduce training costs remains a challenge. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-model Control (CMC), a method that improves multiple LLMs in one-time training with a portable tiny language model. Specifically, we have observed that the logit shift before and after fine-tuning is remarkably similar across different models. Based on this insight, we incorporate a tiny language model with a minimal number of parameters. By training alongside a frozen template LLM, the tiny model gains the capability to alter the logits output by the LLMs. To make this tiny language model applicable to models with different vocabularies, we propose a novel token mapping strategy named PM-MinED. We have conducted extensive experiments on instruction tuning and unlearning tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of CMC. Our code is available at https://github.com/wujwyi/CMC

paragraphs: Many language models need similar behavioral adjustments, such as following instructions or avoiding sensitive information. Training each model separately repeats work, especially when models differ in size and vocabulary. Cross-model Control investigates whether a small trained component can carry an adjustment from one language model to others.

The approach starts from an observed similarity: fine-tuning produces remarkably similar shifts in output logits across different models. Logits are the scores that determine which tokens a model is likely to generate. The authors train a tiny language model alongside a frozen template model so that the small model learns to modify these scores. This component is intended to remain portable after that single training process.

Different vocabularies complicate applying the same controller to multiple models. The paper introduces PM-MinED, a token mapping strategy that supports this transfer. Experiments on instruction tuning and unlearning demonstrate the effectiveness of the overall method. The contribution is a way to reuse learned output adjustments across models, connecting an empirical similarity in fine-tuning behavior to a practical mechanism for reducing repeated training.
summary.tldr: Cross-model Control trains a tiny portable model to adjust multiple language models’ outputs, including across different vocabularies.

title: Cross-model Control: Improving Multiple Large Language Models in One-time Training

abstract: Consistency Models (CMs) have made significant progress in accelerating the generation of diffusion models. However, their application to high-resolution, text-conditioned image generation in the latent space remains unsatisfactory. In this paper, we identify three key flaws in the current design of Latent Consistency Models~(LCMs). We investigate the reasons behind these limitations and propose Phased Consistency Models (PCMs), which generalize the design space and address the identified limitations. Our evaluations demonstrate that PCMs outperform LCMs across 1--16 step generation settings. While PCMs are specifically designed for multi-step refinement, they achieve comparable 1-step generation results to previously state-of-the-art specifically designed 1-step methods. Furthermore, we show the methodology of PCMs is versatile and applicable to video generation, enabling us to train the state-of-the-art few-step text-to-video generator. Our code is available at https://github.com/G-U-N/Phased-Consistency-Model.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to accelerate generation from diffusion models, but applying them to high-resolution images guided by text in latent space remains challenging. This paper examines latent consistency models and identifies three flaws in their design. The authors investigate those problems and introduce Phased Consistency Models, or PCMs, as a broader design that addresses them.

PCMs are designed specifically for refinement across multiple generation steps. This makes performance over a range of step counts central to the proposal. In the reported evaluations, PCMs outperform latent consistency models from one through sixteen steps, showing improvements across both very short generation and settings that allow additional refinement.

Despite their emphasis on multiple steps, PCMs also achieve one-step results comparable to earlier state-of-the-art methods built specifically for one-step generation. The authors extend the methodology to video and report training a state-of-the-art few-step text-to-video generator. Together, these findings suggest that the proposed design supports effective refinement without sacrificing competitive one-step performance, and that its usefulness extends beyond still-image generation in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Phased Consistency Models improve evaluated one-to-sixteen-step image generation and extend to few-step text-to-video generation.

title: Phased Consistency Models

abstract: Co-crystallization is an accessible way to control physicochemical characteristics of organic crystals, which finds many biomedical applications. In this work, we present Generative Method for Co-crystal Design (GEMCODE), a novel pipeline for automated co-crystal screening based on the hybridization of deep generative models and evolutionary optimization for broader exploration of the target chemical space. GEMCODE enables fast *de novo* co-crystal design with target tabletability profiles, which is crucial for the development of pharmaceuticals. With a series of experimental studies highlighting validation and discovery cases, we show that GEMCODE is effective even under realistic computational constraints. Furthermore, we explore the potential of language models in generating co-crystals. Finally, we present numerous previously unknown co-crystals predicted by GEMCODE and discuss its potential in accelerating drug development.

paragraphs: Co-crystallization offers a way to modify the physical and chemical properties of organic crystals. This paper focuses on tabletability, a property important to pharmaceutical development. It introduces GEMCODE, an automated screening and design pipeline intended to generate new co-crystal candidates with desired tabletability profiles.

GEMCODE combines deep generative models with evolutionary optimization to explore the target chemical space more broadly. The generative and optimization components form a hybrid search process directed toward the desired material properties. This connects candidate creation with a specific pharmaceutical design objective, making the pipeline relevant to the search for crystals that can better meet tablet-manufacturing needs.

The authors report experimental studies covering validation and discovery cases, finding the approach effective under realistic computational constraints. They also investigate the potential of language models for co-crystal generation and present numerous previously unknown co-crystals predicted by GEMCODE. These predictions are proposed candidates, while accelerated drug development is discussed as a potential application. The work's stated contribution is an efficient route for exploring co-crystal designs with targeted properties.
summary.tldr: GEMCODE combines generative models and evolutionary optimization to propose co-crystals with targeted tabletability properties.

title: Hybrid Generative AI for De Novo Design of Co-Crystals with Enhanced Tabletability

abstract: Traditional unlearnable strategies have been proposed to prevent unauthorized users from training on the 2D image data. With more 3D point cloud data containing sensitivity information, unauthorized usage of this new type data has also become a serious concern. To address this, we propose the first integral unlearnable framework for 3D point clouds including two processes: (i) we propose an unlearnable data protection scheme, involving a class-wise setting established by a category-adaptive allocation strategy and multi-transformations assigned to samples; (ii) we propose a data restoration scheme that utilizes class-wise inverse matrix transformation, thus enabling authorized-only training for unlearnable data. This restoration process is a practical issue overlooked in most existing unlearnable literature, i.e., even authorized users struggle to gain knowledge from 3D unlearnable data. Both theoretical and empirical results (including 6 datasets, 16 models, and 2 tasks) demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed unlearnable framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/UnlearnablePC.

paragraphs: The paper addresses unauthorized training on 3D point-cloud data that may contain sensitive information. It proposes a framework that makes the distributed data unlearnable while also providing a restoration procedure for authorized use. This second part addresses a practical difficulty: protection is less useful if it also prevents intended users from learning from the data.

The protection scheme uses class-wise settings established through a category-adaptive allocation strategy, with multiple transformations assigned to samples. Restoration applies inverse matrix transformations at the class level. The two procedures are designed together so that transforming the data for protection is paired with a way to recover its usefulness for authorized training.

The authors support the framework with both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation across six datasets, sixteen models, and two tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed protection-and-restoration approach in the studied settings. The central contribution is treating controlled recovery as part of unlearnable-data design, alongside the goal of obstructing unauthorized learning from 3D point clouds.
summary.tldr: The framework protects 3D point clouds through class-wise transformations and restores their training usefulness through corresponding inverse transformations.

title: Unlearnable 3D Point Clouds: Class-wise Transformation Is All You Need

abstract: Multi-label active learning is a crucial yet challenging area in contemporary machine learning, often complicated by a large and sparse label space. This challenge is further exacerbated in active learning scenarios where labeling resources are constrained. Drawing inspiration from existing mixture of Bernoulli models, which efficiently compress the label space into a more manageable weight coefficient space by learning correlated Bernoulli components, we propose a novel model called Evidential Mixture Machines (EMM). Our model leverages mixture components derived from unsupervised learning in the label space and improves prediction accuracy by predicting weight coefficients following the evidential learning paradigm. These coefficients are aggregated as proxy pseudo counts to enhance component offset predictions. The evidential learning approach provides an uncertainty-aware connection between input features and the predicted coefficients and components. Additionally, our method combines evidential uncertainty with predicted label embedding covariances for active sample selection, creating a richer, multi-source uncertainty metric beyond traditional uncertainty scores. Experiments on synthetic datasets show the effectiveness of evidential uncertainty prediction and EMM's capability to capture label correlations through predicted components. Further testing on real-world datasets demonstrates improved performance compared to existing multi-label active learning methods.

paragraphs: In multi-label learning, an example can have several labels, and the space of possible combinations can be large and sparse. Active learning adds a resource constraint: the model must choose which examples are most useful to label. Evidential Mixture Machines address both prediction and selection by modeling relationships among labels together with uncertainty.

The method builds on mixtures of Bernoulli components, which represent correlated label patterns through a smaller space of mixture weights. Components are learned without supervision in the label space, while evidential learning connects input features to uncertain predictions of their weights. The predicted coefficients are also combined into proxy pseudo counts to improve component offset predictions.

For selecting examples, EMM combines evidential uncertainty with predicted covariances in label embeddings. This gives the selection rule information about both uncertainty and label relationships. Synthetic experiments support its uncertainty estimates and ability to capture correlations. Evaluations on real-world datasets report improved performance over existing multi-label active learning methods, supporting the combined prediction-and-selection design.
summary.tldr: Evidential Mixture Machines combine label correlations and uncertainty estimates to improve multi-label prediction and active sample selection.

title: Evidential Mixture Machines: Deciphering Multi-Label Correlations for Active Learning Sensitivity

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach using Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated into an agent framework for flexible and effective personal mobility generation. LLMs overcome the limitations of previous models by effectively processing semantic data and offering versatility in modeling various tasks. Our approach addresses three research questions: aligning LLMs with real-world urban mobility data, developing reliable activity generation strategies, and exploring LLM applications in urban mobility. The key technical contribution is a novel LLM agent framework that accounts for individual activity patterns and motivations, including a self-consistency approach to align LLMs with real-world activity data and a retrieval-augmented strategy for interpretable activity generation. We evaluate our LLM agent framework and compare it with state-of-the-art personal mobility generation approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and its potential applications in urban mobility. Overall, this study marks the pioneering work of designing an LLM agent framework for activity generation based on real-world human activity data, offering a promising tool for urban mobility analysis.

paragraphs: Generating personal mobility involves modeling people's activities and the patterns and motivations behind them. This paper uses a language model within an agent framework to handle that semantic information. The work focuses on aligning generated behavior with real activity data, making activity generation reliable, and exploring the resulting framework's uses in urban mobility analysis.

The framework incorporates individual activity patterns and motivations through two main mechanisms. A self-consistency approach aligns the language model with observed real-world activity data. A retrieval-augmented strategy supports interpretable activity generation by bringing retrieved information into the process. Together, these mechanisms connect the model's flexible handling of language with the empirical patterns it is meant to represent.

The authors evaluate the framework against state-of-the-art personal mobility generators and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is an activity-generation framework grounded in real human activity data, with potential applications in urban analysis. Its importance lies in combining data alignment and interpretable generation within the same agent design, so that semantic modeling is tied to observed behavior.
summary.tldr: An LLM agent framework combines data alignment and retrieval-augmented generation to model individuals' urban activities and mobility.

title: Large Language Models as Urban Residents: An LLM Agent Framework for Personal Mobility Generation

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in 2D vision and language tasks. However, their ability to reason about spatial arrangements remains limited. In this work, we introduce Spatial Region GPT (SpatialRGPT) to enhance VLMs’ spatial perception and reasoning capabilities. SpatialRGPT advances VLMs’ spatial understanding through two key innovations: (i) a data curation pipeline that enables effective learning of regional representation from 3D scene graphs, and (ii) a flexible ``plugin'' module for integrating depth information into the visual encoder of existing VLMs. During inference, when provided with user-specified region proposals, SpatialRGPT can accurately perceive their relative directions and distances. Additionally, we propose SpatialRGBT-Bench, a benchmark with ground-truth 3D annotations encompassing indoor, outdoor, and simulated environments, for evaluating 3D spatial cognition in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Our results demonstrate that SpatialRGPT significantly enhances performance in spatial reasoning tasks, both with and without local region prompts. The model also exhibits strong generalization capabilities, effectively reasoning about complex spatial relations and functioning as a region-aware dense reward annotator for robotic tasks. Code, dataset, and benchmark are released at https://www.anjiecheng.me/SpatialRGPT.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can perform well on image and language tasks while still struggling with spatial arrangements. SpatialRGPT targets the ability to reason about regions' relative directions and distances. It connects regional visual representations with three-dimensional scene information so that spatial relationships become an explicit focus of learning.

The method has two main components: a data-curation pipeline based on 3D scene graphs and a flexible module that adds depth information to an existing model's visual encoder. At inference time, users can specify regions for spatial comparison. The paper also introduces SpatialRGBT-Bench, with ground-truth 3D annotations from indoor, outdoor, and simulated environments.

Results show substantial improvements in spatial reasoning both with and without local region prompts. The authors also report strong generalization to complex spatial relations and demonstrate use as a region-aware dense reward annotator for robotic tasks. These findings connect improved spatial representations to both answering relationship questions and providing spatially grounded feedback for robotics.
summary.tldr: SpatialRGPT combines 3D scene-graph training data and depth integration to improve vision-language models' spatial reasoning.

title: SpatialRGPT: Grounded Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

abstract: What features neural networks learn, and how, remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Alternating Gradient Flows (AGF), an algorithmic framework that describes the dynamics of feature learning in two-layer networks trained from small initialization. Prior works have shown that gradient flow in this regime exhibits a staircase-like loss curve, alternating between plateaus where neurons slowly align to useful directions and sharp drops where neurons rapidly grow in norm. AGF approximates this behavior as an alternating two-step process: maximizing a utility function over dormant neurons and minimizing a cost function over active ones. AGF begins with all neurons dormant, corresponding to an initialization at the origin. At each iteration, a dormant neuron activates, triggering the acquisition of a feature and a drop in the loss. AGF quantifies the order, timing, and magnitude of these drops, matching experiments across several commonly studied architectures. We show that AGF unifies and extends existing saddle-to-saddle analyses in fully connected linear networks and attention-only linear transformers, where the learned features are singular modes and principal components, respectively. In diagonal linear networks, we prove AGF converges to gradient flow in the limit of vanishing initialization. Applying AGF to quadratic networks trained to perform modular addition, we give the first complete characterization of the training dynamics, revealing that networks learn Fourier features in decreasing order of coefficient magnitude. Altogether, AGF offers a promising step towards understanding feature learning in neural networks.

paragraphs: Two-layer neural networks trained from very small initial weights can learn in bursts: progress appears slow before the loss suddenly drops. Alternating Gradient Flows explains this pattern through an approximation that separates the search for useful features from the strengthening of features already acquired. Its starting point treats every neuron as dormant, corresponding to initialization at the origin.

The framework alternates between maximizing a utility function for dormant neurons and minimizing a cost for active neurons. Activating a neuron represents acquiring a feature and produces a loss decrease. This description predicts the order, timing, and size of those decreases, with experimental agreement across several studied architectures.

The framework also extends earlier analyses of fully connected linear networks and attention-only linear transformers. For quadratic networks learning modular addition, it characterizes the full training dynamics and shows Fourier features emerging in descending coefficient magnitude. Together, these results make feature acquisition more explicit in the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: Alternating Gradient Flows explains staged feature learning in several two-layer network settings by alternating neuron activation and active-feature optimization.

title: Alternating Gradient Flows: A Theory of Feature Learning in Two-layer Neural Networks

abstract: Continual learning from unlabeled data streams while effectively combating catastrophic forgetting poses an intractable challenge. Traditional methods predominantly rely on visual clustering techniques to generate pseudo labels, which are frequently plagued by problems such as noise and suboptimal quality, profoundly affecting the impact on the model evolution. To surmount these obstacles, we introduce an innovative approach that synergistically combines both visual and textual information to generate dual space hybrid pseudo labels for reliable model continual evolution. Specifically, by harnessing the capabilities of large multimodal models, we initially generate generalizable text descriptions for a few representative samples. These descriptions then undergo a `Coarse to Fine' refinement process to capture the subtle nuances between different data points, significantly enhancing the semantic accuracy of the descriptions. Simultaneously, a novel cross-modal hybrid approach seamlessly integrates these fine-grained textual descriptions with visual features, thereby creating a more robust and reliable supervisory signal. Finally, such descriptions are employed to alleviate the catastrophic forgetting issue via a semantic alignment distillation, which capitalizes on the stability inherent in language knowledge to effectively prevent the model from forgetting previously learned information. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a variety of benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method attains state-of-the-art performance, and ablation studies further substantiate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Learning continuously from unlabeled examples creates two connected problems: the model needs useful training targets, and new learning can overwrite earlier knowledge. Existing approaches often construct artificial labels by clustering visual representations. The paper argues that noise and poor quality in these labels can undermine the model’s subsequent development.

The proposed method combines visual information with language descriptions. A large multimodal model first describes a small set of representative examples. A coarse-to-fine refinement process then makes those descriptions more sensitive to differences between data points. The refined text is combined with visual features to generate hybrid pseudo labels, giving the learner supervision informed by both appearance and semantic description.

The descriptions also support semantic alignment distillation, which uses the stability of language knowledge to alleviate forgetting as the stream continues. Language therefore contributes both to learning new distinctions and to preserving earlier information. Experiments across several benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, while ablation studies support the effectiveness of the proposed method’s components.
summary.tldr: The method combines refined text descriptions with visual features to improve unlabeled continual learning and alleviate forgetting.

title: Dual-Space Semantic Synergy Distillation for Continual Learning of Unlabeled Streams

abstract: Understanding user intent is essential for situational and context-aware decision-making. Motivated by a real-world scenario, this work addresses intent predictions of smart device users in the vicinity of vehicles by modeling sequential spatiotemporal data. However, in real-world scenarios, environmental factors and sensor limitations can result in non-stationary and irregularly sampled data, posing significant challenges. To address these issues, we propose STaRFormer, a Transformer-based approach that can serve as a universal framework for sequential modeling. STaRFormer utilizes a new dynamic attention-based regional masking scheme combined with a novel semi-supervised contrastive learning paradigm to enhance task-specific latent representations. Comprehensive experiments on 56 datasets varying in types (including non-stationary and irregularly sampled), tasks, domains, sequence lengths, training samples, and applications demonstrate the efficacy of STaRFormer, achieving notable improvements over state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: STaRFormer is motivated by predicting the intentions of smart-device users near vehicles from sequences of spatial and temporal observations. Real sensor data complicates this task: its statistical behavior can change over time, and observations can arrive at irregular intervals. The paper develops a broader sequential-modeling approach around these challenges.

The Transformer-based model combines dynamic attention-based regional masking with semi-supervised contrastive learning. Masking and contrastive learning are used together to improve internal representations for the task being solved. This emphasis on task-informed representations links the training approach to the eventual prediction goal, including intent prediction in the motivating application.

The evaluation covers 56 datasets spanning different tasks, domains, sequence lengths, training-set sizes, and applications, including non-stationary and irregularly sampled data. The authors report notable improvements over state-of-the-art approaches across this broad experimental study. These results support STaRFormer’s usefulness as a general sequential-modeling framework, with evidence extending beyond the vehicle-related scenario that originally motivated its design.
summary.tldr: STaRFormer combines attention-based masking and semi-supervised contrastive learning to improve sequential representations across varied datasets.

title: STaRFormer: Semi-Supervised Task-Informed Representation Learning via Dynamic Attention-Based Regional Masking for Sequential Data

abstract: This paper introduces a general method for the exploration of equivalence classes in the input space of Transformer models. The proposed approach is based on sound mathematical theory which describes the internal layers of a Transformer architecture as sequential deformations of the input manifold. Using eigendecomposition of the pullback of the distance metric defined on the output space through the Jacobian of the model, we are able to reconstruct equivalence classes in the input space and navigate across them. Our method enables two complementary exploration procedures: the first retrieves input instances that produce the same class probability distribution as the original instance—thus identifying elements within the same equivalence class—while the second discovers instances that yield a different class probability distribution, effectively navigating toward distinct equivalence classes. Finally, we demonstrate how the retrieved instances can be meaningfully interpreted by projecting their embeddings back into a human-readable format.

paragraphs: This paper explores which different inputs a Transformer treats as equivalent. Equivalence is defined through the model’s output: inputs belong to the same class when they produce the same probability distribution over predicted classes. The aim is to navigate input space according to the distinctions the model actually makes.

The mathematical framework treats successive Transformer layers as deformations of an input manifold. It takes a distance metric defined at the output and maps it back through the model’s Jacobian, which describes sensitivity to input changes. An eigendecomposition of this pulled-back metric enables the method to reconstruct and move across equivalence classes in input space.

The framework supports two complementary procedures. One finds inputs that preserve the original class-probability distribution; the other finds inputs that produce a different distribution. The authors also show how to project the resulting embeddings into a human-readable form. Together, these operations make it possible to inspect both variations the model treats alike and changes that alter its classification behavior.
summary.tldr: The method uses Transformer geometry to find interpretable input variations that preserve or change the model’s output probability distribution.

title: Unveiling Transformer Perception by Exploring Input Manifolds

abstract: The increasing realism of generated images has raised significant concerns about their potential misuse, necessitating robust detection methods. Current approaches mainly rely on training binary classifiers, which depend heavily on the quantity and quality of available generated images. In this work, we propose a novel framework that exploits geometric differences between the data manifolds of natural and generated images. To exploit this difference, we employ a pair of functions engineered to yield consistent outputs for natural images but divergent outputs for generated ones, leveraging the property that their gradients reside in mutually orthogonal subspaces. This design enables a simple yet effective detection method: an image is identified as generated if a transformation along its data manifold induces a significant change in the loss value of a self-supervised model pre-trained on natural images. Further more, to address diminishing manifold disparities in advanced generative models, we leverage normalizing flows to amplify detectable differences by extruding generated images away from the natural image manifold. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method.

paragraphs: Generated-image detectors commonly learn a binary distinction from examples of natural and generated pictures. Their success can depend heavily on the generated images available for training. This paper instead develops a detector around differences in the geometry of natural and generated image distributions, using a self-supervised model pre-trained on natural images as part of the detection process.

The framework uses two functions designed to agree on natural images and disagree on generated ones. Their construction exploits gradients lying in mutually orthogonal subspaces. Operationally, the detector transforms an image along its data manifold and measures how much the self-supervised model's loss changes. A sufficiently large change is treated as evidence that the image was generated.

The authors also address the shrinking geometric differences associated with more advanced generators. They use normalizing flows to amplify these differences by moving generated images away from the natural-image manifold. Experiments support the method's effectiveness. Its contribution is a detection signal based on responses to geometric transformations, together with a mechanism intended to strengthen that signal when the distributions become harder to distinguish.
summary.tldr: The detector identifies generated images through geometric transformations that change a natural-image model's loss, with normalizing flows amplifying distribution differences.

title: Detecting Generated Images by Fitting Natural Image Distributions

abstract: The rapid advancement of diffusion models has enabled high-fidelity and semantically rich text-to-image generation; however, ensuring fairness and safety remains an open challenge. Existing methods typically improve fairness and safety at the expense of semantic fidelity and image quality. In this work, we propose RespoDiff, a novel framework for responsible text-to-image generation that incorporates a dual-module transformation on the intermediate bottleneck representations of diffusion models. Our approach introduces two distinct learnable modules: one focused on capturing and enforcing responsible concepts, such as fairness and safety, and the other dedicated to maintaining semantic alignment with neutral prompts. To facilitate the dual learning process, we introduce a novel score-matching objective that enables effective coordination between the modules. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in responsible generation by ensuring semantic alignment while optimizing both objectives without compromising image fidelity. Our approach improves responsible and semantically coherent generation by \textasciitilde20\% across diverse, unseen prompts. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly into large-scale models like SDXL, enhancing fairness and safety. The project page is available at https://vssilpa.github.io/respodiff_project_page.

RespoDiff addresses this tension by changing intermediate bottleneck representations inside a diffusion model. Its design gives responsibility-related concepts and semantic preservation separate learnable components.

One module captures and enforces concepts such as fairness and safety. The other maintains semantic alignment with neutral prompts. A new score-matching objective coordinates their learning, so the two modules can pursue their respective goals together. This separation makes preserving the requested meaning an explicit part of the intervention, alongside the desired changes in generated content.

The authors report better responsible-generation performance than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining semantic alignment and image fidelity. They describe an improvement of approximately 20% in responsible and semantically coherent generation across diverse unseen prompts, without identifying a more specific metric in the abstract. The framework also integrates into SDXL. These findings support the dual-module design as a way to improve the evaluated responsibility objectives while retaining the visual and semantic qualities users expect.
summary.tldr: RespoDiff coordinates two bottleneck modules to improve fairness and safety in image generation while preserving prompt alignment and image quality.

title: RespoDiff: Dual-Module Bottleneck Transformation for Responsible & Faithful T2I Generation

abstract: Point cloud registration is a fundamental task in 3D computer vision. Recent advances have shown that graph-based methods are effective for outlier rejection in this context. However, existing clique-based methods impose overly strict constraints and are NP-hard, making it difficult to achieve both robustness and efficiency. While the k-core reduces computational complexity, which only considers node degree and ignores higher-order topological structures such as triangles, limiting its effectiveness in complex scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the $k$-truss from graph theory into point cloud registration, leveraging triangle support as a constraint for inlier selection. We further propose a consensus voting-based low-scale sampling strategy to efficiently extract the structural skeleton of the point cloud prior to $k$-truss decomposition. Additionally, we design a spatial distribution score that balances coverage and uniformity of inliers, preventing selections that concentrate on sparse local clusters. Extensive experiments on KITTI, 3DMatch, and 3DLoMatch demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms both traditional and learning-based approaches in various indoor and outdoor scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns three-dimensional observations, making reliable rejection of incorrect matches important. Graph-based approaches identify mutually compatible matches, but existing structural rules involve trade-offs. Cliques impose very strict constraints and are computationally difficult to find, while k-core methods use node degree and miss higher-order structures such as triangles.

PointTruss introduces the k-truss criterion, using triangle support to select inliers. A consensus voting sampling strategy first extracts a smaller structural skeleton before decomposition, improving efficiency. The method also scores the spatial distribution of inliers to balance coverage and uniformity, helping avoid selections concentrated in sparse local clusters.

Experiments on KITTI, 3DMatch, and 3DLoMatch show reported improvements over traditional and learning-based approaches across indoor and outdoor settings. The authors describe the results as state of the art. The contribution combines a richer graph compatibility criterion with efficient sampling and spatial coverage, addressing both which matches agree structurally and whether the selected matches are distributed usefully across the point cloud.
summary.tldr: PointTruss uses triangle-supported graph structure, efficient sampling, and spatial coverage scoring to improve point cloud registration.

title: PointTruss: K-Truss for Point Cloud Registration

abstract: Recent proposals for regulating frontier AI models have sparked concerns about the cost of safety regulation, and most such regulations have been shelved due to the safety-innovation tradeoff. This paper argues for an alternative regulatory approach that ensures AI safety while actively \textit{promoting} innovation: mandating that large AI laboratories release small, openly accessible "analog models"—scaled-down versions trained similarly to and distilled from their largest proprietary models.Analog models serve as public proxies, allowing broad participation in safety verification, interpretability research, and algorithmic transparency without forcing labs to disclose their full-scale models. Recent research demonstrates that safety and interpretability methods developed using these smaller models generalize effectively to frontier-scale systems. By enabling the wider research community to directly investigate and innovate upon accessible analogs, our policy substantially reduces the regulatory burden and accelerates safety advancements.This mandate promises minimal additional costs, leveraging reusable resources like data and infrastructure, while significantly contributing to the public good. Our hope is not only that this policy be adopted, but that it illustrates a broader principle supporting fundamental research in machine learning: deeper understanding of models relaxes the safety-innovation tradeoff and lets us have more of both.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes requiring frontier AI laboratories to release small, openly accessible analog models. These would be scaled-down models trained similarly to, and distilled from, their largest proprietary systems. The proposal responds to concerns that safety regulation can impose costs that discourage innovation.

The authors argue that accessible analogs would let a broader research community investigate safety, interpretability, and algorithmic transparency. Researchers could work directly with these public proxies while laboratories retain their full-scale models. The argument draws on research described in the abstract showing that safety and interpretability methods developed on smaller models can generalize effectively to frontier-scale systems.

The paper presents reduced regulatory burden and faster safety progress as expected benefits of this policy. It also argues that reusing data and infrastructure would keep additional costs low. These are claims supporting a proposed mandate. The broader position is that expanding fundamental research access can deepen understanding of models and ease the tradeoff between safety and innovation, allowing progress on both objectives.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that mandatory small analog models could broaden safety research while promoting innovation.

title: Position: Require Frontier AI Labs To Release Small "Analog" Models

abstract: The success of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) critically depends on the quality of the reward model. However, while this quality is primarily evaluated through accuracy, it remains unclear whether accuracy fully captures what makes a reward model an effective teacher. We address this question from an optimization perspective. First, we prove that regardless of how accurate a reward model is, if it induces low reward variance, then the RLHF objective suffers from a flat landscape. Consequently, even a perfectly accurate reward model can lead to extremely slow optimization, underperforming less accurate models that induce higher reward variance. We additionally show that a reward model that works well for one language model can induce low reward variance, and thus a flat objective landscape, for another. These results establish a fundamental limitation of evaluating reward models solely based on accuracy or independently of the language model they guide. Experiments using models of up to 8B parameters corroborate our theory, demonstrating the interplay between reward variance, accuracy, and reward maximization rate. Overall, our findings highlight that beyond accuracy, a reward model needs to induce sufficient variance for efficient optimization.
