paragraphs: This paper asks whether reward-model accuracy is enough to predict effective reinforcement learning from human feedback. A reward model supplies the training signal for a language model, so its usefulness depends on how that signal shapes optimization. The authors analyze this teaching role through the variation in rewards it induces.

They prove that low reward variance produces a flat RLHF objective landscape regardless of reward-model accuracy. Consequently, even a perfectly accurate model can lead to very slow optimization and perform worse as a teacher than a less accurate model inducing higher variance. They also show that a reward model can work well with one language model yet induce low variance and a flat landscape with another.

Experiments using models with up to eight billion parameters support the relationship between accuracy, reward variance, and the speed of reward maximization. The findings establish a limitation of evaluating reward models solely by accuracy or separately from the language models they guide. Sufficient reward variance is needed for efficient optimization, making teacher quality a property of the training interaction as well as the reward model.
summary.tldr: Reward-model accuracy alone does not ensure effective RLHF: low induced reward variance can make optimization extremely slow, even with perfect accuracy.

title: What Makes a Reward Model a Good Teacher? An Optimization Perspective

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual understanding but often suffer from visual hallucinations, where they generate descriptions of nonexistent objects, actions, or concepts, posing significant risks in safety-critical applications. Existing hallucination mitigation methods typically follow one of two paradigms: generation adjustment, which modifies decoding behavior to align text with visual inputs, and post-hoc verification, where external models assess and correct outputs. While effective, generation adjustment methods often rely on heuristics and lack correction mechanisms, while post-hoc verification is complicated, typically requiring multiple models and tending to reject outputs rather than refine them. In this work, we introduce REVERSE, a unified framework that integrates hallucination-aware training with on-the-fly self-verification. By leveraging a new hallucination-verification dataset containing over 1.3M semi-synthetic samples, along with a novel inference-time retrospective resampling technique, our approach enables VLMs to both detect hallucinations during generation and dynamically revise those hallucinations. Our evaluations show that REVERSE achieves state-of-the-art hallucination reduction, outperforming the best existing methods by up to 12% on CHAIR-MSCOCO and 34% on HaloQuest.
originalAbstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual understanding but often suffer from visual hallucinations, where they generate descriptions of nonexistent objects, actions, or concepts, posing significant risks in safety-critical applications. Existing hallucination mitigation methods typically follow one of two paradigms: generation adjustment, which modifies decoding behavior to align text with visual inputs, and post-hoc verification, where external models assess and correct outputs. While effective, generation adjustment methods often rely on heuristics and lack correction mechanisms, while post-hoc verification is complicated, typically requiring multiple models and tending to reject outputs rather than refine them. In this work, we introduce REVERSE, a unified framework that integrates hallucination-aware training with on-the-fly self-verification. By leveraging a new hallucination-verification dataset containing over 1.3M semi-synthetic samples, along with a novel inference-time retrospective resampling technique, our approach enables VLMs to both detect hallucinations during generation and dynamically revise those hallucinations. Our evaluations show that REVERSE achieves state-of-the-art hallucination reduction, outperforming the best existing methods by up to 12% on CHAIR-MSCOCO and 34% on HaloQuest.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can describe objects, actions, or concepts that are absent from their visual input. Existing remedies often modify generation or use external models to check completed outputs. The paper identifies a gap between these approaches: generation adjustments may lack correction mechanisms, while external verification can become complicated and emphasize rejecting outputs over improving them.

REVERSE integrates hallucination-aware training with verification during generation. The training uses a new dataset containing more than 1.3 million semi-synthetic hallucination-verification examples. At inference time, retrospective resampling enables the model to revisit and revise hallucinated content. Detection and correction thus become connected parts of the generation process.

Evaluations report state-of-the-art hallucination reduction, with improvements over the best existing methods of up to twelve percent on CHAIR-MSCOCO and thirty-four percent on HaloQuest. These are benchmark-specific reported gains, with 'up to' describing their extent. The approach matters because it equips generation with an active revision mechanism, allowing a model to respond to detected hallucinations by changing its output.
summary.tldr: REVERSE trains vision-language models to detect hallucinations and revise them during generation through retrospective resampling.

title: Generate, but Verify: Reducing Hallucination in Vision-Language Models with Retrospective Resampling

abstract: LLM‑based agents have demonstrated great potential in generating and managing code within complex codebases. In this paper, we introduce WebGen-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to measure an LLM-based agent's ability to create multi-file website codebases from scratch. It contains diverse instructions for website generation, created through the combined efforts of human annotators and GPT-4o. These instructions span three major categories and thirteen minor categories, encompassing nearly all important types of web applications.To assess the quality of the generated websites, we generate test cases targeting each functionality described in the instructions. These test cases are then manually filtered, refined, and organized to ensure accuracy, resulting in a total of 647 test cases. Each test case specifies an operation to be performed on the website and the expected outcome of the operation.To automate testing and improve reproducibility, we employ a powerful web-navigation agent to execute test cases on the generated websites and determine whether the observed responses align with the expected results.We evaluate three high-performance code-agent frameworks—Bolt.diy, OpenHands, and Aider—using multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs as engines. The best-performing combination, Bolt.diy powered by DeepSeek-R1, achieves only 27.8\% accuracy on the test cases, highlighting the challenging nature of our benchmark.Additionally, we construct WebGen-Instruct, a training set consisting of 6,667 website-generation instructions. Training Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct on Bolt.diy trajectories generated from a subset of the training set achieves an accuracy of 38.2\%, surpassing the performance of the best proprietary model.We release our data-generation, training, and testing code, along with both the datasets and model weights at https://github.com/mnluzimu/WebGen-Bench.

paragraphs: WebGen-Bench evaluates whether language-model agents can create working, multi-file websites from instructions. Its focus is functional behavior: whether a user operation produces the expected result. Human annotators and GPT-4o jointly create website requests spanning three broad categories and thirteen narrower categories.

The benchmark contains 647 functionality tests that are manually filtered and refined. A web-navigation agent performs the specified operations and checks the observed outcomes, supporting automated and reproducible assessment. Evaluations combine Bolt.diy, OpenHands, and Aider with proprietary and open-source language models. The strongest evaluated combination, Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-R1, passes 27.8% of the test cases.

The authors also introduce WebGen-Instruct, containing 6,667 website-generation instructions. Training Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct on Bolt.diy trajectories from a subset raises test accuracy to 38.2%, exceeding the best proprietary model evaluated. The results establish both the difficulty of generating functional websites and the value of targeted training on agent trajectories. Success here concerns tested interactions, providing a concrete measure of whether generated applications fulfill their requested functionality.
summary.tldr: WebGen-Bench tests generated websites through 647 functional checks, revealing low initial success rates and gains from targeted agent-trajectory training.

title: WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch

abstract: Recent advancements, such as DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and Kimina-Prover-Preview-72B, demonstrate a prevailing trend in leveraging reinforcement learning (RL)-based large-scale training for automated theorem proving. Surprisingly, we discover that even without any training, careful neuro-symbolic coordination of existing off-the-shelf reasoning models and tactic step provers can achieve comparable performance. This paper introduces DSP+, an improved version of the Draft, Sketch, and Prove framework, featuring a fine-grained and integrated neuro-symbolic enhancement for each phase: (1) In the draft phase, we prompt reasoning models to generate concise natural-language subgoals to benefit the sketch phase, removing thinking tokens and references to human-written proofs; (2) In the sketch phase, subgoals are autoformalized with hypotheses to benefit the proving phase, and sketch lines containing syntactic errors are masked according to predefined rules; (3) In the proving phase, we tightly integrate symbolic search methods like Aesop with step provers to establish proofs for the sketch subgoals. Experimental results show that, without any additional model training or fine-tuning, DSP+ solves 80.7%, 32.8%, and 24 out of 644 problems from miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench, respectively, while requiring fewer budgets compared to state-of-the-arts. DSP+ proves imo_2019_p1, an IMO problem in miniF2F that is not solved by any prior work. Additionally, DSP+ generates proof patterns comprehensible by human experts, facilitating the identification of formalization errors; For example, eight wrongly formalized statements in miniF2F are discovered. Our results highlight the potential of classical reasoning patterns besides the RL-based training. All components will be open-sourced.

paragraphs: Recent automated theorem provers often depend on large-scale reinforcement learning. The results show that inference-time coordination can be competitive with training-intensive approaches on these evaluations.
summary.tldr: DSP+ coordinates existing reasoning models and symbolic provers to achieve competitive theorem-proving results without additional model training.

title: Reviving DSP for Advanced Theorem Proving in the Era of Reasoning Models

abstract: The reward hypothesis states that all goals and purposes can be understood as the maximization of a received scalar reward signal. However, in practice, defining such a reward signal is notoriously difficult, as humans are often unable to predict the optimal behavior corresponding to a reward function. Natural language offers an intuitive alternative for instructing reinforcement learning (RL) agents, yet previous language-conditioned approaches either require costly supervision or test-time training given a language instruction. In this work, we present a new approach that uses a pretrained RL agent trained using only unlabeled, offline interactions—without task-specific supervision or labeled trajectories—to get zero-shot test-time policy inference from arbitrary natural language instructions. We introduce a framework comprising three steps: *imagine*, *project*, and *imitate*. First, the agent imagines a sequence of observations corresponding to the provided language description using video generative models. Next, these imagined observations are projected into the target environment domain. Finally, an agent pretrained in the target environment with unsupervised RL instantly imitates the projected observation sequence through a closed-form solution. To the best of our knowledge, our method, RLZero, is the first approach to show direct language-to-behavior generation abilities on a variety of tasks and environments without any in-domain supervision. We further show that components of RLZero can be used to generate policies zero-shot from cross-embodied videos, such as those available on YouTube, even for complex embodiments like humanoids.

paragraphs: Natural language is a convenient way to describe desired behavior, but translating it into reinforcement-learning policies often requires labeled examples or additional training for each instruction. RLZero instead uses an agent pretrained on unlabeled offline interactions in the target environment. It aims to infer behavior directly from language at test time without task-specific supervision.

The contribution is a connection between generated visual descriptions and unsupervised policy learning: language specifies an imagined outcome, and prior environment experience enables the agent to act on that representation.
summary.tldr: RLZero converts language into imagined observations that a pretrained unsupervised RL agent can imitate without task-specific test-time training.

title: RLZero: Direct Policy Inference from Language Without In-Domain Supervision

abstract: The reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, particularly following the release of DeepSeek-R1, which has inspired a surge of research into data quality and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. Despite the pivotal role diversity plays in RL, its influence on LLM reasoning remains largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, this work presents a systematic investigation into the impact of diversity in RL-based training for LLM reasoning, and proposes a novel diversity-aware policy optimization method. Across evaluations on 12 LLMs, we observe a strong positive correlation between the solution diversity and potential@k (a novel metric quantifying an LLM’s reasoning potential) in high-performing models. This finding motivates our method to explicitly promote diversity during RL training. Specifically, we design a token-level diversity and reformulate it into a practical objective, then we selectively apply it to positive samples. Integrated into the R1-zero training framework, our method achieves a 3.5\% average improvement across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, while generating more diverse and robust solutions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve language-model reasoning, but training also shapes how many different solutions a model explores. This paper studies solution diversity as a factor in reasoning performance. Its starting point is that producing a wider range of useful approaches may reveal capabilities that repeated, similar answers fail to expose.

Across 12 language models, the authors find a strong positive correlation between solution diversity and potential@k, their measure of reasoning potential, among high-performing models. That relationship motivates a training method that explicitly rewards diversity. They define diversity at the token level, convert it into a practical optimization objective, and apply it selectively to positive samples.

When incorporated into the R1-zero training framework, the method produces a reported average improvement of 3.5% across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, alongside more diverse and robust solutions. The correlation provides motivation, while the training experiments provide evidence for the proposed intervention. The central contribution is a concrete way to encourage variation among positive samples during reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: A diversity objective applied to positive training samples improves mathematical reasoning in the evaluated reinforcement-learning framework.

title: Diversity-Aware Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Reasoning

abstract: We introduce a novel framework for AI-generated image detection through epistemic uncertainty, aiming to address critical security concerns in the era of generative models. Our key insight stems from the observation that distributional discrepancies between training and testing data manifest distinctively in the epistemic uncertainty space of machine learning models. In this context, the distribution shift between natural and generated images leads to elevated epistemic uncertainty in models trained on natural images when evaluating generated ones. Hence, we exploit this phenomenon by using epistemic uncertainty as a proxy for detecting generated images. This converts the challenge of generated image detection into the problem of uncertainty estimation, underscoring the generalization performance of the model used for uncertainty estimation. Fortunately, advanced large-scale vision models pre-trained on extensive natural images have shown excellent generalization performance for various scenarios. Thus, we utilize these pre-trained models to estimate the epistemic uncertainty of images and flag those with high uncertainty as generated. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our method.

paragraphs: This paper approaches generated-image detection through a model's uncertainty about unfamiliar inputs. Its starting observation is that differences between training and test distributions can appear in epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty associated with the model's knowledge. The framework therefore makes uncertainty estimation central to deciding whether an image was generated. It uses large vision models pretrained on extensive collections of natural images, drawing on their ability to generalize across different scenarios. Images receiving high epistemic uncertainty are flagged as generated. The detector's effectiveness consequently depends on the generalization behavior of the model supplying those uncertainty estimates.

Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of this approach. The stated contribution is the connection between a distribution difference and a measurable uncertainty signal that can serve as a detection proxy. It offers a way to use the knowledge already present in pretrained vision models to identify generated imagery through how uncertain those models become.
summary.tldr: The framework detects generated images using elevated epistemic uncertainty in vision models pretrained on natural images.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty for Generated Image Detection

abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) are confronted with overwhelming information volume when comprehending long-form documents. This challenge raises the imperative of a cohesive memory module, which can elevate vanilla LLMs into autonomous reading agents. Despite the emergence of some heuristic approaches, a systematic design principle remains absent. To fill this void, we draw inspiration from Jean Piaget's Constructivist Theory, illuminating three traits of the agentic memory---structured schemata, flexible assimilation, and dynamic accommodation. This blueprint forges a clear path toward a more robust and efficient memory system for LLM-based reading comprehension. To this end, we develop CAM, a prototype implementation of Constructivist Agentic Memory that simultaneously embodies the structurality, flexibility, and dynamicity. At its core, CAM is endowed with an incremental overlapping clustering algorithm for structured memory development, supporting both coherent hierarchical summarization and online batch integration. During inference, CAM adaptively explores the memory structure to activate query-relevant information for contextual response, akin to the human associative process. Compared to existing approaches, our design demonstrates dual advantages in both performance and efficiency across diverse long-text reading comprehension tasks, including question answering, query-based summarization, and claim verification.

paragraphs: Reading long documents requires an LLM to organize more information than it can conveniently use at once. This paper approaches that problem through an explicit memory system. Drawing on Piaget's constructivist theory, it proposes three design principles: structured knowledge organization, flexible incorporation of information, and dynamic adjustment as information accumulates.

CAM implements these principles with an incremental clustering algorithm whose groups can overlap. This structure supports hierarchical summaries while allowing new batches of information to enter the memory during operation. The combination matters because a reading agent needs both an organized account of what it has encountered and a way to incorporate additional material into that account.

When answering a query, CAM adaptively explores its memory to activate relevant information for the response. The authors report advantages in both performance and efficiency over existing approaches across question answering, query-based summarization, and claim verification on long texts. The contribution connects a proposed memory-design framework to a working system and evaluates its usefulness across several forms of reading comprehension.
summary.tldr: CAM organizes and updates document memory through overlapping clusters, improving long-text reading performance and efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: CAM: A Constructivist View of Agentic Memory for LLM-Based Reading Comprehension

abstract: We present **Brain Harmony (BrainHarmonix)**, the first multimodal brain foundation model that unifies structural morphology and functional dynamics into compact 1D token representations. The model was pretrained on two of the largest neuroimaging datasets to date, encompassing 64,594 T1-weighted structural MRI 3D volumes (～ 14 million images) and 70,933 functional MRI (fMRI) time series. BrainHarmonix is grounded in two foundational neuroscience principles: *structure complements function* - structural and functional modalities offer distinct yet synergistic insights into brain organization; *function follows structure* - brain functional dynamics are shaped by cortical morphology. The modular pretraining process involves single-modality training with geometric pre-alignment followed by modality fusion through shared brain hub tokens. Notably, our dynamics encoder uniquely handles fMRI time series with heterogeneous repetition times (TRs), addressing a major limitation in existing models. BrainHarmonix is also the first to deeply compress high-dimensional neuroimaging signals into unified, continuous 1D tokens, forming a compact latent space of the human brain. BrainHarmonix achieves strong generalization across diverse downstream tasks, including neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder classification and cognition prediction - consistently outperforming previous approaches. Our models - pretrained on 8 H100 GPUs - aim to catalyze a new era of AI-driven neuroscience powered by large-scale multimodal neuroimaging.

paragraphs: Brain Harmony, also called BrainHarmonix, combines information about brain structure and activity in a shared representation. Structural MRI describes morphology, while functional MRI records changing activity. The model follows two motivating principles: these modalities supply complementary information, and brain structure shapes functional dynamics. Its goal is to capture both within compact, continuous one-dimensional tokens.

Pretraining first develops each modality separately with geometric pre-alignment, then connects them through shared brain hub tokens. A dynamics encoder accommodates functional scans collected with different repetition times, allowing it to handle variation in their temporal sampling. The training data include 64,594 structural MRI volumes and 70,933 functional MRI time series.

The resulting latent representation compresses high-dimensional neuroimaging signals into a common space for downstream tasks. The authors report strong generalization and consistent improvements over previous approaches in disorder classification and cognition prediction. These findings support combining morphology and function for reusable brain representations, with the reported benefits spanning both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative classification tasks.
summary.tldr: BrainHarmonix compresses structural and functional brain scans into shared tokens, improving reported results on disorder classification and cognition prediction.

title: Brain Harmony: A Multimodal Foundation Model Unifying Morphology and Function into 1D Tokens

abstract: We study online decision making problems under resource constraints, where both reward and cost functions are drawn from distributions that may change adversarially over time. We focus on two canonical settings: $(i)$ online resource allocation where rewards and costs are observed before action selection, and $(ii)$ online learning with resource constraints where they are observed after action selection, under full feedback or bandit feedback. It is well known that achieving sublinear regret in these settings is impossible when the rewards and cost distributions may change arbitrarily over time. To address this challenge, we analyze a framework in which the learner is guided by a spending plan—a sequence prescribing expected resource usage across rounds. We design general (primal-)dual methods that achieve sublinear regret with respect to baselines that follow the spending plan. Crucially, the performance of our algorithms improves when the spending plan ensures a well-balanced distribution of the budget across rounds. We additionally provide a robust variant of our methods to handle worst-case scenarios where the spending plan is highly imbalanced. To conclude, we study the regret of our algorithms when competing against benchmarks that deviate from the prescribed spending plan.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions made under a limited resource budget when reward and cost distributions can change adversarially. It covers both allocation problems where rewards and costs are visible before choosing an action and learning problems where they become available afterward. In the latter setting, feedback may be full or bandit.

Arbitrary changes make sublinear regret impossible in the unrestricted setting. The authors introduce guidance through a spending plan that specifies expected resource use across rounds. Their primal–dual methods achieve sublinear regret relative to baselines that follow that plan. The comparator restriction is central: the guarantee depends on which resource-use patterns the competing baseline follows.

Performance improves when the plan distributes the budget in a well-balanced way across rounds. The paper also provides a robust variant for highly imbalanced plans and studies comparisons against benchmarks that depart from the prescribed plan. Together, these results clarify how guidance about spending can support learning guarantees despite adversarial changes in rewards and costs.
summary.tldr: A spending plan enables sublinear regret against plan-following baselines under adversarially changing rewards and resource costs.

title: No-Regret Learning Under Adversarial Resource Constraints: A Spending Plan Is All You Need!

abstract: As training billion-scale transformers becomes increasingly common, employing multiple distributed GPUs along with parallel training methods has become a standard practice. However, existing transformer designs suffer from significant communication overhead, especially in Tensor Parallelism (TP), where each block’s MHA–MLP connection requires an all-reduce communication. Through our investigation, we show that the MHA-MLP connections can be bypassed for efficiency, while the attention output of the first layer can serve as an alternative signal for the bypassed connection. Motivated by the observations, we propose FAL (First Attentions Last), an efficient transformer architecture that redirects the first MHA output to the MLP inputs of the following layers, eliminating the per-block MHA-MLP connections. This removes the all-reduce communication and enables parallel execution of MHA and MLP on a single GPU. We also introduce FAL+, which adds the normalized first attention output to the MHA outputs of the following layers to augment the MLP input for the model quality. Our evaluation shows that FAL reduces multi-GPU training time by up to 44%, improves single-GPU throughput by up to 1.18×, and achieves better perplexity compared to the baseline GPT. FAL+ achieves even lower perplexity without increasing the training time than the baseline.

Through our investigation, we show that the MHA-MLP connections can be bypassed for efficiency, while the attention output of the first layer can serve as an alternative signal for the bypassed connection. This removes the all-reduce communication and enables parallel execution of MHA and MLP on a single GPU. We also introduce FAL+, which adds the normalized first attention output to the MHA outputs of the following layers to augment the MLP input for the model quality. Our evaluation shows that FAL reduces multi-GPU training time by up to 44%, improves single-GPU throughput by up to 1.18×, and achieves better perplexity compared to the baseline GPT. FAL+ achieves even lower perplexity without increasing the training time than the baseline.

paragraphs: Training large transformers across multiple GPUs involves communication as well as computation. Under tensor parallelism, the connection between each block’s attention module and its multilayer perceptron requires an all-reduce operation. This paper investigates whether that repeated connection can be bypassed while still giving the model a useful signal.

The proposed FAL architecture sends the first layer’s attention output to the multilayer perceptron inputs of later layers. Reusing that signal eliminates the usual per-block attention-to-perceptron connections and their associated all-reduce communication. It also permits attention and perceptron computation to execute in parallel on a single GPU. A second version, FAL+, combines normalized first-layer attention output with later attention outputs to enrich the input and improve model quality.

In the reported evaluation, FAL reduces multi-GPU training time by up to 44% and improves single-GPU throughput by up to 1.18 times while achieving better perplexity than the GPT baseline. FAL+ achieves still lower perplexity without exceeding the baseline’s training time. The results show that architectural information routing can improve both training efficiency and measured language-model quality.
summary.tldr: FAL reuses first-layer attention across later layers to reduce communication and enable parallel computation, improving training speed and perplexity in evaluations.

title: First Attentions Last: Better Exploiting First Attentions for Efficient Parallel Training

abstract: Online ride-hailing platforms aim to deliver efficient mobility-on-demand services, often facing challenges in balancing dynamic and spatially heterogeneous supply and demand. Existing methods typically fall into two categories: reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, which suffer from data inefficiency, oversimplified modeling of real-world dynamics, and difficulty enforcing operational constraints; or decomposed online optimization methods, which rely on manually designed high-level objectives that lack awareness of low-level routing dynamics. To address this issue, we propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates large language model (LLM) with mathematical optimization in a dynamic hierarchical system: (1) it is training-free, removing the need for large-scale interaction data as in RL, and (2) it leverages LLM to bridge cognitive limitations caused by problem decomposition by adaptively generating high-level objectives. Within this framework, LLM serves as a meta-optimizer, producing semantic heuristics that guide a low-level optimizer responsible for constraint enforcement and real-time decision execution. These heuristics are refined through a closed-loop evolutionary process, driven by harmony search, which iteratively adapts the LLM prompts based on feasibility and performance feedback from the optimization layer. Extensive experiments based on scenarios derived from both the New York and Chicago taxi datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving an average improvement of 16% compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

summary.tldr: A training-free framework evolves LLM-generated objectives using optimizer feedback and reports a 16% average improvement in taxi-derived scenarios.

title: Hierarchical Optimization via LLM-Guided Objective Evolution for Mobility-on-Demand Systems

abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing have enabled high-resolution profiling of diverse molecular modalities, while integrating unpaired multi-omics single-cell data remains challenging. Existing approaches either rely on pair information or prior correspondences, or require computing a global pairwise coupling matrix, limiting their scalability and flexibility. In this paper, we introduce a scalable and flexible generative framework called single-cell Multi-omics Regularized Disentangled Representations (scMRDR) for unpaired multi-omics integration. Specifically, we disentangle each cell’s latent representations into modality-shared and modality-specific components using a well-designed $\beta$-VAE architecture, which are augmented with isometric regularization to preserve intra-omics biological heterogeneity, adversarial objective to encourage cross-modal alignment, and masked reconstruction loss strategy to address the issue of missing features across modalities. Our method achieves excellent performance on benchmark datasets in terms of batch correction, modality alignment, and biological signal preservation. Crucially, it scales effectively to large-level datasets and supports integration of more than two omics, offering a powerful and flexible solution for large-scale multi-omics data integration and downstream biological discovery.

paragraphs: Single-cell experiments measure different molecular modalities, but combining unpaired measurements is difficult. Existing integration approaches may depend on known correspondences or on a global matrix coupling pairs of observations, restricting flexibility and scale. scMRDR introduces a generative framework for integrating unpaired multi-omics data through structured latent representations.

A beta-variational autoencoder separates each cell’s representation into information shared across modalities and information specific to its modality. Three objectives support this separation: isometric regularization preserves biological variation within each omics dataset, adversarial training encourages alignment across modalities, and masked reconstruction handles features missing across modalities. These components aim to reconcile shared structure without erasing meaningful differences.

Benchmark results show strong performance in batch correction, modality alignment, and preservation of biological signals. The framework also scales to large datasets and supports more than two omics. Its contribution is a combination of representational separation and complementary training objectives that makes integration more flexible while retaining information useful for downstream biological analysis.
summary.tldr: scMRDR integrates unpaired single-cell modalities by separating shared and modality-specific information while preserving biological variation.

title: scMRDR: A scalable and flexible framework for unpaired single-cell multi-omics data integration

abstract: Reconstructing detailed hand avatars plays a crucial role in various applications. While prior works have focused on capturing high-fidelity hand geometry, they heavily rely on high-resolution multi-view image inputs and struggle to generalize on low-resolution images. Multi-view image super-resolution methods have been proposed to enforce 3D view consistency. These methods, however, are limited to static objects/scenes with fixed resolutions and are not applicable to articulated deformable hands. In this paper, we propose SRHand (Super-Resolution Hand), the method for reconstructing detailed 3D geometry as well as textured images of hands from low-resolution images. SRHand leverages the advantages of implicit image representation with explicit hand meshes. Specifically, we introduce a geometric-aware implicit image function (GIIF) that learns detailed hand prior by upsampling the coarse input images. By jointly optimizing the implicit image function and explicit 3D hand shapes, our method preserves multi-view and pose consistency among upsampled hand images, and achieves fine-detailed 3D reconstruction (wrinkles, nails). In experiments using the InterHand2.6M and Goliath datasets, our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art image upsampling methods adapted to hand datasets, and 3D hand reconstruction methods, quantitatively and qualitatively. The code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: SRHand reconstructs detailed hand geometry and textured images from low-resolution inputs. Hands are challenging because they deform and articulate, so methods designed for static scenes cannot simply ensure consistency across changing poses. Existing detailed reconstruction methods also rely heavily on high-resolution images from multiple viewpoints.

The method combines an implicit image representation with an explicit three-dimensional hand mesh. Its geometry-aware implicit image function learns detailed hand priors while enlarging coarse input images. Jointly optimizing that function and the hand shape connects image enhancement to geometry, helping the resulting images stay consistent across viewpoints and poses.

This coordinated optimization produces fine geometric details such as wrinkles and nails. Experiments on InterHand2.6M and Goliath report significant quantitative and qualitative improvements over state-of-the-art image-upscaling methods adapted to hands and over three-dimensional hand reconstruction methods. The findings show the value of solving image enhancement and shape recovery together when the subject is deformable, rather than treating enhanced images as independent views of an unchanged object.
summary.tldr: SRHand jointly enhances low-resolution hand images and explicit meshes to reconstruct fine details consistently across viewpoints and poses.

title: SRHand: Super-Resolving Hand Images and 3D Shapes via View/Pose-aware Neural Image Representations and Explicit Meshes

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) typically process a large number of visual tokens, leading to considerable computational overhead, even though many of these tokens are redundant. Existing visual token pruning methods primarily focus on selecting the most salient tokens based on attention scores, resulting in the semantic incompleteness of the selected tokens. In this paper, we propose a novel visual token pruning strategy, called **S**aliency-**C**overage **O**riented token **P**runing for **E**fficient MLLMs (SCOPE), to jointly model both the saliency and coverage of the selected visual tokens to better preserve semantic completeness. Specifically, we introduce a set-coverage for a given set of selected tokens, computed based on the token relationships. We then define a token-coverage gain for each unselected token, quantifying how much additional coverage would be obtained by including it. By integrating the saliency score into the token-coverage gain, we propose our SCOPE score and iteratively select the token with the highest SCOPE score. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple vision-language understanding benchmarks using the LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-Next models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms prior approaches.

paragraphs: SCOPE reduces the number of visual tokens processed by a multimodal language model. Many tokens contain redundant information, but simply keeping those with the highest attention-based importance can leave the retained set semantically incomplete. The paper treats token selection as a joint problem of preserving salient information and covering the image's represented content.

The method defines coverage for a selected group of tokens using relationships among tokens. For every token not yet selected, it calculates how much additional coverage that token would provide. It combines this gain with the token's saliency to form a SCOPE score, then repeatedly selects the highest-scoring candidate. Selection therefore depends on what the retained set already represents, as well as each token's importance.

Experiments use LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-Next across multiple vision-language understanding benchmarks. The authors report consistent improvements over prior pruning approaches. The findings support considering the selected tokens collectively: a useful additional token is one that contributes important information while extending the coverage of the tokens already kept.
summary.tldr: SCOPE prunes visual tokens by balancing individual saliency with added coverage, improving results over prior methods on evaluated vision-language benchmarks.

title: SCOPE: Saliency-Coverage Oriented Token Pruning for Efficient Multimodel LLMs

abstract: We give algorithms with provable guarantees that learn a class of deep nets in the generative model view popularized by Hinton and others. Our generative model is an n node multilayer neural net that has degree at most n^γ for some γ< 1 and each edge has a random edge weight in [-1,1]. Our algorithm learns almost all networks in this class with polynomial running time. The sample complexity is quadratic or cubic depending upon the details of the model. The algorithm uses layerwise learning. It is based upon a novel idea of observing correlations among features and using these to infer the underlying edge structure via a global graph recovery procedure. The analysis of the algorithm reveals interesting structure of neural nets with random edge weights.

Our generative model is an n node multilayer neural net that has degree at most n^γ for some γ< 1 and each edge has a random edge weight in [-1,1]. Our algorithm learns almost all networks in this class with polynomial running time. The sample complexity is quadratic or cubic depending upon the details of the model. The algorithm uses layerwise learning. It is based upon a novel idea of observing correlations among features and using these to infer the underlying edge structure via a global graph recovery procedure. The analysis of the algorithm reveals interesting structure of neural nets with random edge weights.

paragraphs: This paper establishes learning guarantees for a particular class of deep generative neural networks. The networks contain n nodes, have degree at most n raised to a power γ below one, and use random edge weights in the interval [-1, 1]. These structural and randomness assumptions define the class covered by the results.

The proposed algorithm learns one layer at a time. It observes correlations among features and uses them to infer the underlying connections through a global graph recovery procedure. This connects a statistical signal in the observations to the network's hidden edge structure, providing a concrete mechanism for recovering successive layers.

The authors prove polynomial running time for learning almost all networks in this class. Depending on the model details, the required number of samples grows quadratically or cubically. The analysis also reveals structure in neural networks with random weights. The contribution is therefore a rigorous learnability result for a specified family of deep representations, with explicit computational and sample requirements tied to that family.
summary.tldr: Layerwise correlation analysis provably learns almost all networks in a specified bounded-degree, random-weight generative class in polynomial time.

title: Provable Bounds for Learning Some Deep Representations

abstract: Transfer learning has received a lot of attention in the machine learning community over the last years, and several effective algorithms have been developed. However, relatively little is known about their theoretical properties, especially in the setting of lifelong learning, where the goal is to transfer information to tasks for which no data have been observed so far. In this work we study lifelong learning from a theoretical perspective. Our main result is a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound that offers a unified view on existing paradigms for transfer learning, such as the transfer of parameters or the transfer of low-dimensional representations. We also use the bound to derive two principled lifelong learning algorithms, and we show that these yield results comparable with existing methods.

We also use the bound to derive two principled lifelong learning algorithms, and we show that these yield results comparable with existing methods.

paragraphs: Lifelong learning asks how experience with earlier tasks can help with future tasks whose data have not yet been observed. This makes the theoretical question broader than explaining performance on the tasks already available. The paper studies how information transferred across tasks can be connected to a generalization guarantee.

Its main contribution is a PAC-Bayesian bound that places different transfer strategies within one theoretical framework. In particular, the bound covers transferring model parameters and transferring low-dimensional representations. These approaches share different kinds of information, but the analysis offers a common way to understand their role in learning future tasks.

The authors also use the bound to derive two learning algorithms, so the theoretical result serves as a basis for designing procedures. Their reported results are comparable with existing methods. The contribution therefore combines a unified account of transfer with algorithms motivated by that account, without claiming an empirical advantage over all existing approaches.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian generalization bound unifies parameter and representation transfer and yields two lifelong learning algorithms with results comparable to existing methods.

title: A PAC-Bayesian bound for Lifelong Learning

abstract: We explore a novel approach to upper bound the misclassification error for problems with data comprising a small number of positive samples and a large number of negative samples. We assign the hinge-loss to upper bound the misclassification error of the positive examples and use the minimax risk to upper bound the misclassification error with respect to the worst case distribution that generates the negative examples. This approach is computationally appealing since the majority of training examples (belonging to the negative class) are represented by the statistics of their distribution, in contrast to kernel SVM which produces a very large number of support vectors in such settings. We derive empirical risk bounds for linear and non-linear classification and show that they are dimensionally independent and decay as 1/\sqrtm for m samples. We propose an efficient algorithm for training an intersection of finite number of hyperplane and demonstrate its effectiveness on real data, including letter and scene recognition.

Its approach treats the two classes differently when bounding classification errors. Positive examples are handled with hinge loss, while negative examples are handled through a minimax risk representing a worst-case generating distribution.

The computational motivation is to summarize the many negative examples through distributional statistics. This avoids the large collection of support vectors that the abstract identifies as a difficulty for kernel support-vector machines in this setting. The formulation combines sample-based treatment of the small positive class with a distribution-based treatment of the large negative class.

The authors derive empirical risk bounds for linear and nonlinear classification that do not depend on dimension and decrease at a rate of 1/√m for m samples. They also propose an efficient training algorithm for a classifier formed from an intersection of finitely many hyperplanes. Experiments on real data, including letter and scene recognition, demonstrate effectiveness. The results combine theoretical error control with a computational strategy tailored to class imbalance.
summary.tldr: A hinge-minimax classifier handles scarce positives and abundant negatives using class-specific error bounds and statistical summaries of the negative class.

title: K-hyperplane Hinge-Minimax Classifier

abstract: With the rapid growth of crowdsourcing platforms it has become easy and relatively inexpensive to collect a dataset labeled by multiple annotators in a short time. However due to the lack of control over the quality of the annotators, some abnormal annotators may be affected by position bias which can potentially degrade the quality of the final consensus labels. In this paper we introduce a statistical framework to model and detect annotator’s position bias in order to control the false discovery rate (FDR) without a prior knowledge on the amount of biased annotators–the expected fraction of false discoveries among all discoveries being not too high, in order to assure that most of the discoveries are indeed true and replicable. The key technical development relies on some new knockoff filters adapted to our problem and new algorithms based on the Inverse Scale Space dynamics whose discretization is potentially suitable for large scale crowdsourcing data analysis. Our studies are supported by experiments with both simulated examples and real-world data. The proposed framework provides us a useful tool for quantitatively studying annotator’s abnormal behavior in crowdsourcing.

paragraphs: The paper addresses position bias in crowdsourced ranking: some annotators may respond partly to where an option appears, potentially degrading the final consensus labels. Collecting many annotations cheaply does not by itself resolve this problem. The authors develop a statistical framework for modeling and detecting this particular form of abnormal annotation behavior.

The framework controls the false discovery rate without requiring advance knowledge of how many annotators are biased. This targets the expected fraction of incorrect flags among all flagged annotators. It therefore evaluates the reliability of the collection of discoveries, rather than promising that each individual flag must be correct.

The technical approach adapts knockoff filters and introduces algorithms based on inverse scale space dynamics. Their discretization is described as potentially suitable for large-scale crowdsourcing analysis, preserving a distinction between proposed scalability and an unconditional scalability guarantee. Experiments with simulated and real-world data support the approach. The resulting tool makes annotator assessment quantitative while explicitly accounting for false accusations of position bias.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework detects position-biased annotators while controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries.

title: False Discovery Rate Control and Statistical Quality Assessment of Annotators in Crowdsourced Ranking

abstract: In many settings, we have multiple data sets (also called views) that capture different and overlapping aspects of the same phenomenon. We are often interested in finding patterns that are unique to one or to a subset of the views. For example, we might have one set of molecular observations and one set of physiological observations on the same group of individuals, and we want to quantify molecular patterns that are uncorrelated with physiology. Despite being a common problem, this is highly challenging when the correlations come from complex distributions. In this paper, we develop the general framework of Rich Component Analysis (RCA) to model settings where the observations from different views are driven by different sets of latent components, and each component can be a complex, high-dimensional distribution. We introduce algorithms based on cumulant extraction that provably learn each of the components without having to model the other components. We show how to integrate RCA with stochastic gradient descent into a meta-algorithm for learning general models, and demonstrate substantial improvement in accuracy on several synthetic and real datasets in both supervised and unsupervised tasks. Our method makes it possible to learn latent variable models when we don’t have samples from the true model but only samples after complex perturbations.

paragraphs: Rich Component Analysis addresses multiple datasets that describe overlapping aspects of the same phenomenon. The goal is to recover patterns belonging to one view or a subset of views. For example, molecular and physiological measurements may share some structure, while a researcher wants to isolate molecular patterns uncorrelated with physiology.

The framework models each view as driven by a different collection of latent components. Each component may itself be a complex, high-dimensional distribution. The authors introduce algorithms based on cumulant extraction that provably learn individual components without requiring the other components to be modeled. This makes selective recovery of structure the central operation of the method.

The paper combines RCA with stochastic gradient descent in a general model-learning procedure. Experiments show substantial accuracy improvements on synthetic and real datasets in supervised and unsupervised tasks. The framework also enables learning latent-variable models from samples altered by complex perturbations, extending its use to situations where samples from the unperturbed model are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Rich Component Analysis recovers latent components from overlapping data views without needing to model the other components.

title: Rich Component Analysis

abstract: A long-standing obstacle to progress in deep learning is the problem of vanishing and exploding gradients. Although, the problem has largely been overcome via carefully constructed initializations and batch normalization, architectures incorporating skip-connections such as highway and resnets perform much better than standard feedforward architectures despite well-chosen initialization and batch normalization. In this paper, we identify the shattered gradients problem. Specifically, we show that the correlation between gradients in standard feedforward networks decays exponentially with depth resulting in gradients that resemble white noise whereas, in contrast, the gradients in architectures with skip-connections are far more resistant to shattering, decaying sublinearly. Detailed empirical evidence is presented in support of the analysis, on both fully-connected networks and convnets. Finally, we present a new “looks linear” (LL) initialization that prevents shattering, with preliminary experiments showing the new initialization allows to train very deep networks without the addition of skip-connections.

Although, the problem has largely been overcome via carefully constructed initializations and batch normalization, architectures incorporating skip-connections such as highway and resnets perform much better than standard feedforward architectures despite well-chosen initialization and batch normalization. In this paper, we identify the shattered gradients problem. Specifically, we show that the correlation between gradients in standard feedforward networks decays exponentially with depth resulting in gradients that resemble white noise whereas, in contrast, the gradients in architectures with skip-connections are far more resistant to shattering, decaying sublinearly. Detailed empirical evidence is presented in support of the analysis, on both fully-connected networks and convnets. Finally, we present a new “looks linear” (LL) initialization that prevents shattering, with preliminary experiments showing the new initialization allows to train very deep networks without the addition of skip-connections.

paragraphs: Keeping gradients from vanishing or exploding does not fully explain why very deep networks can be difficult to train. This paper identifies another problem: gradients can lose their correlation as depth increases, eventually resembling white noise. The authors call this phenomenon gradient shattering and use it to investigate the advantages of skip connections.

Their analysis shows exponential decay of gradient correlations with depth in standard feedforward networks. Architectures with skip connections are more resistant, with sublinear decay. Empirical evidence from both fully connected networks and convolutional networks supports the analysis. This shifts attention from gradient magnitude alone to the structure of the gradients that guide learning.

The authors also introduce a looks-linear initialization designed to prevent shattering. Preliminary experiments show that this initialization allows very deep networks to be trained without adding skip connections. Those early results suggest initialization can address the identified problem, while the broader contribution explains an optimization difficulty that remains relevant even when gradient magnitudes are well controlled.
summary.tldr: Gradient correlations can shatter with depth; skip connections resist this effect, and a new initialization shows preliminary promise in preventing it.

title: The Shattered Gradients Problem: If resnets are the answer, then what is the question?

abstract: This paper introduces a new general framework for forest-type regression which allows the development of robust forest regressors by selecting from a large family of robust loss functions. In particular, when plugged in the squared error and quantile losses, it will recover the classical random forest and quantile random forest. We then use robust loss functions to develop more robust forest-type regression algorithms. In the experiments, we show by simulation and real data that our robust forests are indeed much more insensitive to outliers, and choosing the right number of nearest neighbors can quickly improve the generalization performance of random forest.

In particular, when plugged in the squared error and quantile losses, it will recover the classical random forest and quantile random forest. We then use robust loss functions to develop more robust forest-type regression algorithms. In the experiments, we show by simulation and real data that our robust forests are indeed much more insensitive to outliers, and choosing the right number of nearest neighbors can quickly improve the generalization performance of random forest.

paragraphs: A regression loss determines which prediction errors a method treats as costly. This paper introduces a general framework for forest-type regression in which that loss can be selected from a broad family. The flexibility makes it possible to construct forest regressors specifically intended to reduce sensitivity to outliers.

The framework also includes familiar methods: choosing squared-error loss recovers classical random forests, while choosing quantile loss recovers quantile random forests. These connections show how different forest estimators fit within one formulation. The authors then use robust losses to develop additional regressors, making robustness an explicit modeling choice within the same framework.

Experiments with simulated and real data find that the robust forests are substantially less sensitive to outliers. The authors also report that selecting an appropriate number of nearest neighbors can quickly improve random-forest generalization. The findings identify both loss selection and neighborhood size as useful choices in the studied forest methods, with the robustness improvements demonstrated empirically.
summary.tldr: A general-loss framework unifies familiar forest regressors and produces robust variants that are less sensitive to outliers in experiments.

title: Forest-type Regression with General Losses and Robust Forest

abstract: The past few years have witnessed a growth in size and computational requirements for training and inference with neural networks. Currently, a common approach to address these requirements is to use a heterogeneous distributed environment with a mixture of hardware devices such as CPUs and GPUs. Importantly, the decision of placing parts of the neural models on devices is often made by human experts based on simple heuristics and intuitions. In this paper, we propose a method which learns to optimize device placement for TensorFlow computational graphs. Key to our method is the use of a sequence-to-sequence model to predict which subsets of operations in a TensorFlow graph should run on which of the available devices. The execution time of the predicted placements is then used as the reward signal to optimize the parameters of the sequence-to-sequence model. Our main result is that on Inception-V3 for ImageNet classification, and on RNN LSTM, for language modeling and neural machine translation, our model finds non-trivial device placements that outperform hand-crafted heuristics and traditional algo-rithmic methods.

paragraphs: Running a neural network across different hardware devices requires deciding where its computations should execute. Those choices are often made by experts using heuristics and intuition. This paper treats placement as a learning problem for TensorFlow computational graphs, aiming to automate decisions about distributing operations across available devices.

A sequence-to-sequence model predicts placements for subsets of graph operations. The proposed placement is executed, and its execution time supplies the reward signal used to optimize the placement model. This connects the learning objective directly to runtime: the model receives feedback from how its proposed allocation actually performs.

The reported results cover Inception-V3 for ImageNet classification and LSTM recurrent networks for language modeling and neural machine translation. On those workloads, the method discovers nontrivial placements that outperform handcrafted heuristics and traditional algorithmic approaches. These findings show that learned placement can improve execution decisions in the evaluated settings, making hardware allocation another part of the neural-network workflow that can be optimized from experience.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-trained sequence model learns device placements that improve runtime over manual and algorithmic alternatives on the evaluated networks.

title: Device Placement Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have recently received increasing attention for their ability to provide well-calibrated posterior uncertainties. However, model selection—even choosing the number of nodes—remains an open question. Recent work has proposed the use of a horseshoe prior over node pre-activations of a Bayesian neural network, which effectively turns off nodes that do not help explain the data. In this work, we propose several modeling and inference advances that consistently improve the compactness of the model learned while maintaining predictive performance, especially in smaller-sample settings including reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks are attractive for their ability to express calibrated uncertainty, but deciding how large a network should be remains a model-selection problem. This paper focuses on compactness, including the question of how many nodes are needed. The goal is to reduce unnecessary model capacity while preserving useful predictive performance.

The starting point is earlier work placing a horseshoe prior over node pre-activations. That prior can effectively deactivate nodes that do not contribute to explaining the data. It therefore provides a mechanism for choosing an effective network size within learning, with the data helping determine which nodes remain useful.

The authors propose several advances in modeling and inference within this approach. They report that these changes consistently produce more compact learned models while maintaining prediction quality, especially when samples are limited, including reinforcement-learning settings. The stated result links network-size reduction with preserved performance: the value comes from removing unhelpful nodes without paying a corresponding predictive cost in the settings considered.
summary.tldr: Modeling and inference advances for horseshoe-prior Bayesian networks improve compactness while maintaining predictive performance, especially with limited samples.

title: Structured Variational Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks with Horseshoe Priors

abstract: Despite recent advances in training recurrent neural networks (RNNs), capturing long-term dependencies in sequences remains a fundamental challenge. Most approaches use backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is difficult to scale to very long sequences. This paper proposes a simple method that improves the ability to capture long term dependencies in RNNs by adding an unsupervised auxiliary loss to the original objective. This auxiliary loss forces RNNs to either reconstruct previous events or predict next events in a sequence, making truncated backpropagation feasible for long sequences and also improving full BPTT. We evaluate our method on a variety of settings, including pixel-by-pixel image classification with sequence lengths up to 16000, and a real document classification benchmark. Our results highlight good performance and resource efficiency of this approach over competitive baselines, including other recurrent models and a comparable sized Transformer. Further analyses reveal beneficial effects of the auxiliary loss on optimization and regularization, as well as extreme cases where there is little to no backpropagation.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the difficulty of learning relationships across very long sequences with recurrent neural networks. Standard backpropagation through time becomes difficult to scale as sequences lengthen. The authors add an unsupervised auxiliary loss to the main training objective, giving the network an additional task connected to the sequence itself.

That task asks the network either to reconstruct earlier events or predict upcoming ones. The added learning signal improves the ability to capture long-term dependencies, makes truncated backpropagation feasible for long sequences, and also benefits full backpropagation through time. The approach changes the training objective to help the recurrent model retain useful sequential information.

Experiments include pixel-by-pixel image classification with sequences up to 16,000 steps and a document classification benchmark. The reported results show good performance and resource efficiency against competitive recurrent models and a similarly sized Transformer. Further analysis identifies optimization and regularization benefits and examines extreme settings with little or no backpropagation, broadening the evidence about how the auxiliary objective helps.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary reconstruction or prediction losses help recurrent networks learn long-term dependencies efficiently.

title: Learning Longer-term Dependencies in RNNs with Auxiliary Losses

abstract: This paper develops coding techniques to reduce the running time of distributed learning tasks. It characterizes the fundamental tradeoff to compute gradients in terms of three parameters: computation load, straggler tolerance and communication cost. It further gives an explicit coding scheme that achieves the optimal tradeoff based on recursive polynomial constructions, coding both across data subsets and vector components. As a result, the proposed scheme allows to minimize the running time for gradient computations. Implementations are made on Amazon EC2 clusters using Python with mpi4py package. Results show that the proposed scheme maintains the same generalization error while reducing the running time by $32%$ compared to uncoded schemes and $23%$ compared to prior coded schemes focusing only on stragglers (Tandon et al., ICML 2017).

paragraphs: Distributed gradient computation can be slowed both by workers that finish late and by the amount of information workers must send. Adding redundant computation can tolerate slow workers, but redundancy also has a cost. This paper studies those competing demands together rather than optimizing straggler tolerance alone.

The authors characterize a fundamental tradeoff among computation load, straggler tolerance, and communication cost. They construct a coding scheme that achieves the optimal tradeoff using recursive polynomials. The scheme codes across both data subsets and gradient-vector components, giving it control over the amount of work assigned and the amount of information communicated.

Implementations on Amazon EC2 use Python and mpi4py. The reported experiments preserve generalization error while reducing running time by 32% relative to uncoded schemes and 23% relative to a prior straggler-focused coded method. These results support the practical value of jointly managing communication and redundant computation for the distributed learning workloads evaluated.
summary.tldr: Gradient coding jointly optimizes computation, communication, and straggler tolerance to reduce distributed training time.

title: Communication-Computation Efficient Gradient Coding

abstract: Interpretable modeling of heterogeneous data channels is essential in medical applications, for example when jointly analyzing clinical scores and medical images. Variational Autoencoders (VAE) are powerful generative models that learn representations of complex data. The flexibility of VAE may come at the expense of lack of interpretability in describing the joint relationship between heterogeneous data. To tackle this problem, in this work we extend the variational framework of VAE to bring parsimony and interpretability when jointly account for latent relationships across multiple channels. In the latent space, this is achieved by constraining the variational distribution of each channel to a common target prior. Parsimonious latent representations are enforced by variational dropout. Experiments on synthetic data show that our model correctly identifies the prescribed latent dimensions and data relationships across multiple testing scenarios. When applied to imaging and clinical data, our method allows to identify the joint effect of age and pathology in describing clinical condition in a large scale clinical cohort.

paragraphs: Combining different kinds of medical data can reveal relationships that are difficult to see within one source alone. A model might jointly analyze clinical scores and medical images, for example. Variational autoencoders can represent such complex data, but their flexibility can make the learned relationships between data channels difficult to interpret.

This paper extends the variational autoencoder framework to encourage compact, interpretable latent representations across multiple channels. Each channel’s variational distribution is constrained toward a shared target prior. Variational dropout further encourages a parsimonious representation, so the joint model is pushed to describe the data through a restrained set of latent dimensions.

In synthetic experiments, the model identifies the intended latent dimensions and relationships across several testing scenarios. Applied to imaging and clinical measurements from a large clinical cohort, it identifies joint effects of age and pathology in describing clinical condition. These results support the use of the representation for examining relationships across heterogeneous measurements, with the synthetic experiments checking recovery of known structure and the clinical application demonstrating joint analysis of real data.
summary.tldr: A sparse multi-channel variational autoencoder learns compact shared representations that help interpret relationships between heterogeneous clinical and imaging data.

title: Sparse Multi-Channel Variational Autoencoder for the Joint Analysis of Heterogeneous Data

abstract: Suppose an agent is in a (possibly unknown) Markov Decision Process in the absence of a reward signal, what might we hope that an agent can efficiently learn to do? This work studies a broad class of objectives that are defined solely as functions of the state-visitation frequencies that are induced by how the agent behaves. For example, one natural, intrinsically defined, objective problem is for the agent to learn a policy which induces a distribution over state space that is as uniform as possible, which can be measured in an entropic sense. We provide an efficient algorithm to optimize such such intrinsically defined objectives, when given access to a black box planning oracle (which is robust to function approximation). Furthermore, when restricted to the tabular setting where we have sample based access to the MDP, our proposed algorithm is provably efficient, both in terms of its sample and computational complexities. Key to our algorithmic methodology is utilizing the conditional gradient method (a.k.a. the Frank-Wolfe algorithm) which utilizes an approximate MDP solver.

paragraphs: Without a reward signal, an agent still needs an objective if it is to explore purposefully. This paper studies objectives determined entirely by how often the agent visits different states. One example is making the state-visitation distribution as uniform as possible, with entropy measuring how broadly visits are spread.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm for these intrinsically defined objectives using a black-box planning oracle that is robust to function approximation. The central optimization tool is the conditional gradient, or Frank-Wolfe, method, combined with an approximate solver for the Markov decision process. This connects a desired visitation pattern to the policies needed to produce it.

For tabular environments with sample-based access, the authors prove efficiency in both sample requirements and computation. These guarantees apply to the specified setting, while the broader algorithm is framed through access to the planning oracle. The contribution establishes that reward-free exploration can be organized around explicit distributional objectives and, under the stated access conditions, optimized with provable efficiency.
summary.tldr: A planning-based algorithm optimizes reward-free state-visitation objectives, including maximum entropy, with sample and computational guarantees in the tabular setting.

title: Provably Efficient Maximum Entropy Exploration

abstract: Many tasks, including language generation, benefit from learning the structure of the output space, particularly when the space of output labels is large and the data is sparse. State-of-the-art neural language models indirectly capture the output space structure in their classifier weights since they lack parameter sharing across output labels. Learning shared output label mappings helps, but existing methods have limited expressivity and are prone to overfitting. In this paper, we investigate the usefulness of more powerful shared mappings for output labels, and propose a deep residual output mapping with dropout between layers to better capture the structure of the output space and avoid overfitting. Evaluations on three language generation tasks show that our output label mapping can match or improve state-of-the-art recurrent and self-attention architectures, and suggest that the classifier does not necessarily need to be high-rank to better model natural language if it is better at capturing the structure of the output space.

paragraphs: Language generation requires choosing among many output labels, often with limited data for individual labels. This paper focuses on learning relationships within that output space. Standard classifier weights capture those relationships indirectly, while existing shared mappings across labels offer limited expressiveness and can overfit.

The proposed approach uses a deep residual mapping shared across output labels. Its additional depth provides a more expressive way to represent output structure, while dropout between layers addresses overfitting. This changes how the model represents and relates its possible outputs, making the output mapping itself a focus of architectural design.

Evaluations across three language-generation tasks show that this mapping can match or improve leading recurrent and self-attention architectures. The findings also suggest that a classifier need not have high rank to model language better when its representation captures output structure more effectively. This is a qualified empirical conclusion about the value of a better shared mapping, rather than a universal claim that classifier rank is unimportant.
summary.tldr: Deep residual mappings shared across output labels improve language-generation modeling by capturing output structure while using dropout to reduce overfitting.

title: Deep Residual Output Layers for Neural Language Generation

abstract: Multivariate Hawkes processes (MHP) are widely used in a variety of fields to model the occurrence of discrete events. Prior work on learning MHPs has only focused on inference in the presence of perfect traces without noise. We address the problem of learning the causal structure of MHPs when observations are subject to an unknown delay. In particular, we introduce the so-called synchronization noise, where the stream of events generated by each dimension is subject to a random and unknown time shift. We characterize the robustness of the classic maximum likelihood estimator to synchronization noise, and we introduce a new approach for learning the causal structure in the presence of noise. Our experimental results show that our approach accurately recovers the causal structure of MHPs for a wide range of noise levels, and significantly outperforms classic estimation methods.

We characterize the robustness of the classic maximum likelihood estimator to synchronization noise, and we introduce a new approach for learning the causal structure in the presence of noise.
