paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model discrete events occurring across multiple streams. This paper studies learning their causal structure when the streams are not correctly aligned in time. The problem is relevant to inference from observations whose timing differs from the underlying event process because of unknown delays.

The authors formalize synchronization noise by giving each dimension's event stream a random, unknown time shift. This is a specific observation model: uncertainty concerns the alignment of streams. They characterize how robust the classical maximum likelihood estimator is to this noise and introduce a new approach for recovering causal structure when synchronization noise is present.

Experiments show accurate recovery across a wide range of noise levels and substantial improvements over classical estimation methods. These findings support explicitly addressing timing misalignment when learning relationships between event streams. The contribution includes both an analysis of an established estimator under the proposed noise model and a learning approach whose reported empirical performance remains strong across the tested noise levels.
summary.tldr: A new method recovers Hawkes process causal structure under unknown time shifts, outperforming classical estimators across tested noise levels.

title: Learning Hawkes Processes Under Synchronization Noise

abstract: We present an extension to the disjoint paths problem in which additional lifted edges are introduced to provide path connectivity priors. We call the resulting optimization problem the lifted disjoint paths problem. We show that this problem is NP-hard by reduction from integer multicommodity flow and 3-SAT. To enable practical global optimization, we propose several classes of linear inequalities that produce a high-quality LP-relaxation. Additionally, we propose efficient cutting plane algorithms for separating the proposed linear inequalities. The lifted disjoint path problem is a natural model for multiple object tracking and allows an elegant mathematical formulation for long range temporal interactions. Lifted edges help to prevent id switches and to re-identify persons. Our lifted disjoint paths tracker achieves nearly optimal assignments with respect to input detections. As a consequence, it leads on all three main benchmarks of the MOT challenge, improving significantly over state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Multiple-object tracking requires linking detections across time into consistent object trajectories. This paper extends the disjoint paths problem with lifted edges that express preferences about path connectivity. These additional connections provide a mathematical way to include interactions between detections that are far apart in time.

The resulting lifted disjoint paths problem is NP-hard, as shown through reductions from integer multicommodity flow and 3-SAT. To make optimization practical, the authors develop classes of linear inequalities that strengthen a linear-programming relaxation. Efficient cutting-plane algorithms identify relevant inequalities, allowing the optimization procedure to use these constraints effectively.

In tracking, lifted edges help maintain identities and re-identify people, addressing decisions that depend on more than nearby frames. The proposed tracker obtains assignments that are nearly optimal relative to its input detections. The authors report leading performance on all three main MOT challenge benchmarks, with significant gains over prior methods. This ties the richer connectivity model and its optimization machinery to improved tracking outcomes.
summary.tldr: Lifted edges model long-range tracking relationships, while strong relaxations and cutting planes make the resulting hard optimization problem practical.

title: Lifted Disjoint Paths with Application in Multiple Object Tracking

abstract: For an explanation of a deep learning model to be effective, it must provide both insight into a model and suggest a corresponding action in order to achieve some objective. Too often, the litany of proposed explainable deep learning methods stop at the first step, providing practitioners with insight into a model, but no way to act on it. In this paper, we propose contextual decomposition explanation penalization (CDEP), a method which enables practitioners to leverage existing explanation methods to increase the predictive accuracy of a deep learning model. In particular, when shown that a model has incorrectly assigned importance to some features, CDEP enables practitioners to correct these errors by inserting domain knowledge into the model via explanations. We demonstrate the ability of CDEP to increase performance on an array of toy and real datasets.

In this paper, we propose contextual decomposition explanation penalization (CDEP), a method which enables practitioners to leverage existing explanation methods to increase the predictive accuracy of a deep learning model. In particular, when shown that a model has incorrectly assigned importance to some features, CDEP enables practitioners to correct these errors by inserting domain knowledge into the model via explanations. paragraphs: An explanation can reveal that a neural network gives importance to the wrong features, yet that insight alone does not change the model. This paper focuses on the next step: giving practitioners a way to act on what an explanation reveals. Its objective is to improve predictions by incorporating relevant domain knowledge during learning.

The proposed method, contextual decomposition explanation penalization, or CDEP, uses explanations as a channel for that knowledge. When a practitioner identifies an incorrect assignment of feature importance, explanation penalties provide a means to correct it. The approach connects the diagnosis of a model's behavior to a training intervention aimed at changing that behavior.

The authors demonstrate improved performance across toy and real datasets. These findings show that explanations can have a practical role in model development beyond helping people inspect predictions. The contribution is a method for translating knowledge about inappropriate feature importance into learning guidance, with empirical evidence that doing so can improve predictive accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: CDEP turns explanation-based judgments about incorrect feature importance into training penalties that can improve predictive accuracy.

title: Interpretations are Useful: Penalizing Explanations to Align Neural Networks with Prior Knowledge

abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful approach to learn behaviour through interactions with an environment. However, behaviours are usually learned in a purely reactive fashion, where an appropriate action is selected based on an observation. In this form, it is challenging to learn when it is necessary to execute new decisions. This makes learning inefficient especially in environments that need various degrees of fine and coarse control. To address this, we propose a proactive setting in which the agent not only selects an action in a state but also for how long to commit to that action. Our TempoRL approach introduces skip connections between states and learns a skip-policy for repeating the same action along these skips. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TempoRL on a variety of traditional and deep RL environments, showing that our approach is capable of learning successful policies up to an order of magnitude faster than vanilla Q-learning.

However, behaviours are usually learned in a purely reactive fashion, where an appropriate action is selected based on an observation. In this form, it is challenging to learn when it is necessary to execute new decisions. This makes learning inefficient especially in environments that need various degrees of fine and coarse control. To address this, we propose a proactive setting in which the agent not only selects an action in a state but also for how long to commit to that action. Our TempoRL approach introduces skip connections between states and learns a skip-policy for repeating the same action along these skips. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TempoRL on a variety of traditional and deep RL environments, showing that our approach is capable of learning successful policies up to an order of magnitude faster than vanilla Q-learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents usually select an action in response to each observation. That reactive setup does not directly teach them when another decision is needed. Environments may require close control in some situations and sustained actions in others, so repeatedly deciding at the same temporal granularity can make learning inefficient.

TempoRL expands the decision to include both an action and how long to continue it. It introduces skip connections between states and learns a skip-policy that repeats the selected action across those skips. This gives the agent a learned way to commit to an action for a period of time, making action duration part of its behavior.

The authors evaluate TempoRL in a variety of traditional and deep reinforcement-learning environments. They show that it can learn successful policies up to an order of magnitude faster than vanilla Q-learning. The finding supports learning when to reconsider an action as a useful component of reinforcement learning, with the largest reported speed improvement representing an achieved outcome rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: TempoRL learns how long to repeat actions, enabling successful policy learning up to ten times faster than vanilla Q-learning.

title: TempoRL: Learning When to Act

abstract: This paper tackles the problem of adversarial examples from a game theoretic point of view. We study the open question of the existence of mixed Nash equilibria in the zero-sum game formed by the attacker and the classifier. While previous works usually allow only one player to use randomized strategies, we show the necessity of considering randomization for both the classifier and the attacker. We demonstrate that this game has no duality gap, meaning that it always admits approximate Nash equilibria. We also provide the first optimization algorithms to learn a mixture of classifiers that approximately realizes the value of this game, \emph{i.e.} procedures to build an optimally robust randomized classifier.

We study the open question of the existence of mixed Nash equilibria in the zero-sum game formed by the attacker and the classifier. While previous works usually allow only one player to use randomized strategies, we show the necessity of considering randomization for both the classifier and the attacker. We demonstrate that this game has no duality gap, meaning that it always admits approximate Nash equilibria. We also provide the first optimization algorithms to learn a mixture of classifiers that approximately realizes the value of this game, \emph{i.e.} procedures to build an optimally robust randomized classifier.

paragraphs: This paper views adversarial examples as a zero-sum game between an attacker and a classifier. The attacker seeks outcomes that harm classification, while the classifier seeks robustness. The central question is whether the game has mixed Nash equilibria, which allow players to randomize their strategies instead of committing to a single choice.

The authors show the necessity of considering randomization for both players, whereas earlier work usually allowed it for only one. They establish that the game has no duality gap: the two opposing optimization perspectives agree on its value. The stated consequence is that approximate Nash equilibria always exist, providing a theoretical target for robust learning.

The paper also supplies optimization algorithms that learn a mixture of classifiers approximately achieving the game’s value. This connects the equilibrium analysis to procedures for constructing an optimally robust randomized classifier in the studied formulation. The approximation qualification matters: the algorithms aim to approach the game value, and the existence result explicitly guarantees approximate equilibria.
summary.tldr: Allowing both attacker and classifier to randomize yields approximate-equilibrium guarantees and algorithms for learning robust classifier mixtures.

title: Mixed Nash Equilibria in the Adversarial Examples Game

abstract: With the development of graph kernels and graph representation learning, many superior methods have been proposed to handle scalability and oversmoothing issues on graph structure learning. However, most of those strategies are designed based on practical experience rather than theoretical analysis. In this paper, we use a particular dummy node connecting to all existing vertices without affecting original vertex and edge properties. We further prove that such the dummy node can help build an efficient monomorphic edge-to-vertex transform and an epimorphic inverse to recover the original graph back. It also indicates that adding dummy nodes can preserve local and global structures for better graph representation learning. We extend graph kernels and graph neural networks with dummy nodes and conduct experiments on graph classification and subgraph isomorphism matching tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that taking graphs with dummy nodes as input significantly boosts graph structure learning, and using their edge-to-vertex graphs can also achieve similar results. We also discuss the gain of expressive power from the dummy in neural networks.
originalAbstract: With the development of graph kernels and graph representation learning, many superior methods have been proposed to handle scalability and oversmoothing issues on graph structure learning. However, most of those strategies are designed based on practical experience rather than theoretical analysis. In this paper, we use a particular dummy node connecting to all existing vertices without affecting original vertex and edge properties. We further prove that such the dummy node can help build an efficient monomorphic edge-to-vertex transform and an epimorphic inverse to recover the original graph back. It also indicates that adding dummy nodes can preserve local and global structures for better graph representation learning. We extend graph kernels and graph neural networks with dummy nodes and conduct experiments on graph classification and subgraph isomorphism matching tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that taking graphs with dummy nodes as input significantly boosts graph structure learning, and using their edge-to-vertex graphs can also achieve similar results. We also discuss the gain of expressive power from the dummy in neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a simple modification to graph inputs: adding a dummy node connected to every existing vertex. The original vertices and edges retain their properties. The goal is to strengthen graph structure learning while providing a theoretical explanation for the modification, rather than relying only on an architectural choice that works in practice.

The authors prove that the additional node supports an efficient transformation from edges to vertices, together with an inverse that recovers the original graph. The analysis indicates that the construction can preserve both local and global structure. This gives the added node a structural role beyond simply introducing another place for a model to aggregate information.

The authors incorporate dummy nodes into graph kernels and graph neural networks, testing graph classification and subgraph isomorphism matching. Their experiments report significant improvements when models receive the augmented graphs, with similar results from the corresponding edge-to-vertex graphs. They also discuss increased neural-network expressive power, linking the empirical gains to how graph structure can be represented.
summary.tldr: Adding a universally connected dummy node supports structure-preserving graph transformations and improves graph learning in the reported experiments.

title: Boosting Graph Structure Learning with Dummy Nodes

abstract: Robust overfitting widely exists in adversarial training of deep networks. The exact underlying reasons for this are still not completely understood. Here, we explore the causes of robust overfitting by comparing the data distribution of non-overfit (weak adversary) and overfitted (strong adversary) adversarial training, and observe that the distribution of the adversarial data generated by weak adversary mainly contain small-loss data. However, the adversarial data generated by strong adversary is more diversely distributed on the large-loss data and the small-loss data. Given these observations, we further designed data ablation adversarial training and identify that some small-loss data which are not worthy of the adversary strength cause robust overfitting in the strong adversary mode. To relieve this issue, we propose minimum loss constrained adversarial training (MLCAT): in a minibatch, we learn large-loss data as usual, and adopt additional measures to increase the loss of the small-loss data. Technically, MLCAT hinders data fitting when they become easy to learn to prevent robust overfitting; philosophically, MLCAT reflects the spirit of turning waste into treasure and making the best use of each adversarial data; algorithmically, we designed two realizations of MLCAT, and extensive experiments demonstrate that MLCAT can eliminate robust overfitting and further boost adversarial robustness.

This paper investigates the issue by comparing training examples produced by weak and strong adversaries. Weak-adversary examples mainly have small losses, while strong-adversary examples include a more varied mixture of small-loss and large-loss cases.

Through data ablation experiments, the authors identify some small-loss examples as a cause of robust overfitting in the strong-adversary setting. They propose minimum loss constrained adversarial training, or MLCAT. Within each minibatch, large-loss examples are learned normally, while additional measures increase the loss of small-loss examples, hindering fitting once those examples become easy to learn.

The authors develop two realizations of this principle. Extensive experiments show that MLCAT can eliminate robust overfitting and further improve adversarial robustness. The contribution links an observed difference in loss distributions to a targeted change in training behavior. Its empirical success supports treating easy adversarial examples differently within the studied setting, without turning the identified mechanism into a complete explanation of every instance of robust overfitting.
summary.tldr: MLCAT counteracts robust overfitting by increasing losses on easy adversarial examples, with experiments showing improved adversarial robustness.

title: Understanding Robust Overfitting of Adversarial Training and Beyond

abstract: We initiate the study of strategic behavior in screening processes with multiple classifiers. We focus on two contrasting settings: a "conjunctive” setting in which an individual must satisfy all classifiers simultaneously, and a sequential setting in which an individual to succeed must satisfy classifiers one at a time. In other words, we introduce the combination of strategic classificationwith screening processes. We show that sequential screening pipelines exhibit new and surprising behavior where individuals can exploit the sequential ordering of the tests to "zig-zag” between classifiers without having to simultaneously satisfy all of them. We demonstrate an individual can obtain a positive outcome using a limited manipulation budget even when far from the intersection of the positive regions of every classifier. Finally, we consider a learner whose goal is to design a sequential screening process that is robust to such manipulations, and provide a construction for the learner that optimizes a natural objective.

paragraphs: A screening process may require someone to pass several classifiers. This paper studies how strategic behavior changes when those classifiers are applied simultaneously or in sequence. In the simultaneous setting, success requires satisfying all classifiers at once. In a sequential pipeline, a person needs to satisfy each classifier when its turn arrives.

The authors show that ordering creates a distinctive opportunity for manipulation. An individual can zig-zag between the classifiers' positive regions, making changes that pass the current stage without ever satisfying every classifier simultaneously. They demonstrate that a limited manipulation budget can suffice even when the individual starts far from the intersection of all positive regions.

The paper also studies the process designer's side of this interaction. It provides a construction for a sequential screening process that is robust to such manipulation and optimizes a natural objective. The central implication is that the behavior of a pipeline depends on its sequence: analyzing the conditions for passing all tests simultaneously can miss strategies available when decisions happen over time.
summary.tldr: Sequential screening can let individuals manipulate their way through tests without satisfying them all at once, motivating robust pipeline design.

title: Sequential Strategic Screening

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a way for machines to learn from data that is kept locally, in order to protect the privacy of clients. This is typically done using local SGD, which helps to improve communication efficiency. However, such a scheme is currently constrained by slow and unstable convergence due to the variety of data on different clients’ devices. In this work, we identify three under-explored phenomena of biased local learning that may explain these challenges caused by local updates in supervised FL. As a remedy, we propose FedBR, a novel unified algorithm that reduces the local learning bias on features and classifiers to tackle these challenges. FedBR has two components. The first component helps to reduce bias in local classifiers by balancing the output of the models. The second component helps to learn local features that are similar to global features, but different from those learned from other data sources. We conducted several experiments to test FedBR and found that it consistently outperforms other SOTA FL methods. Both of its components also individually show performance gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/lins-lab/fedbr.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models while keeping each client's data local. Performing several local optimization steps can reduce communication, but differences between clients' data can make convergence slow and unstable. This paper identifies three underexplored forms of biased local learning that may help explain these difficulties in supervised federated learning.

The proposed FedBR algorithm addresses bias in both classifiers and learned features. One component balances model outputs to reduce bias in local classifiers. The other encourages local features to resemble global features while remaining different from features learned from other data sources. The two components target different parts of the local learning process within a unified method.

Across the reported experiments, FedBR consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated methods used for comparison. Each component also produces gains when assessed individually, providing evidence that both contribute to the result. The paper's explanation of the original convergence problem remains qualified: the identified phenomena may explain the challenges. Its empirical findings support reducing these biases as a useful response to heterogeneous client data.
summary.tldr: FedBR improves federated learning on heterogeneous data by reducing bias in local classifiers and feature representations.

title: FedBR: Improving Federated Learning on Heterogeneous Data via Local Learning Bias Reduction

abstract: There is a growing gap between the impressive results of deep image generative models and classical algorithms that offer theoretical guarantees. The former suffer from mode collapse or memorization issues, limiting their application to scientific data. The latter require restrictive assumptions such as log-concavity to escape the curse of dimensionality. We partially bridge this gap by introducing conditionally strongly log-concave (CSLC) models, which factorize the data distribution into a product of conditional probability distributions that are strongly log-concave. This factorization is obtained with orthogonal projectors adapted to the data distribution. It leads to efficient parameter estimation and sampling algorithms, with theoretical guarantees, although the data distribution is not globally log-concave. We show that several challenging multiscale processes are conditionally log-concave using wavelet packet orthogonal projectors. Numerical results are shown for physical fields such as the $\varphi^4$ model and weak lensing convergence maps with higher resolution than in previous works.

paragraphs: The paper seeks generative models that combine useful modeling flexibility with mathematical guarantees. Deep image generators can suffer from memorization or mode collapse, while classical methods often need restrictive assumptions about the entire data distribution. The authors partially bridge this gap by imposing structure on conditional distributions instead.

Their conditionally strongly log-concave models express a distribution as a product of conditional probability distributions, each satisfying strong log-concavity. Orthogonal projectors adapted to the data produce this factorization. This permits efficient parameter estimation and sampling with theoretical guarantees even when the full distribution is not globally log-concave. The key is that the required regularity holds within the conditional pieces.

Using wavelet packet projectors, the authors show conditional log-concavity for several challenging multiscale processes. Numerical demonstrations include the phi-four physical model and weak lensing convergence maps, at higher resolutions than previous work. These results illustrate how conditional structure can make scientifically relevant distributions accessible to principled generative modeling without requiring global log-concavity.
summary.tldr: Factoring distributions into strongly log-concave conditional pieces enables generative modeling with guarantees beyond globally log-concave distributions.

title: Conditionally Strongly Log-Concave Generative Models

abstract: In this paper, we consider non-convex multi-block bilevel optimization (MBBO) problems, which involve $m\gg 1$ lower level problems and have important applications in machine learning. Designing a stochastic gradient and controlling its variance is more intricate due to the hierarchical sampling of blocks and data and the unique challenge of estimating hyper-gradient. We aim to achieve three nice properties for our algorithm: (a) matching the state-of-the-art complexity of standard BO problems with a single block; (b) achieving parallel speedup by sampling $I$ blocks and sampling $B$ samples for each sampled block per-iteration; (c) avoiding the computation of the inverse of a high-dimensional Hessian matrix estimator. However, it is non-trivial to achieve all of these by observing that existing works only achieve one or two of these properties. To address the involved challenges for achieving (a, b, c), we propose two stochastic algorithms by using advanced blockwise variance-reduction techniques for tracking the Hessian matrices (for low-dimensional problems) or the Hessian-vector products (for high-dimensional problems), and prove an iteration complexity of $O(\frac{m\epsilon^{-3}\mathbb{I}(I \textless m)}{I\sqrt{I}}+\frac{m\epsilon^{-3}}{I\sqrt{B}})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point under appropriate conditions. We also conduct experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms comparing with existing MBBO algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper considers bilevel optimization with many lower-level problems feeding into an upper-level objective. This structure makes stochastic optimization difficult because an iteration may sample both problem blocks and data within those blocks. Estimating the upper-level gradient must account for the lower-level problems, introducing additional sources of uncertainty.

The authors propose two algorithms that reduce this uncertainty through blockwise variance reduction. One tracks Hessian matrices for lower-dimensional problems, while the other tracks Hessian-vector products for higher-dimensional problems. These choices support an approach that avoids inverting a high-dimensional estimated Hessian, a potentially costly part of computing the required gradient information.

Under appropriate conditions, the analysis establishes an iteration bound for reaching an approximately stationary point. The bound reflects benefits from sampling more blocks and more examples per sampled block, supporting parallel speedup while matching the stated complexity target for standard single-block bilevel optimization. Experiments compare the proposed methods with existing multi-block algorithms. Together, the results address gradient estimation, computational cost, and parallel processing within one framework.
summary.tldr: Two blockwise variance-reduced algorithms provide conditional convergence guarantees and parallel speedup for bilevel optimization with many lower-level problems.

title: Blockwise Stochastic Variance-Reduced Methods with Parallel Speedup for Multi-Block Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Reconstructing the 3D shape of objects observed in a single image is a challenging task. Recent approaches rely on visual cues extracted from a given image learned from a deep net. In this work, we leverage recent advances in monocular scene understanding to incorporate an additional geometric cue of surface normals. For this, we proposed a novel optimization layer that encourages the face normals of the reconstructed shape to be aligned with estimated surface normals. We develop a computationally efficient conjugate-gradient-based method that avoids the computation of a high-dimensional sparse matrix. We show this framework to achieve compelling shape reconstruction results on the challenging Pix3D and ShapeNet datasets.

We develop a computationally efficient conjugate-gradient-based method that avoids the computation of a high-dimensional sparse matrix. We show this framework to achieve compelling shape reconstruction results on the challenging Pix3D and ShapeNet datasets.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a three-dimensional object from one image requires turning visual evidence into a geometric shape. This paper adds surface-normal information to that process. A surface normal describes the orientation of a surface, so estimated normals provide a geometric cue about how different parts of the reconstructed object should face.

The authors introduce an optimization layer that encourages the face normals of the reconstructed shape to align with normals estimated from the image. This links the reconstruction to geometric information obtained through monocular scene understanding. The alignment is encouraged by the optimization, giving the shape-reconstruction framework an additional source of guidance beyond its existing learned visual cues.

To make the computation efficient, the paper develops a conjugate-gradient-based method that avoids computing a high-dimensional sparse matrix. The framework produces compelling reconstruction results on Pix3D and ShapeNet in the reported evaluation. Its contribution combines a geometric consistency objective with an efficient optimization procedure, allowing estimated surface orientations to influence the reconstructed shape within the model.
summary.tldr: An efficient optimization layer improves single-image shape reconstruction by encouraging reconstructed face orientations to match estimated surface normals.

title: Surface Snapping Optimization Layer for Single Image Object Shape Reconstruction

abstract: Molecular relational learning, whose goal is to learn the interaction behavior between molecular pairs, got a surge of interest in molecular sciences due to its wide range of applications. Recently, graph neural networks have recently shown great success in molecular relational learning by modeling a molecule as a graph structure, and considering atom-level interactions between two molecules. Despite their success, existing molecular relational learning methods tend to overlook the nature of chemistry, i.e., a chemical compound is composed of multiple substructures such as functional groups that cause distinctive chemical reactions. In this work, we propose a novel relational learning framework, called CGIB, that predicts the interaction behavior between a pair of graphs by detecting core subgraphs therein. The main idea is, given a pair of graphs, to find a subgraph from a graph that contains the minimal sufficient information regarding the task at hand conditioned on the paired graph based on the principle of conditional graph information bottleneck. We argue that our proposed method mimics the nature of chemical reactions, i.e., the core substructure of a molecule varies depending on which other molecule it interacts with. Extensive experiments on various tasks with real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of CGIB over state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/Namkyeong/CGIB.

paragraphs: Predicting how two molecules interact requires deciding which parts of each molecule matter for that particular pairing. Existing graph-based approaches model molecules through their atoms and interactions, but the authors argue that they tend to overlook the role of larger substructures, such as functional groups. Those substructures can be central to distinctive chemical reactions.

CGIB approaches the problem by identifying core subgraphs within a pair of molecular graphs. Its objective is to retain the smallest amount of information sufficient for the prediction task, with relevance determined by the other graph in the pair. This conditional information bottleneck allows the selected part of a molecule to depend on its interaction partner.

The authors argue that this partner-dependent selection reflects how chemically relevant substructures can change across interactions. They evaluate CGIB on multiple tasks using real-world datasets and report stronger performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using conditional substructure selection for molecular relational prediction, with the paired molecule helping determine which information should be preserved in the representation.
summary.tldr: CGIB predicts molecular interactions by selecting compact, task-relevant subgraphs whose importance depends on the molecule they are paired with.

title: Conditional Graph Information Bottleneck for Molecular Relational Learning

abstract: In human-interactive applications of online learning, a human’s preferences or abilities are often a function of the algorithm’s recent actions. Motivated by this, a significant line of work has formalized settings where an action’s loss is a function of the number of times it was played in the prior $m$ timesteps, where $m$ corresponds to a bound on human memory capacity. To more faithfully capture decay of human memory with time, we introduce the Weighted Tallying Bandit (WTB), which generalizes this setting by requiring that an action’s loss is a function of a weighted summation of the number of times it was played in the last $m$ timesteps. WTB is intractable without further assumption. So we study it under Repeated Exposure Optimality (REO), a condition requiring the existence of an action that when repetitively played will eventually yield smaller loss than any other action sequence. We study the minimization of complete policy regret (CPR), which is the strongest notion of regret, in WTB under REO. Since $m$ is often unknown, we only assume access to an upper bound $M$ on $m$. We show that for problems with $K$ actions and horizon $T$, a simple modification of the successive elimination algorithm has $\mathcal{O} \left( \sqrt{KT} + (m+M)K \right)$ CPR. Upto an additive (in lieu of mutliplicative) factor in $(m+M)K$, this recovers the classical guarantee for the far simpler stochastic multi-armed bandit with traditional regret. We additionally show that in our setting, any algorithm will suffer additive CPR of $\Omega \left( mK + M \right)$, demonstrating our result is near optimal. Our method is computationally efficient, and we experimentally demonstrate its practicality and superiority over various baselines.

paragraphs: In systems interacting with people, an action’s effect can depend on recent exposure to that action. Weighted Tallying Bandits models this by making loss depend on a weighted count of past plays within a memory window. The weights allow recent history to capture memory decay more faithfully than an unweighted count.

The general problem is intractable, so the paper assumes Repeated Exposure Optimality: some action, when repeated, eventually produces lower loss than any other action sequence. The learner need not know the actual memory length m, only an upper bound M. Under these conditions, a modified successive-elimination algorithm minimizes complete policy regret.

For K actions over T rounds, the regret bound is O(√(KT) + (m+M)K). Thus memory contributes an additive term to the familiar square-root bandit rate. A lower bound of Ω(mK+M) on the additive cost shows near optimality in the stated setting. The algorithm is computationally efficient, and experiments support its practicality and advantages over evaluated baselines. Its guarantee depends centrally on the repeated-exposure assumption.
summary.tldr: Under Repeated Exposure Optimality, weighted-memory bandits admit efficient learning with near-optimal complete policy regret.

title: Weighted Tallying Bandits: Overcoming Intractability via Repeated Exposure Optimality

abstract: Deep networks for computer vision are not reliable when they encounter adversarial examples. In this paper, we introduce a framework that uses the dense intrinsic constraints in natural images to robustify inference. By introducing constraints at inference time, we can shift the burden of robustness from training to testing, thereby allowing the model to dynamically adjust to each individual image’s unique and potentially novel characteristics at inference time. Our theoretical results show the importance of having dense constraints at inference time. In contrast to existing single-constraint methods, we propose to use equivariance, which naturally allows dense constraints at a fine-grained level in the feature space. Our empirical experiments show that restoring feature equivariance at inference time defends against worst-case adversarial perturbations. The method obtains improved adversarial robustness on four datasets (ImageNet, Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and MS-COCO) on image recognition, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Computer-vision networks can make unreliable predictions when images contain adversarial perturbations. This paper introduces a framework that enforces constraints during inference, allowing the model to adjust to the particular image being processed. The approach places part of the robustness effort at testing time, where an image’s distinctive or unfamiliar characteristics are available.

The authors argue theoretically for using many constraints at inference rather than relying on a single one. Their method uses feature equivariance, which supplies fine-grained relationships in the feature space that can serve as dense constraints. Restoring those relationships provides the mechanism for making inference more robust on each input.

Experiments show that restoring feature equivariance defends against the evaluated worst-case adversarial perturbations. The reported improvements span ImageNet, Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and MS-COCO, covering image recognition, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation. This breadth supports the usefulness of the inference-time framework across the examined visual tasks. The theoretical emphasis on dense constraints and the empirical robustness results together motivate equivariance as a practical source of image-specific corrective information.
summary.tldr: Enforcing dense feature-equivariance constraints at inference improves adversarial robustness across several recognition and segmentation benchmarks.

title: Robust Perception through Equivariance

abstract: Anomaly detection methods identify examples that do not follow the expected behaviour, typically in an unsupervised fashion, by assigning real-valued anomaly scores to the examples based on various heuristics. These scores need to be transformed into actual predictions by thresholding so that the proportion of examples marked as anomalies equals the expected proportion of anomalies, called contamination factor. Unfortunately, there are no good methods for estimating the contamination factor itself. We address this need from a Bayesian perspective, introducing a method for estimating the posterior distribution of the contamination factor for a given unlabeled dataset. We leverage several anomaly detectors to capture the basic notion of anomalousness and estimate the contamination using a specific mixture formulation. Empirically on 22 datasets, we show that the estimated distribution is well-calibrated and that setting the threshold using the posterior mean improves the detectors’ performance over several alternative methods.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector often assigns each example a numerical score rather than a final normal-or-anomalous decision. Turning those scores into decisions requires a threshold. One way to choose it is to specify the expected fraction of anomalies, called the contamination factor, but that fraction is itself unknown in an unlabeled dataset.

This paper estimates a posterior distribution over the contamination factor using a Bayesian approach. It combines information from several anomaly detectors to capture what appears anomalous, then uses a mixture formulation to infer the contamination level. Producing a distribution makes uncertainty about the fraction of anomalies part of the result, instead of supplying only a single estimate.

Across 22 datasets, the authors find that the estimated distributions are well-calibrated. They also use the posterior mean to set detection thresholds and report better detector performance than several alternative methods. The contribution addresses the decision step between anomaly scores and actionable labels: estimating how many examples to flag, while also representing uncertainty about that quantity.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method estimates uncertainty in the anomaly fraction and improves detection thresholds in experiments across 22 datasets.

title: Estimating the Contamination Factor’s Distribution in Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

abstract: This paper revisits Gaussian Mixture Copula Model (GMCM), a more expressive alternative to the widely used Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), with the goal to make its parameter estimation tractable. Both the Expectation Maximization and the direct Likelihood Maximization frameworks for GMCM have to grapple with a likelihood function that lacks a closed form. This has led to a few approximation schemes that alleviate the problem, nonetheless leaving the issue still unresolved. Additionally, past works have alluded to an additional challenge of parameter non-identifiability, but none has offered a rigorous treatment and a commensurate solution framework to overcome the same. This work offers solutions to each of these issues in an attempt to help GMCM realize its full potential. The source of non-identifiability is not only proven but also suitable priors are proposed that eliminate the problem. Additionally, an efficient numerical framework is proposed to evaluate the intractable likelihood function, while also providing its analytical derivatives. Finally, a view of GMCM as a series of bijective mappings from a base distribution is presented, which paves the way to synthesize GMCM using modern, probabilistic programming languages (PPLs). The main claims of this work are supported by empirical evidence gathered on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture copula models offer greater expressiveness than Gaussian mixture models, but estimating their parameters presents difficult obstacles. Their likelihood lacks a closed-form expression, complicating both expectation-maximization and direct likelihood optimization. This paper addresses that computational obstacle together with a separate problem: different parameter choices can be non-identifiable.

The authors prove the source of non-identifiability and propose suitable priors that eliminate it. They also develop an efficient numerical framework for evaluating the otherwise intractable likelihood and provide analytical derivatives. These contributions address two different needs in estimation: making the objective computable and resolving ambiguity in its parameterization.

The paper further describes the model as a sequence of invertible transformations starting from a base distribution. This viewpoint opens a route to expressing Gaussian mixture copula models in modern probabilistic programming languages. Empirical evidence from synthetic and real-world datasets supports the main claims. Together, the results aim to make a flexible model more practical by improving its estimation foundations and its compatibility with probabilistic modeling tools.
summary.tldr: The paper addresses Gaussian mixture copula estimation through identifiability-resolving priors, numerical likelihood evaluation, and analytical derivatives.

title: On the Estimation of Gaussian Mixture Copula Models

abstract: The design of novel protein structures remains a challenge in protein engineering for applications across biomedicine and chemistry. In this line of work, a diffusion model over rigid bodies in 3D (referred to as frames) has shown success in generating novel, functional protein backbones that have not been observed in nature. However, there exists no principled methodological framework for diffusion on SE(3), the space of orientation preserving rigid motions in R3, that operates on frames and confers the group invariance. We address these shortcomings by developing theoretical foundations of SE(3) invariant diffusion models on multiple frames followed by a novel framework, FrameDiff, for estimating the SE(3) equivariant score over multiple frames. We apply FrameDiff on monomer backbone generation and find it can generate designable monomers up to 500 amino acids without relying on a pretrained protein structure prediction network that has been integral to previous methods. We find our samples are capable of generalizing beyond any known protein structure.

paragraphs: Protein-backbone generation can represent structures through three-dimensional rigid frames, each carrying position and orientation information. Diffusion models operating on such frames had shown promise, but the paper identifies a missing principled framework for diffusion on SE(3), the space of orientation-preserving rigid motions, with the appropriate invariance.

The authors develop theoretical foundations for invariant diffusion over multiple frames and introduce FrameDiff to estimate an equivariant score. These symmetry properties connect the model’s behavior to how structures transform under rigid motion. The framework therefore addresses the geometric foundations of generation as well as providing a method for learning the required score.

Applied to monomer backbone generation, FrameDiff produces designable structures containing up to 500 amino acids without using a pretrained protein-structure prediction network. The authors also find that generated samples can go beyond known protein structures. These findings support FrameDiff as a route to novel, designable backbones while reducing dependence on a pretrained prediction component that had been central to earlier methods.
summary.tldr: FrameDiff provides a symmetry-aware diffusion framework that generates designable protein backbones up to 500 amino acids.

title: SE(3) diffusion model with application to protein backbone generation

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts a source model to the distribution shift in testing data without using any source data. There have been plenty of algorithms concentrated on covariate shift in the last decade, i.e., $\mathcal{D}_t(X)$, the distribution of the test data is different from the source data. Nonetheless, in real application scenarios, it is necessary to consider the influence of label distribution shift, i.e., both $\mathcal{D}_t(X)$ and $\mathcal{D}_t(Y)$ are shifted, which has not been sufficiently explored yet. To remedy this, we study a new problem setup, namely, TTA with Open-world Data Shift (AODS). The goal of AODS is simultaneously adapting a model to covariate and label distribution shifts in the test phase. In this paper, we first analyze the relationship between classification error and distribution shifts. Motivated by this, we hence propose a new framework, namely ODS, which decouples the mixed distribution shift and then addresses covariate and label distribution shifts accordingly. We conduct experiments on multiple benchmarks with different types of shifts, and the results demonstrate the superior performance of our method against the state of the arts. Moreover, ODS is suitable for many TTA algorithms.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model to changing test data without access to its original training data. Many approaches focus on changes in the input distribution. This paper studies a broader setting in which both the inputs and the distribution of labels change, so adaptation must address two sources of mismatch together.

The authors call this problem test-time adaptation with Open-world Data Shift. They first analyze how classification error relates to distribution shifts, then use that analysis to motivate ODS. The framework separates the mixed shift into covariate and label components and handles each accordingly. This makes the distinction between the two kinds of change part of the adaptation procedure.

Experiments cover multiple benchmarks and different shift types, with ODS outperforming the state-of-the-art methods included in the comparisons. The authors also state that the framework is suitable for many test-time adaptation algorithms. Its contribution is thus both a problem formulation that explicitly includes changing label distributions and a broadly applicable framework for addressing that change alongside shifts in the inputs.
summary.tldr: ODS separates input and label distribution shifts so test-time adaptation can address both without revisiting source data.

title: ODS: Test-Time Adaptation in the Presence of Open-World Data Shift

abstract: Automatically generating high-quality code descriptions greatly improves the readability and maintainability of the codebase. Recently, retrieval augmented code-to-text generation has proven to be an effective solution, which has achieved state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks. It brings out the potential to leverage large unlabeled code descriptions to further improve the generation quality. Despite the promising performance, retrieval-augmented models however suffer from being deluded by inconducive retrieved references, due to irrelevant or even misleading information contained therein. To this end, we design PinNet, a new framework for code-to-text generation. PinNet relies on a discriminator to measure how well the retrievals match the semantics of the input code. Remarkably, the hidden representation of the reference before the output layer of the discriminator can be leveraged to significantly improve the code-to-text generation by modifying the attention weights. It essentially pays high attention to valuable information and eliminates misleadingness. To effectively execute this idea, we also propose a novel contrastive learning method to quantify the semantical similarities between unlabeled references. Using extensive experiments on code summarization and SQL-to-text generation, we demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly outperform all of the baselines.

paragraphs: PinNet addresses a failure mode in generating descriptions of code with retrieved references. Retrieval can provide useful material, but a reference may also contain irrelevant or misleading information. A generator that gives this material too much influence can produce a worse description despite having access to additional examples.

The framework uses a discriminator to assess how well retrieved material matches the meaning of the input code. It then uses the discriminator’s hidden representation, taken before its output layer, to modify the generator’s attention weights. This makes semantic matching influence which parts of a reference receive attention during generation.

The authors also introduce a contrastive learning method for measuring semantic similarity among unlabeled references. Experiments on code summarization and SQL-to-text generation show significant improvements over all compared baselines. The findings support using the internal representation of a relevance-assessing model to guide generation, helping useful reference information receive more attention while reducing the influence of misleading content.
summary.tldr: PinNet uses a discriminator’s semantic representations to guide attention toward useful retrieved information when generating descriptions of code.

title: PinNet: Pinpoint Instructive Information for Retrieval Augmented Code-to-Text Generation

abstract: Given a collection of probability measures, a practitioner sometimes needs to find an "average" distribution which adequately aggregates reference distributions. A theoretically appealing notion of such an average is the Wasserstein barycenter, which is the primal focus of our work. By building upon the dual formulation of Optimal Transport (OT), we propose a new scalable approach for solving the Wasserstein barycenter problem. Our methodology is based on the recent Neural OT solver: it has bi-level adversarial learning objective and works for general cost functions. These are key advantages of our method since the typical adversarial algorithms leveraging barycenter tasks utilize tri-level optimization and focus mostly on quadratic cost. We also establish theoretical error bounds for our proposed approach and showcase its applicability and effectiveness in illustrative scenarios and image data setups. Our source code is available at https://github.com/justkolesov/NOTBarycenters.

paragraphs: When several probability distributions describe reference data, combining them may require an average distribution rather than an average of individual numbers. This paper studies the Wasserstein barycenter, an averaging concept grounded in optimal transport. The objective is to aggregate reference distributions in a way that reflects the cost of transporting probability mass between them.

The proposed method builds on the dual formulation of optimal transport and a neural optimal-transport solver. Its adversarial learning objective has two optimization levels and supports general cost functions. These features distinguish it from typical adversarial approaches to barycenters that use three optimization levels and concentrate primarily on quadratic costs.

The authors establish theoretical error bounds and demonstrate the approach in illustrative examples and image-data settings. The contribution therefore combines a scalable computational formulation with analysis of its error. Supporting broader costs makes the averaging procedure more flexible about how differences between distributions are measured, while the two-level objective simplifies the optimization structure relative to the approaches described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: A neural optimal-transport method estimates Wasserstein barycenters using two-level adversarial optimization, general costs, and theoretical error bounds.

title: Estimating Barycenters of Distributions with Neural Optimal Transport

abstract: We propose an approach to do learning in Gaussian factor graphs. We treat all relevant quantities (inputs, outputs, parameters, activations) as random variables in a graphical model, and view training and prediction as inference problems with different observed nodes. Our experiments show that these problems can be efficiently solved with belief propagation (BP), whose updates are inherently local, presenting exciting opportunities for distributed and asynchronous training. Our approach can be scaled to deep networks and provides a natural means to do continual learning: use the BP-estimated posterior of the current task as a prior for the next. On a video denoising task we demonstrate the benefit of learnable parameters over a classical factor graph approach and we show encouraging performance of deep factor graphs for continual image classification.

Our approach can be scaled to deep networks and provides a natural means to do continual learning: use the BP-estimated posterior of the current task as a prior for the next. paragraphs: This paper represents learning as inference in a Gaussian factor graph. Inputs, outputs, parameters, and intermediate activations are all treated as random variables within one graphical model. Training and prediction become related inference problems, distinguished by which quantities are observed and which must be inferred.

The authors use belief propagation to solve these problems, and their experiments show that it can do so efficiently. Its updates are local, meaning computation proceeds through interactions within the graph. That locality creates opportunities for distributed and asynchronous training. The approach also scales to deep networks, extending the graphical formulation beyond shallow models.

Continual learning follows naturally from the probabilistic representation: the estimated posterior after one task becomes the prior for the next. In video denoising, the authors demonstrate benefits from learnable parameters compared with a classical factor graph approach. They also report encouraging continual image classification results. Together, these experiments support the framework's ability to combine deep learning, local inference, and transfer of learned uncertainty between successive tasks.
summary.tldr: Deep Gaussian factor graphs unify training and prediction as local belief-propagation inference and carry learned posteriors between tasks.

title: Learning in Deep Factor Graphs with Gaussian Belief Propagation

abstract: Much of the recent discourse within the ML community has been centered around Large Language Models (LLMs), their functionality and potential -- yet not only do we not have a working definition of LLMs, but much of this discourse relies on claims and assumptions that are worth re-examining. We contribute a definition of LLMs, critically examine five common claims regarding their properties (including 'emergent properties'), and conclude with suggestions for future research directions and their framing.
originalAbstract: Much of the recent discourse within the ML community has been centered around Large Language Models (LLMs), their functionality and potential -- yet not only do we not have a working definition of LLMs, but much of this discourse relies on claims and assumptions that are worth re-examining. paragraphs: Discussions of large language models often make broad claims about what these systems are and what they can do. This position paper argues that the discussion lacks a shared working definition and depends on assumptions that deserve closer examination. Its starting point is conceptual clarity: claims about a category of models are harder to assess when that category is not clearly defined.

The authors contribute a definition of large language models and critically examine five common claims about their properties. These include claims concerning emergent properties. The aim is to revisit the reasoning and assumptions behind familiar statements, making the framing of research claims itself an object of analysis.

The paper concludes with suggestions for future research and for how that research should be presented. Its contribution is therefore a proposed definition, a critical examination of common claims, and a discussion of research direction. The central implication is that productive debate about language-model capabilities requires attention to both the meaning of the terms used and the qualifications attached to claims.
summary.tldr: This position paper proposes an LLM definition and reexamines five common claims, including claims about emergent properties.

title: Position: Key Claims in LLM Research Have a Long Tail of Footnotes

abstract: Post-hoc explainability methods such as Grad-CAM are popular because they do not influence the performance of a trained model. However, they mainly reveal ”where” a model looks at for a given input, fail to explain ”what” the model looks for (e.g., what is important to classify a bird image to a Scott Oriole?). Existing part-prototype networks leverage part-prototypes (e.g., characteristic Scott Oriole’s wing and head) to answer both ”where" and ”what", but often under-perform their black box counterparts in the accuracy. Therefore, a natural question is: can one construct a network that answers both ”where” and ”what" in a post-hoc manner to guarantee the model’s performance? To this end, we propose the first post-hoc part-prototype network via decomposing the classification head of a trained model into a set of interpretable part-prototypes. Concretely, we propose an unsupervised prototype discovery and refining strategy to obtain prototypes that can precisely reconstruct the classification head, yet being interpretable. Besides guaranteeing the performance, we show that our network offers more faithful explanations qualitatively and yields even better part-prototypes quantitatively than prior part-prototype networks.

paragraphs: An explanation that highlights an image region can show where a classifier focuses without identifying what visual feature it recognizes there. Part-prototype networks address both questions by representing recognizable parts, such as characteristic wings or heads. However, existing versions often sacrifice accuracy compared with their black-box counterparts.

This paper constructs part-prototype explanations after a model has already been trained. It decomposes the classification head into interpretable prototypes using an unsupervised discovery and refinement strategy. The crucial requirement is that the prototypes precisely reconstruct the original classification head. That reconstruction is how the method preserves the trained model’s performance while providing an interpretable representation of its classification mechanism.

The authors report more faithful explanations in qualitative comparisons and better part-prototypes in quantitative comparisons with prior part-prototype networks. The contribution brings together two properties that had been difficult to combine: explanations of both feature identity and location, and preservation of the original classifier’s performance through a post-hoc decomposition.
summary.tldr: A post-hoc decomposition reconstructs a trained classifier’s head with interpretable part-prototypes, preserving performance while explaining what features matter and where.

title: Post-hoc Part-Prototype Networks

abstract: Mixup is a highly successful technique to improve generalization by augmenting training data with combinations of random pairs. Selective mixup is a family of methods that apply mixup to specific pairs e.g. combining examples across classes or domains. Despite remarkable performance on benchmarks with distribution shifts, these methods are still poorly understood. We find that an overlooked aspect of selective mixup explains some of its success in a completely new light. The non-random selection of pairs affects the training distribution and improves generalization by means completely unrelated to the mixing. For example in binary classification, mixup across classes implicitly resamples the data to uniform class distribution - a classical solution to label shift. We verify empirically that this resampling explains some of the improvements reported in prior work. Theoretically, the effect relies on a “regression toward the mean”, an accidental property we find in several datasets. Outcomes. We now better understand why selective mixup works. This lets us predict a yet-unknown failure mode and conditions where the method is detrimental. We also use the equivalence with resampling to design better variants that combine mixing and resampling effects.

paragraphs: Mixup augments training data by combining pairs of examples. Selective mixup chooses particular pairs, such as examples from different classes or domains, and has performed well under distribution shifts. This paper examines an overlooked consequence of that selection: choosing pairs non-randomly also changes the distribution of examples used during training.

The authors show that this resampling effect can improve generalization independently of the mixing operation. In binary classification, for instance, selecting pairs across classes implicitly produces a uniform class distribution, connecting the method to a classical response to label shift. Experiments verify that resampling accounts for some improvements previously attributed to selective mixup.

The theoretical account depends on a regression-toward-the-mean property that the authors find in several datasets and describe as accidental. Their analysis predicts a previously unrecognized failure mode and conditions under which selective mixup can hurt performance. It also motivates improved variants that deliberately combine mixing and resampling, making pair selection an explicit part of the method’s explanation and design.
summary.tldr: Selective mixup gains partly arise from implicit resampling, an insight that explains some successes, predicts failures, and guides improved variants.

title: Selective Mixup Helps with Distribution Shifts, But Not (Only) because of Mixup

abstract: The massive developments of generative model frameworks require principled methods for the evaluation of a model’s novelty compared to a reference dataset. While the literature has extensively studied the evaluation of the quality, diversity, and generalizability of generative models, the assessment of a model’s novelty compared to a reference model has not been adequately explored in the machine learning community. In this work, we focus on the novelty assessment for multi-modal distributions and attempt to address the following differential clustering task: Given samples of a generative model $P_\mathcal{G}$ and a reference model $P_\mathrm{ref}$, how can we discover the sample types expressed by $P_\mathcal{G}$ more frequently than in $P_\mathrm{ref}$? We introduce a spectral approach to the differential clustering task and propose the Kernel-based Entropic Novelty (KEN) score to quantify the mode-based novelty of $P_\mathcal{G}$ with respect to $P_\mathrm{ref}$. We analyze the KEN score for mixture distributions with well-separable components and develop a kernel-based method to compute the KEN score from empirical data. We support the KEN framework by presenting numerical results on synthetic and real image datasets, indicating the framework’s effectiveness in detecting novel modes and comparing generative models. The paper’s code is available at: github.com/buyeah1109/KEN.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce good-looking, varied samples without making it clear what is novel relative to a reference collection. This paper makes that comparison more specific: which types of samples occur more frequently in the generated distribution than in the reference distribution? Novelty here concerns the relative presence of different modes, or groups of similar samples.

The authors introduce a spectral approach to this differential clustering problem and propose the Kernel-based Entropic Novelty score, abbreviated KEN. The framework connects a numerical novelty assessment with identifying the sample groups responsible for the difference. That makes the comparison more interpretable than a score that does not indicate what kinds of outputs distinguish the two distributions.

The theoretical analysis considers mixture distributions whose components are well separated. The paper also develops a kernel-based procedure for estimating KEN from samples. Numerical studies using synthetic data and real image datasets indicate that the framework can detect novel modes and compare generative models. These findings concern novelty relative to a chosen reference, rather than an absolute judgment of originality.
summary.tldr: KEN measures a generative model’s novelty relative to a reference by identifying sample types that the model produces more frequently.

title: An Interpretable Evaluation of Entropy-based Novelty of Generative Models

abstract: Bridging the gap between diffusion models and human preferences is crucial for their integration into practical generative workflows. While optimizing downstream reward models has emerged as a promising alignment strategy, concerns arise regarding the risk of excessive optimization with learned reward models, which potentially compromises ground-truth performance. In this work, we confront the reward overoptimization problem in diffusion model alignment through the lenses of both inductive and primacy biases. We first identify a mismatch between current methods and the temporal inductive bias inherent in the multi-step denoising process of diffusion models, as a potential source of reward overoptimization. Then, we surprisingly discover that dormant neurons in our critic model act as a regularization against reward overoptimization while active neurons reflect primacy bias. Motivated by these observations, we propose Temporal Diffusion Policy Optimization with critic active neuron Reset (TDPO-R), a policy gradient algorithm that exploits the temporal inductive bias of diffusion models and mitigates the primacy bias stemming from active neurons. Empirical results demonstrate the superior efficacy of our methods in mitigating reward overoptimization. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/ZiyiZhang27/tdpo.

However, pushing that reward too hard can potentially worsen the underlying performance the reward is meant to represent. This paper investigates that problem through the structure of diffusion generation and the learning behavior of the critic used during optimization.

The authors identify a mismatch between existing alignment methods and the temporal structure of successive denoising steps as a possible source of overoptimization. They also find different roles for dormant and active neurons in their critic: dormant neurons act as a regularizing influence, while active neurons reflect primacy bias, or an influence of earlier learning on subsequent behavior.

These observations motivate TDPO-R, a policy-gradient method that uses the temporal inductive bias of diffusion models and resets active critic neurons to mitigate primacy bias. Experiments report better mitigation of reward overoptimization. The contribution links the organization of denoising steps with the critic’s internal learning dynamics, offering two concrete places to intervene when improving a learned reward stops reliably improving the intended outcome.
summary.tldr: TDPO-R reduces reward overoptimization in diffusion-model alignment by using denoising’s temporal structure and resetting active critic neurons.

title: Confronting Reward Overoptimization for Diffusion Models: A Perspective of Inductive and Primacy Biases

abstract: Open-Ended object Detection (OED) is a novel and challenging task that detects objects and generates their category names in a free-form manner, without requiring additional vocabularies during inference. However, the existing OED models, such as GenerateU, require large-scale datasets for training, suffer from slow convergence, and exhibit limited performance. To address these issues, we present a novel and efficient Open-Det framework, consisting of four collaborative parts. Specifically, Open-Det accelerates model training in both the bounding box and object name generation process by reconstructing the Object Detector and the Object Name Generator. To bridge the semantic gap between Vision and Language modalities, we propose a Vision-Language Aligner with V-to-L and L-to-V alignment mechanisms, incorporating with the Prompts Distiller to transfer knowledge from the VLM into VL-prompts, enabling accurate object name generation for the LLM. In addition, we design a Masked Alignment Loss to eliminate contradictory supervision and introduce a Joint Loss to enhance classification, resulting in more efficient training. Compared to GenerateU, Open-Det, using only 1.5% of the training data (0.077M vs. 5.077M), 20.8% of the training epochs (31 vs. 149), and fewer GPU resources (4 V100 vs. 16 A100), achieves even higher performance (+1.0% in APr). The source codes are available at: https://github.com/Med-Process/Open-Det.

summary.tldr: Open-Det combines improved detection, name generation, alignment, and distillation to outperform GenerateU with substantially fewer training resources.

title: Open-Det: An Efficient Learning Framework for Open-Ended Detection

abstract: In the maximum coverage problem we are given $d$ subsets from a universe $[n]$, and the goal is to output $k$ subsets such that their union covers the largest possible number of distinct items. We present the first algorithm for maximum coverage in the turnstile streaming model, where updates which insert or delete an item from a subset come one-by-one. Notably our algorithm only uses $poly\log n$ update time. We also present turnstile streaming algorithms for targeted and general fingerprinting for risk management where the goal is to determine which features pose the greatest re-identification risk in a dataset. As part of our work, we give a result of independent interest: an algorithm to estimate the complement of the $p^{\text{th}}$ frequency moment of a vector for $p \geq 2$. Empirical evaluation confirms the practicality of our fingerprinting algorithms demonstrating a speedup of up to $210$x over prior work.

paragraphs: Maximum coverage asks which k subsets together contain the largest number of distinct items. This paper studies the problem when subset membership changes through a stream of individual insertions and deletions. That turnstile setting requires an algorithm to maintain useful information as memberships change, including when previously observed items are removed.

The authors present the first maximum coverage algorithm for this streaming model, with update time polynomial in the logarithm of the universe size. They also develop streaming algorithms for targeted and general fingerprinting, where the aim is to identify features that create the greatest risk of re-identifying people in a dataset. A further contribution estimates the complement of the pth frequency moment of a vector for p at least two.

Empirical evaluation of the fingerprinting algorithms reports speedups of up to 210 times over prior work. This supports their practicality for the evaluated risk-management computations. The paper links efficient handling of changing set memberships with the assessment of which combinations of dataset features create identification risk.
summary.tldr: New turnstile streaming algorithms support maximum coverage and re-identification risk analysis, with fingerprinting speedups reaching 210 times in evaluation.

title: Maximum Coverage in Turnstile Streams with Applications to Fingerprinting Measures

abstract: As LLMs continue to become more powerful and versatile, human evaluation has become intractable at scale and reliance on automatic metrics has become the norm. Recently, it has been shown that LLMs are themselves state-of-the-art evaluators for many tasks. These Autoraters are typically designed so that they generalize to new systems and test sets. In practice, however, evaluation is performed on a small set of fixed, canonical test sets, which are carefully curated to measure the capabilities of interest and are not changed frequently. In this work, we design a method which specializes a prompted Autorater to a given test set, by leveraging historical ratings on the test set to construct in-context learning (ICL) examples. We evaluate our Specialist method on the task of fine-grained machine translation evaluation, and show that it dramatically outperforms the state-of-the-art XCOMET metric by 54% and 119% on the WMT’23 and WMT’24 test sets, respectively. We perform extensive analyses to understand the representations learned by our Specialist metrics, and how variability in rater behavior affects their performance. We also verify the generalizability and robustness of our Specialist method across different numbers of ICL examples, LLM backbones, systems to evaluate, and evaluation tasks.
