paragraphs: Dataset pruning reduces training cost by retaining a useful subset of examples. Some methods judge each example independently, while others focus on relationships between examples to encourage diversity. This paper argues that relying on either signal alone can make pruning less robust as the retained fraction or data distribution changes.

The proposed framework represents the dataset as a weighted graph. Node weights encode an example’s individual value, and edge weights encode its relational value. Selection becomes a maximum-weight clique problem. Although that problem is NP-hard, the authors exploit its structure to derive a greedy procedure that adds samples according to their marginal contribution.

Under a few mild conditions, the unified objective has a formal approximation guarantee covering a broad family of importance metrics. The guarantee is conditional on those requirements, rather than a claim that greedy selection always finds the optimum. Experiments report improvements over existing pruning methods, including more than 40% less training time without accuracy loss for ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1k. The result demonstrates the value of combining individual informativeness with relationships between samples.
summary.tldr: A graph-based pruning objective combines individual sample value with relational diversity, cutting ImageNet-1k training time by over 40% without accuracy loss.

title: Selecting Samples on Graphs: A Unified Dataset Pruning Framework for Lossless Training Acceleration

abstract: Unified visual tokenization faces a fundamental trade-off: optimizing for high-fidelity pixel reconstruction (spatial equivariance) inherently conflicts with semantic abstraction (conceptual invariance). We identify the root cause as Manifold Misalignment, where naive joint optimization leads to conflicting gradients that force a zero-sum game between these two objectives. In this paper, we propose MUSE, a framework that resolves this deadlock via Topological Orthogonality. Recognizing Structure as the orthogonal bridge, MUSE physically decouples the optimization subspaces within Transformers. We route structural gradients to refine attention topology and semantic gradients to update feature values, transforming destructive interference into Mutual Reinforcement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUSE breaks the trade-off, matching state-of-the-art generation (gFID 3.08) while notably outperforming its own teacher InternViT-300M in linear probing (85.2% vs. 82.5%), proving that structurally aligned reconstruction actively refines semantic perception.

It supports the paper’s claim that appropriately structured reconstruction training can actively improve semantic perception.
summary.tldr: MUSE separates structural and semantic training signals within Transformers, combining strong image generation with improved semantic representation quality.

title: MUSE: Resolving Manifold Misalignment in Visual Tokenization via Topological Orthogonality

abstract: Recently, a line of works can generate impressive 3D objects from a single image, but they are limited by restricted representation resolution, making them unsuitable for 3D scene generation. In this work, we introduce HIVE-3D, a novel method for high-quality 3D scene generation based on hierarchical voxel enhancement framework. Specifically, given a single scene image as input, we first produce a coarse initial scene, then introduce image segmentation and attention-based retrieval to align 2D image components with 3D scene components. Subsequently, we organize these scene relations into a hierarchical component tree, where nodes closer to the leaves denote finer-grained components. Finally, we propose a voxel super-resolution model that generates refined voxels for the target instance while maintaining strong consistency with the coarse voxels. Equipped with this model, we perform coarse-to-fine hierarchical super-resolution on images and voxels for each component, producing a high-resolution and high-quality 3D scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Subsequently, we organize these scene relations into a hierarchical component tree, where nodes closer to the leaves denote finer-grained components. paragraphs: Generating a whole 3D scene from one image requires representing both the overall arrangement and fine details within individual components. The paper identifies limited representation resolution as a barrier for methods developed around individual objects. HIVE-3D addresses this through a hierarchy that progressively refines scene components.

The process begins with a coarse 3D scene. Image segmentation and attention-based retrieval then connect components in the input image with components in the generated scene. These relationships form a tree, with increasingly fine components nearer its leaves. The tree gives the refinement process an explicit organization across different levels of scene detail.

A voxel super-resolution model generates finer spatial detail for a target instance while maintaining consistency with its coarse voxels. HIVE-3D applies this refinement to images and voxels component by component, moving from coarse structure toward finer resolution. Experiments report significant improvements over prior approaches and state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because local detail is developed within the existing scene structure, allowing hierarchical refinement to support a high-resolution scene as a whole.
summary.tldr: HIVE-3D builds detailed 3D scenes from single images by hierarchically refining components while preserving coarse scene consistency.

title: HIVE-3D: Hierarchical Voxel Enhancement for High-Quality 3D Scene Generation

abstract: Few-shot classification aims to adapt a pretrained model to novel classes with limited examples. While current methods often heuristically combine pretrained knowledge and few-shot evidence, we seek a more principled understanding of their relationship. In this paper, we propose a Bayesian-inspired optimal integration framework(BOIF) that interprets pretrained models as priors and few-shot evidence as likelihoods. Under conditional independence approximation, we show that the optimal log-posterior decomposes into the sum of prior logits and likelihood logits. This leads to a simple yet effective design principle: decouple the prior and likelihood pathways and combine their logits additively. Guided by this principle, we implement BOIF using CLIP with two novel enhancements: (1) a multi-level feature adapter to enrich visual representations, and (2) a simplified cache module for likelihood estimation. Extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks show BOIF achieves state-of-the-art performance (e.g., 80.61% average accuracy at 16-shot) and strong out-of-distribution robustness. Our work provides both a principled perspective and an effective instantiation for few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification adapts an existing model to unfamiliar classes using only a small set of labeled examples. A central design question is how much to rely on pretrained knowledge and how much to rely on the new examples. This paper develops a Bayesian-inspired framework that gives these two information sources distinct roles.

BOIF treats pretrained knowledge as a prior and the few-shot observations as likelihood evidence. Under a conditional independence approximation, the authors show that the optimal log-posterior separates into a sum of prior and likelihood logits. This motivates separate processing pathways whose scores are added together. Their CLIP implementation enriches visual features through a multilevel adapter and estimates likelihood evidence using a simplified cache.

Across 11 benchmarks, BOIF achieves reported state-of-the-art results, including 80.61% average accuracy with 16 examples per class, alongside strong out-of-distribution robustness. The result supports the practical value of separating and then combining pretrained knowledge and new evidence. The theoretical justification specifically depends on the stated conditional independence approximation.
summary.tldr: BOIF separates pretrained knowledge from few-shot evidence and combines their scores using a Bayesian-inspired rule.

title: Bayes-inspired Integration of Pretrained Priors and Few-Shot Evidence for Few-Shot Classification

abstract: Prompt learning for vision-language models (VLMs) often suffers from performance degradation when adapting to downstream tasks with noisy labels. Existing methods that rely on filtering or reconstructing supervision can propagate errors, leading to sharp performance drops. We observe that pre-trained embeddings are resilient to label noise, offering stable references despite limited adaptation. Based on this insight, we propose Evidence-Prompt, a framework built on the evidence prior that enhances prompt learning by integrating stable pre-trained knowledge. We treat prompt learning as a Bayesian reasoning task, where credibility is derived from both supervision-agnostic and supervision-conditioned evidence. This framework effectively combines these sources to infer robust training targets under noisy conditions, enabling stable learning even with high noise levels. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks with both synthetic and real-world noisy labels demonstrate that our method flattens the accuracy–noise curve and consistently outperforms SOTA methods, with notable gains on OxfordPets dataset at a 75% noise rate (+36.6% under Asym and +14.4% under Sym). Additionally, transferability experiments reveal that incorporating our evidence prior into other SOTA methods results in accuracy improvements ranging from 2.6% to 15.66%.

paragraphs: Adapting a vision-language model through prompt learning becomes unreliable when training labels are wrong. Filtering or rebuilding those labels can propagate mistakes. Evidence-Prompt starts from the authors’ observation that pretrained embeddings remain resilient to label noise, making them useful references even though their direct adaptation to a new task is limited.

The method frames prompt learning as Bayesian reasoning. It combines evidence that does not depend on the supplied supervision with evidence conditioned on that supervision, using both to assess credibility and infer training targets. summary.tldr: Evidence-Prompt combines stable pretrained knowledge with supervision-dependent evidence to improve prompt learning when labels are noisy.

abstract: We present a statistical analysis of the AUC as an evaluation criterion for classification scoring models. First, we consider significance tests for the difference between AUC scores of two algorithms on the same test set. We derive exact moments under simplifying assumptions and use them to examine approximate practical methods from the literature. We then compare AUC to empirical misclassification error when the prediction goal is to {\em minimize future error rate}. We show that the AUC may be preferable to empirical error even in this case and discuss the tradeoff between approximation error and estimation error underlying this phenomenon.

We derive exact moments under simplifying assumptions and use them to examine approximate practical methods from the literature. We then compare AUC to empirical misclassification error when the prediction goal is to {\em minimize future error rate}. We show that the AUC may be preferable to empirical error even in this case and discuss the tradeoff between approximation error and estimation error underlying this phenomenon.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes AUC as a statistical criterion for evaluating classification models that produce scores. Its first question is how to judge whether two algorithms have meaningfully different AUC values when evaluated on the same test set. This makes uncertainty in a comparison part of the evaluation, rather than relying only on the observed difference.

Under simplifying assumptions, the authors derive exact moments and use them to assess approximate significance-testing methods from the literature. The assumptions qualify the analytical result, while the comparison with practical approximations connects the theory to procedures used for evaluating scoring models. The focus is on understanding the reliability of the comparison.

The second question concerns model selection when the eventual goal is to minimize future classification error. The authors show that AUC may be preferable to observed misclassification error even for that goal. They explain this through a tradeoff between approximation error and estimation error. Thus, the criterion most directly resembling the final objective need not always be the preferable selection criterion when estimated from data.
summary.tldr: A statistical analysis examines AUC comparisons and shows why AUC may sometimes guide model selection better than empirical classification error.

title: Model selection via the AUC

abstract: In this paper, we present a new interpretation of AdaBoost.ECC and AdaBoost.OC. We show that AdaBoost.ECC performs stage-wise functional gradient descent on a cost function, defined in the domain of margin values, and that AdaBoost.OC is a shrinkage version of AdaBoost.ECC. These findings strictly explain some properties of the two algorithms. The gradient-minimization formulation of AdaBoost.ECC allows us to derive a new algorithm, referred to as AdaBoost.SECC, by explicitly exploiting shrinkage as regularization in AdaBoost.ECC. Experiments on diverse databases confirm our theoretical findings. Empirical results show that AdaBoost.SECC performs significantly better than AdaBoost.ECC and AdaBoost.OC.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common interpretation of AdaBoost.ECC and AdaBoost.OC through margins. It shows that AdaBoost.ECC performs stage-wise functional gradient descent on a cost defined over margin values. This identifies an optimization objective behind the algorithm’s successive updates and provides a basis for explaining properties of the method.

Within that interpretation, AdaBoost.OC is a shrinkage version of AdaBoost.ECC. Shrinkage reduces the size of updates, and the paper explicitly uses it as regularization to derive a new algorithm called AdaBoost.SECC. The shared optimization formulation therefore does two jobs: it relates existing algorithms and guides the construction of a further variant.

Experiments across diverse databases support the theoretical findings. In those experiments, AdaBoost.SECC performs significantly better than both AdaBoost.ECC and AdaBoost.OC. The reported advantage is empirical, while the connection between the earlier algorithms comes from the analysis. Together, the results show how identifying the margin-based objective can lead to a practically useful change in the boosting procedure.
summary.tldr: A margin-based optimization view unifies AdaBoost.ECC and AdaBoost.OC and yields AdaBoost.SECC, which performs better in the reported experiments.

abstract: We often seek to identify co-occurring hidden features in a set of observations. The Indian Buffet Process (IBP) provides a non-parametric prior on the features present in each observation, but current inference techniques for the IBP often scale poorly. The collapsed Gibbs sampler for the IBP has a running time cubic in the number of observations, and the uncollapsed Gibbs sampler, while linear, is often slow to mix. We present a new linear-time collapsed Gibbs sampler for conjugate models and demonstrate its efficacy on several large real-world data-sets.

paragraphs: An observation can contain several hidden features at once, and the same feature can recur across observations. The Indian Buffet Process provides a nonparametric prior for representing which features are present. The paper addresses the computational difficulty of inferring these hidden feature assignments when the number of observations becomes large.

Existing Gibbs sampling approaches present a tradeoff. The collapsed sampler has a running time that grows cubically with the number of observations. The uncollapsed sampler scales linearly, but often mixes slowly, meaning it can take time to move effectively through the possibilities being considered. Thus, cheaper computation alone does not resolve the inference problem.

The authors introduce a collapsed Gibbs sampler with linear running time for conjugate models. This retains the collapsed approach while changing its dependence on dataset size from cubic to linear in the stated setting. They demonstrate its effectiveness on several large real-world datasets. The contribution is therefore an inference improvement for an established hidden-feature model, with the linear-time claim specifically tied to conjugate models.
summary.tldr: A new collapsed Gibbs sampler makes Indian Buffet Process inference scale linearly with observation count for conjugate models.

title: Accelerated sampling for the Indian Buffet Process

abstract: Learning multiple tasks across heterogeneous domains is a challenging problem since the feature space may not be the same for different tasks. We assume the data in multiple tasks are generated from a latent common domain via sparse domain transforms and propose a latent probit model (LPM) to jointly learn the domain transforms, and the shared probit classifier in the common domain. To learn meaningful task relatedness and avoid over-fitting in classification, we introduce sparsity in the domain transforms matrices, as well as in the common classifier. We derive theoretical bounds for the estimation error of the classifier in terms of the sparsity of domain transforms. An expectation-maximization algorithm is derived for learning the LPM. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated on several real datasets.

We derive theoretical bounds for the estimation error of the classifier in terms of the sparsity of domain transforms. An expectation-maximization algorithm is derived for learning the LPM. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated on several real datasets.

paragraphs: Sharing information across tasks becomes difficult when those tasks use different feature spaces. This paper approaches that problem by assuming that data from the different domains originate in a common hidden domain through sparse transformations. The common domain provides a place where the tasks can share a classifier despite differences in their observed representations.

The proposed latent probit model learns the domain transformations and the shared classifier together. It encourages sparsity in both the transformation matrices and the classifier. This means restricting how many connections or coefficients are active, with the stated aims of capturing meaningful task relationships and reducing overfitting. An expectation-maximization algorithm performs the learning.

The authors derive bounds on classifier estimation error that depend on the sparsity of the domain transformations. These results tie a central modeling choice to the quality of estimation. Tests on several real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Both the construction and its interpretation rely on the stated common-domain assumption, which supplies the structure enabling knowledge sharing.
summary.tldr: A latent probit model shares a classifier across heterogeneous tasks by jointly learning sparse transformations from a common hidden domain.

title: Cross-Domain Multitask Learning with Latent Probit Models

abstract: A wide variety of machine learning algorithms such as support vector machine (SVM), minimax probability machine (MPM), and Fisher discriminant analysis (FDA), exist for binary classification. The purpose of this paper is to provide a unified classification model that includes the above models through a robust optimization approach. This unified model has several benefits. One is that the extensions and improvements intended for SVM become applicable to MPM and FDA, and vice versa. Another benefit is to provide theoretical results to above learning methods at once by dealing with the unified model. We give a statistical interpretation of the unified classification model and propose a non-convex optimization algorithm that can be applied to non-convex variants of existing learning methods.

paragraphs: Support vector machines, minimax probability machines, and Fisher discriminant analysis are established approaches to separating two classes. This paper develops a robust optimization framework that includes all three. Its purpose is to expose a shared mathematical structure behind methods that are often studied separately.

That common structure creates a route for transferring ideas across methods. The authors explain that extensions and improvements developed for one included method can become applicable to the others. Likewise, theoretical results established for the unified model can address several learning methods together. The framework therefore offers a common starting point for both modifying classifiers and analyzing their behavior.

The paper also gives the unified model a statistical interpretation and proposes an optimization algorithm for non-convex variants of existing methods. This connects the unifying formulation to both its meaning as a learning model and the problem of computing solutions. The stated contribution is a shared theoretical and algorithmic framework, with benefits arising from connections among classifiers rather than a reported ranking of their predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: A robust optimization framework unifies SVM, minimax probability machines, and Fisher discriminant analysis, enabling shared extensions and theoretical analysis.

title: A Unified Robust Classification Model

abstract: Tensor decomposition is a powerful computational tool for multiway data analysis. Many popular tensor decomposition approaches—such as the Tucker decomposition and CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP)—amount to multi-linear factorization. They are insufficient to model (i) complex interactions between data entities, (ii) various data types (eg missing data and binary data), and (iii) noisy observations and outliers. To address these issues, we propose tensor-variate latent nonparametric Bayesian models, coupled with efficient inference methods, for multiway data analysis. We name these models InfTucker. Using these InfTucker, we conduct Tucker decomposition in an infinite feature space. Unlike classical tensor decomposition models, our new approaches handle both continuous and binary data in a probabilistic framework. Unlike previous Bayesian models on matrices and tensors, our models are based on latent Gaussian or t processes with nonlinear covariance functions. To efficiently learn the InfTucker from data, we develop a variational inference technique on tensors. Compared with classical implementation, the new technique reduces both time and space complexities by several orders of magnitude. Our experimental results on chemometrics and social network datasets demonstrate that our new models achieved significantly higher prediction accuracy than the most state-of-art tensor decomposition approaches.

paragraphs: InfTucker extends tensor decomposition for multiway data beyond multilinear factorization. The paper is motivated by difficulties modeling complex interactions, varied data types, noisy observations, and outliers with popular decompositions such as Tucker and CP. It proposes nonparametric Bayesian latent models that perform Tucker decomposition in an infinite feature space.

The models use latent Gaussian or t processes with nonlinear covariance functions. This provides a probabilistic approach to representing interactions, and the framework handles both continuous and binary observations. The infinite-feature formulation is paired with tensor-specific variational inference, making computation an explicit part of the contribution rather than leaving the richer representation without an efficient learning procedure.

Compared with a classical implementation, the inference technique reduces both time and space complexities by several orders of magnitude. Experiments on chemometrics and social network datasets report significantly higher prediction accuracy than leading tensor decomposition approaches. The reported findings therefore support both the computational design and the predictive usefulness of the models on the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: InfTucker combines nonlinear Bayesian tensor models with efficient variational inference and reports improved prediction on chemometrics and social network data.

title: Infinite Tucker Decomposition: Nonparametric Bayesian Models for Multiway Data Analysis
